End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Warning: This article discusses suicide and PTSD. If you need help, contact Lifeline on 0800 543 354 or text 4357 (HELP).

The sound of water splashing was enough to trigger former cop Haydn Korach after he attended a drowning while working.

At the time, it seemed like a routine job.

Years later, Korach realises it’s one of many that contributed to a Post Traumatic Stress Disorder diagnosis after two decades on the frontline.

Despite hallmark symptoms like irritability, avoidance and depression, Korach was in denial even in front of a psychologist.

“For me, PTSD was something that soldiers got,” he said.

“People that have been shot at, they get PTSD. And I was like, ‘it’s not me’.”

Korach’s wife believed otherwise.

He compared himself to colleagues who’d been confronted with traumatic situations, wondering why, or if they were going through the same.

Korach described PTSD as an “invisible prison”, and began avoiding things because of paranoia and hypervigilance.

Sitting at a cafe with his back to people left him tense, and some towns in Northland triggered anxiety.

He even stopped diving, something he felt had held him together toward the end of his career.

The sound of sirens and water lapping were triggers too, and nightmares still came regularly.

Korach medically retired from the force once he accepted his diagnosis.

But he grieved the loss of what was supposed to be a lifetime career.

His experience made him feel people didn’t know enough about PTSD.

Some colleagues and other emergency workers couldn’t understand what he was going through, he said.

About a year ago, Korach recorded a private YouTube video about his ordeal and sent it to friends and family.

Motivated by his late grandfather who served in the Navy, Korach began filming and posting episodes publicly this year.

The work, dubbed Behind the Uniform, gave him purpose.

“I lost that when I lost my job, and maybe in a small way this can help me get a bit of that back as well.”

Though he felt his videos were going “into the void” at times, positive feedback kept him going.

People from all walks of life attended his seminars, whether in emergency services or working as funeral directors.

His ability to share his testimony with a room full of strangers was evidence of the strides he’d made in two years.

Korach’s dream was to help young people recognise symptoms early, something he wished for himself.

“If it’s just starting or you’re just noticing it, there’s no reason why you might not even be able to continue working.

“I’d love to be able to help out some cops ... because we should be investing in our young staff and we should be making sure they can do a full career.”

Korach knew he would never be in uniform again.

Becoming a police officer kick-started his dream after he was robbed in the Whangārei Rose Gardens at 14.

When he went to the police station to report the crime, he was chucked in the passenger seat of a police car and watched the arrest unfold.

He was hooked.

By 18, Korach was in the police force, but the allure of fast cars and getting bad guys off the street turned into something more.

A standout moment was when he helped a woman on holiday in New Zealand break free from an abusive marriage.

“She sent me an email, and she was like, ‘I think I would have died if I had stayed in that situation’.”

Korach worked across the North Island during his career, including as a Wellington Police College instructor.

He worked mostly on the frontline and became a supervisor for Kaikohe and Kaitāia before being promoted to senior sergeant.

Korach hoped to one day study psychology or work in the welfare space, though he knew there was work still needed and triggers he hadn’t quite figured out.

Despite that, there was tangible proof of his recovery.

With the aid of his psychologist, Korach was able to reclaim a love of the ocean that PTSD once stole from him.

It took 18 months, but he was now able to take his children snorkelling.

Behind the Uniform had helped too.

“I think it’s helping me therapeutically as well because it’s helping me kind of become who I wanted to be again,” he said.

Brodie Stone covers crime and emergency for the Northern Advocate. She has spent most of her life in Whangārei and is passionate about delving into issues that matter to Northlanders and beyond.

After years of construction, disruption and anticipation, Auckland’s City Rail Link is carrying its first passengers.

The first trains rolled through Auckland’s long-awaited City Rail Link from just before 5am, opening the new underground stations and dramatically reshaping how thousands travel around the city.

Herald reporter Rachel Maher was among the first passengers as Auckland wakes to a transformed rail network.

Contact us

The first passenger service through the CRL tunnels departed Ōtāhuhu Station at 4:57am this morning.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon was effusive with praise about Auckland’s new rail extension and the prospect of it shaping the city’s economic growth.

The network experienced its first emergency after 6am as a small fire led to evacuation announcements.

Commuters will face new timetables and route changes on the three main services: the East West, South City and Onehunga West lines.

The first weekday timetable will operate on the new CRL-enabled rail network with trains scheduled to run from just after 5am.

‘Auckland deserves this’: CRL to finally open after over 100 years of talk

City Rail Link opening: New train lines, stations and routes explained

Follow our live coverage of the opening of the CRL below.

Auckland Transport boss Stacey van der Putten said a few thousand people had already used the train service this morning.

More accurate numbers would be given later, she said, adding that the opening had brought a lot of joy to people on the first train.

She said: "It was really cool to see. A lot of anticipation, a lot of excitement. You don't usually get that many people on a train, you know, pre-5am on a Sunday."

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten says the fire at Waitematā Station this morning was unrelated to the City Rail Link itself.

She told media that it was "one of those unforeseen things".

She added: "It's an active railway, you can't predict these things. What we were really impressed with was how the system responded and it responded quickly, which is good."

Van der Putten said it would be investigated further.

The incident showed that all the testing went to good use, as all processes went to plan.

Assistant Area Commander Dave Woon

Fire and Emergency crews are still at Waitematā Station because the fire alarms can not be isolated.

Assistant Area Commander Dave Woon said the fire was quickly put out with a dry powder extinguisher by station staff.

He added: "Our people are still here because we can't isolate the bells, can't isolate the evacuation signals.

"We have called for an alarm agent, that agent is on site and we're endeavouring to sort that out.

"The rail was de-energised following the fire, which was behind a decorative panel, but has been re-activated since.

"The on-station staff have done a great job in putting the fire out and getting things going as quickly as possible."

Woon said his colleague at the Auckland Rail Operations Centre told him trains would be up and running "very soon".

The electrical fire that caused all the disruption this morning. Photo / Richard Hills

Trains have started running through Auckland’s City Rail Link tunnels and new stations again after a fire halted operations this morning.

A small fire was located in a panel lighting cable above one of the platforms at Waitematā Station, which caused the services to stop and passengers to be evacuated around 6am.

Fire and Emergency was immediately notified and its crews responded quickly, an Auckland Transport (AT) spokesperson confirmed.

The fire has now been extinguished, and services "are resuming".

The spokesperson said AT would work to get usual services back up and running as quickly as possible "but this will take time because trains will need to be moved back to the right position".

The spokesperson added: "We’d like to thank Aucklanders for their patience and understanding as we’ve worked through this issue this morning."

Fire crews found an electrical control box on fire at Waitematā Station

Cheers broke out at Te Waihorotiu Station as passengers began disembarking from the first train to pull in following this morning’s disruption.

There was a sense of relief as people stepped off the train.

“That was longer than expected,” one passenger said as they disembarked.

Passengers at Te Waihorotiu Station are being warned to expect “slight delays and cancellations” following this morning’s fire at Waitematā Station.

An announcement over the loudspeaker apologised to passengers for the disruption as people returned to the platforms.

The network is beginning to get moving again, but the morning’s incident is continuing to have flow-on effects for services.

Nelson District Court: Father jailed for repeated sexual offending against daughter

WARNING: This story references child sexual abuse and may be upsetting to readers

The comfort a young girl sought from a nightmare when she climbed into her parents’ bed led to her being raped by her father as her mother slept beside her.

It was the beginning of a four-year nightmare of repeated violations that ended only when the girl left home as soon as she was legally able.

The man, who has permanent name suppression to protect his daughter’s identity, has been sentenced in the Nelson District Court to 12 years in prison with no chance of parole for six years.

The sentence might have been longer but for the offender’s guilty pleas to seven charges ranging from rape to sexual violations and indecencies.

Despite the gravity of the offending, Judge Chris Macklin said the offender’s guilty pleas had spared the victim the trauma of a trial.

“Say what you like about the seriousness of the offending, the deep sense of shame that you no doubt feel, the sheer ugliness of the scale of what has occurred,” the judge said.

“You have, after a time, come to accept what was alleged and you have taken responsibility for it without forcing upon your victim the further indignity of trial.”

Judge Macklin credited the young woman, whom he termed a survivor as opposed to a victim, saying she had survived the offending and the various burdens and obstacles placed in her way.

According to facts summarised by Judge Macklin in sentencing notes provided to NZME, the offending started in 2013.

The young girl had a nightmare and went to her parents’ bed seeking comfort. She cuddled her mother, who was asleep.

Her father got into bed naked and performed indecencies on the girl while covering her mouth with his hand and telling her to be quiet.

He then raped her, causing significant pain and prompting her to cry and ask him to stop.

She was unable to wake her mother.

The facts stated the father then told his daughter, “I love you”, before he rolled over and went to sleep.

Soon after, the child had a nightmare about being raped, went to her parents’ room and tried to wake her mother.

Her father woke first and was “immediately angry” with her.

“You told her that you would come and sleep with her. She responded ‘no’ because she was afraid,” Judge Macklin said in the notes.

The father followed his daughter to her room, where she fell asleep in bed with him and later woke to an indecency he performed on her.

Another indecency occurred while the girl was showering in an outside shower at home.

Contact the Open Justice team

One charge of unlawful sexual connection related to an incident in which he tried to force his daughter into an act which left her “very scared” during and after what happened, Judge Macklin said.

It happened again one morning after the girl’s siblings, with whom she had been playing, left the room.

She was alone with her father, who grabbed her by the head and forced her under a blanket.

“She was scared and she thought you might not let her out of the room,” Judge Macklin said.

The final charge involved an indecent act committed after the girl felt unable to refuse because she did not want to make her father angry.

Afterwards, he told her to go and make him coffee.

In fixing a sentencing outcome, Judge Macklin said the scale of offending and degree of violation were at the top end for offending involving a single victim.

Two matters he emphasised were the vulnerability of the child and the breach of trust.

“Because this was not any child, this was your daughter,” he said.

Judge Macklin said the breach of trust was remarkable and one of the most significant aggravating factors because the relationship of parent and child required the utmost care and protection.

Crown prosecutor Sophie O’Donoghue submitted the offending was premeditated and planned.

Judge Macklin said there was an element of persistence in the offending that suggested some degree of premeditation, but he did not find the offending was planned.

Instead, it was “impulsive and opportunistic offending”, but that did not mitigate the assessment of culpability.

From a 15-year prison starting point, Judge Macklin said defence counsel John Sandston’s request for a guilty plea reduction was appropriate.

O’Donoghue did not dispute the 15% credit, described by the judge as “somewhat generous” given the lateness of the pleas, but he said it reflected the “significant further trauma” the victim and the wider whānau had been spared by not having to go to trial.

In assessing the offender’s personal circumstances, Judge Macklin acknowledged his conduct was grounded in a “tragic back-story” of his own issues with sexual norms and misconduct.

He said allowing a 5% reduction in sentence to reflect his background circumstances did not excuse his behaviour.

In setting the minimum period of imprisonment, which was not automatically applied, O’Donoghue for the Crown submitted that a minimum period was appropriate.

Sandston, for the defence, opposed it.

Judge Macklin said a pre-sentence report showed an “incredible lack of insight” into the seriousness of what occurred and that the offender posed a moderate risk of further sexual offending and a high risk of harm to others.

He fixed half the 12-year sentence as the minimum term of imprisonment before parole could be considered.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

At last: the CRL is open for business - Editorial

New Zealand Herald September 12, 2026

The Maungawhau Station (left) reflects its proximity to Mt Eden while the Karanga-a-hape Station (right) tells the mana whenua's origin story.

At last, the day has come.

A project that has been decades in the making, and characterised by controversy, determination, ambition, and a vast amount of public money: the CRL opened for business today.

Ribbons have been cut, speeches made; naysayers have naysayed. But above the noise, the buzz has been palpable.

Thousands have streamed into the stations - Karanga-a-Hape, Maungawhau and Te Waihorotiu - before the official opening. If the mood of the city can be reliably read, it is a time of celebration.

Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland is a rapidly growing city. This is not news to anyone, especially those who live here. It has languished in a woeful public transport system, wheezing along a mire of clogged motorways; travelling along arterial routes as if through wet cement. For the wider and inner-city inhabitants, and for those just passing through, it’s not an exaggeration to say the CRL promises to be revolutionary.

What is also not news to anyone is that the gestation, from the preliminary plans 11 years ago to now, has been, at times very painful. Retailers and business owners have suffered during the network’s construction, and some have not survived. For those who have, and for those buoyed by the promise of better things to come, there is excitement, and they are on board. New businesses, ventures and dreams will develop.

The economic growth and benefits from this monumental innovation will ensure Auckland has a modern network that enables and serves, rather than suffocates, progress and success. For some, the business of just getting to work will be revelatory.

Public transport done well isn’t just a means from A to B. It provides people with experience, connection, and it can reshape a city.

The legacy of public infrastructure, and of the stations themselves (both functional and impressive architectural destinations in their own right), will prevail far beyond the shrill rhetoric of politicians.

Many – including politicians – have grumbled about the budget blow-out, the time taken.

Yet some of the most audacious global public infrastructural achievements have also had the motherlode of shade thrown at them. The London-France channel tunnel (the Chunnel) for example, was cited as doomed to fail; no one would use it, they said at the time; it was a waste of money. It changed travel in Europe.

Across the ditch, the Sydney Opera House was sledged for its radical design. It is now a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts millions of tourists.

Aside from national wealth and population base, the comparisons stand.

Public and political scepticism is rife around any mega infrastructural endeavour. It takes its foothold in cynicism, red tape, financial strictures, and the understandably very real public perception that in times of difficulty and economic struggle, it might not be worth it all in the end.

When we consider the logistical construction nightmare of the CRL, which involved digging foundations under skyscrapers, contending with a live network in a densely populated city - not to mention contending with a global pandemic - the fact that we can celebrate its opening is no small thing. We are here.

To err on the side of optimism is essential for growth; otherwise, nothing would ever happen.

The German philosopher Goethe is quoted for something that also prevails, hundreds of years later: “Whatever you can do, or dream you can, begin it. Boldness has genius, power and magic in it.”

There is no greater example in recent history in New Zealand of this level of bold and magical thinking.

The only thing now to do is get on board so that the benefits of that endeavour will unfold and embolden greater visions for the future.

Letters: Ministry of Social Development strikes the gold standard of ‘whoopsies’

New Zealand Herald September 12, 2026

Social Development Minister Louise Upston should apologise to beneficiaries denied emergency grants after a Government error, a reader says. Photo / Dean Purcell

Letter of the week: Ministry’s gold standard ‘whoopsies’

There have been some notable Government cock-ups over the years, but the Ministry of Social Development stating that food wasn’t an essential need for beneficiaries achieved the gold standard of mistakes.

MSD’s excuse for offending people coming to them for help was an administrative error, one, which evidently, they didn’t learn from as the “error” was repeated for six years before they had a “whoops” moment.

Their credibility was further stretched by entrenching their position that the code was wrong but not the underlying decision to deny some 8000 emergency grants.

What is most concerning is that MSD has no understanding of what it means to live on a knife edge and how one unexpected expense can push someone over the edge into hunger and despair.

Beneficiaries are people who, for a number of reasons, have fallen on hard times and deserve respect. They are owed an apology by the minister in charge of this fiasco, Louise Upston.

Mary Hearn, Glendowie.

Authority’s poor behaviour

Roger Hawkins (Sept 7) is so correct in taking to task the Real Estate Authority’s action to exclude Janet Dickson from earning her living as a real estate agent because she refused to take a tikanga Māori course.

Her background, such as growing up among Māori families, teaching at a school with predominantly Māori students and having passed School Certificate Māori, should have precluded her from doing the course.

Her experiences with Māori and in education would suggest that she is far more qualified than most New Zealanders in things Māori.

Dickson mentions the outrage among the real estate profession when the course was introduced in 2023. The fact that the Real Estate Authority sent threatening letters and ultimatums to “either do the course or don’t work” shows an organisation totally at odds with the feelings of those it represents. Broadly speaking, tikanga means correct and appropriate behaviour.

The Real Estate Authority’s actions would appear to be otherwise and it is they that should be taking the course.

Bernard Walker, Mount Maunganui.

‘Deeply troubling’ decision

Janet Dickson’s reasons for refusing to undertake a 90-minute module on tikanga Māori are deeply troubling to me. I am a 43-year-old Pākehā New Zealander. I challenge Dickson’s use of her Christian faith as a reason for not wanting to engage with this course.

It was Christian missionaries and early Māori Christian converts who advocated strongly for Te Tīriti o Waitangi on the grounds that it was the best option available to protect Māori customs, land and their way of life.

If Dickson was as sympathetic with Māori culture as she claims to be she would logically jump at the chance to learn more about the indigenous people whose land she inhabits.

My brother, who is also a real estate agent, said the tikanga module was an informative and welcome addition from the other nine hours of compliance-heavy Real Estate Authority education.

Dickson’s reaction appears to reflect the attitude of a minority in our country who simply don’t like being told what to do, especially if it involves being open to a Māori worldview, which challenges their superiority complex.

Reverend Joel Carpenter, Glen Innes.

Same Great Lakes, new acronym

To this day, I always remember the names of the Great Lakes by the acronym Homes – Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior.

Now Trump wants to rename Ontario to America which changes the acronym to Shame – perhaps appropriate?

Peter Jeffares, Auckland Central.

Waiheke Island resort

While I don’t wish to be a Nimby, I can’t think of anything worse than having a luxury hotel on Waiheke Island.

Many residents leave the island in the summer to get away from the impacts of the island’s summer congestion.

Last I heard, the population swelled from 8000 to 30,000 in the summer. A large increase on our poor roads and general infrastructure.

Imagine what it would be like with the 180 hotel rooms, Ryokan villas, spa, and various other facilities a hotel would bring.

Waiheke Island is a charming place that doesn’t need any more capitalism. .

Mayor Wayne Brown needs to come here in the height of the summer season and decide whether we need more people, infrastructure, etc or whether we leave the island as the special place it is albeit with congestion in the touristy months.

Susan Wilson, Waiheke Island.

9/11 tribute ‘magnificent’

Occasionally there is an event that is so atrocious it shocks the world, and the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the Twin Towers was one of these.

It is etched in my memory, and those memories came flooding back as I watched the artwork titled 2977 Lights over New York Harbour.

What a magnificent tribute to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks. To see 2977 drone lights recreating the outline of the Twin Towers, one light to honour each victim who died in the attacks, was incredibly moving and beautiful.

Lorraine Kidd, Warkworth.

Bay of Plenty wild kiwifruit: 12,506 vines destroyed

While commercial kiwifruit is a boon for the economy – particularly in the Bay of Plenty – the wild variety is a serious plant pest.

“Wild kiwifruit are a serious threat to the environment,” Chris McKay, Bay of Plenty Regional Council biosecurity officer responsible for the wild kiwifruit programme, said.

“These fast-growing climbers can form dense, heavy mats that overwhelm and strangle trees, eventually causing them to collapse or die.

“They can also smother forestry plantations and native bush, disrupting natural ecosystems.

“Their ability to thrive across a wide range of temperatures and habitats makes them particularly difficult to control.

“They can also be hosts for pests that impact the industry.”

Wild kiwifruit is classified as a “progressive containment species” by the regional council within the Bay of Plenty Regional Pest Management Plan (RPMP), which aims to prevent them from spreading, reduce their distribution or eradicate them within parts of the region over time.

While landowners or occupiers are responsible for the control of progressive containment species on their property under the RPMP, in 2020, industry body Kiwifruit Vine Health (KVH) and Bay of Plenty Regional Council developed a joint management plan for wild kiwifruit over 10 years.

As part of the agreement, the regional council and KVH work collaboratively to support landowners by engaging contractors to control wild kiwifruit at a subsidised cost, to help them meet the requirements of the RPMP.

KVH co-ordinates the administration involved in the running of the programme as well as managing the control component, while also contributing annually towards control and surveillance costs.

Bay of Plenty Regional Council contributes $120,000 annually to support KVH in managing the control programme and currently spends an additional $60,000 per annum on surveillance and small-scale control work.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Bay of Plenty Regional Council completed more than 180 inspections of wild kiwifruit infestations, which are known to be on 1000 properties across the region.

While the pest plant cover is recorded as 358,687sq m, McKay said: “the likelihood is that the true coverage is much higher, due to birds depositing seed in relatively inaccessible gullies, native bush, scrubland and pine plantations”.

“Continued surveillance and control efforts will be required on an ongoing basis to achieve the long-term goal of progressively containing wild kiwifruit,” he said.

“The public are asked to report any infestations and landowners are encouraged to control any vines on their property or seek out advice in the case of multiple plants being present.”

KVH – the kiwifruit industry’s dedicated biosecurity organisation – works collaboratively with industry organisations, regional councils and landowners to manage wild kiwifruit populations in all growing regions (in both the North and South Islands) to reduce biosecurity risk.

Chief executive Leanne Stewart said the reason wild kiwifruit vines were a biosecurity risk to New Zealand’s kiwifruit industry was that they could act as a reservoir for pests and diseases, undermining eradication and control efforts on commercially productive vines.

“They are also a threat to our environment,” she said.

“Wild kiwifruit vines are vigorous climbers, and if left uncontrolled, can form dense heavy blankets of vines that strangle trees, causing them to die or collapse.”

In the Bay of Plenty particularly, Stewart said a significant increase in the population of wild kiwifruit was recorded in the mid to late 1990s and a control programme in the region began in 2000.

Over time, KVH and the council continued to work together with landowners to manage this pest plant and contribute costs, she said.

KVH has also partnered with Zespri and the Kiwifruit Breeding Centre.

“Through their significant contributions, the programme has been able to expand and control wild kiwifruit infestations previously left unchecked,” Stewart said.

“The programme has achieved significant success over the years through ongoing surveillance and control, with thousands of wild vines removed and infestations identified and managed.

“Over the last year alone (our 2025/26 reporting period), 12,506 individual vines on 91 properties were destroyed, including 10,430 individual vines in the Bay of Plenty on 78 properties – no small task for landowners and our contractors.

“However, wild kiwifruit has not been eradicated, and continued vigilance remains important.

“Wild vines continue to emerge from seed spread by birds and human activity, which is why ongoing control, surveillance and public awareness are still required.”

Growers are asked to remove unpicked fruit from vines and mulch as soon as possible.

Stewart said this prevented mass feeding by birds and allowed the fruit to compost as quickly as possible.

“If anyone knows the location of any unrecorded wild kiwifruit infestations, we ask they contact their local regional council or unitary authority with details so the infestation can be assessed and programmed for control or visit www. kvh. org. nz for more information.”

I’ve noticed certain things happen when you’re getting older.

Some are obvious, like hair suddenly deciding to grow in places where you don’t particularly want it, while becoming increasingly reluctant in the one place you do.

Then there are the noises.

At some point in life, getting out of a chair stops being a silent activity.

Standing up requires a small grunt, stretching produces a noise you definitely didn’t intend to make, and occasionally you bend down to tie your shoelaces and make a sound concerning enough for someone in the next room to ask if you’re all right.

Another sign is that you start talking about technology that younger people look at in much the same way you look at a rotary telephone in a museum.

They understand it was once cutting-edge technology, but can’t quite believe people had the patience to wait for the dial to come all the way back around.

Take floppy disks. Try explaining to someone under 25 that we used to save our important documents on a little plastic square that had less storage capacity than a photograph of their lunch.

Then there were cassette tapes, fax machines and dial-up internet.

For those under 40, dial-up was a system where your computer screamed at another computer for about 30 seconds before allowing you onto the internet, and while this was happening, nobody in the house could use the phone.

We thought this was incredible technology.

Anyway, with the noises, the disappearing hair and finding yourself starting sentences with “Back in my day”, something else starts to happen.

You start thinking about the things you’d still really like to do.

Your bucket list.

I have to say, I’ve never been particularly fond of the term “bucket list”.

Don’t get me wrong, I have absolutely nothing against a water-containing vessel. Buckets have served us incredibly well over the years.

They’ve carried water, washed cars, provided emergency seating when turned upside down and, if you’re from Manawatū, become an integral part of supporting your rugby team.

It’s the implication of kicking the bucket that bothers me.

It gives the whole exercise an unnecessary sense of urgency. But the idea behind it, I love.

What are the things you’d really like to do?

Not the things you think you should do, or the places Instagram has decided you need to be photographed standing in front of.

Just those experiences that, for whatever reason, have always made you think, “Yep, I’d love to do that”.

So, I had a think.

I’d love to ice skate at Rockefeller Centre in New York at Christmas.

I should point out that I can’t ice skate, but that hasn’t stopped me from constructing a fairly detailed version of this event in my head.

I’m gliding elegantly around the rink, the enormous Christmas tree is lit up behind me, snow is gently falling, and New York is twinkling away in the background.

It’s basically Blades of Glory, just with slightly less lycra and considerably more Christmas spirit.

In reality, I’ll probably be clinging to the side while an 8-year-old American child skates backwards past me.

So, while my lack of co-ordination, complete absence of skating ability and general dislike of the cold might come at this dream like Tonya Harding’s associates came at Nancy Kerrigan’s knee, I’m not giving up on it.

I’d also love to see the Northern Lights.

I know the science. Charged particles, solar wind, Earth’s magnetic field, oxygen and nitrogen atoms all getting excited and lighting up the sky.

But I don’t want to be standing there thinking about any of that.

I just want to look up and see those enormous green curtains dancing across the sky while standing somewhere ridiculously cold with my mouth hanging open, wondering how on earth nature came up with that.

Closer to home, but still on the nature theme. I want to walk the Hollyford Track.

Three days travelling from the mountains to the sea, starting beneath the Southern Alps and following the Hollyford River through ancient native forest, past pristine lakes and waterfalls, before eventually reaching the wild West Coast at Martins Bay.

Along the way there are 1000-year-old forest giants, fur seals, the chance of seeing rare Fiordland crested penguins and even dolphins that occasionally make their way into Lake McKerrow.

It’s one of those walks where I suspect you’d quickly run out of adjectives. Spectacular. Incredible. Majestic. By day three I’d probably just be pointing at things and saying, “Look at THAT”.

And there’s something I really like about spending a few days doing nothing more complicated than putting one foot in front of the other, not having to think, just enjoying the view as New Zealand shows off around you.

It really is a Great Walk … although the only other great walk I have any real experience with is the great Hamilton Walk of Shame home from The Outback.

It may not have ancient forests, pristine lakes or Fiordland crested penguins, but there was plenty of wildlife; the footing could be treacherous and reaching the end always felt like a significant personal achievement.

Then there’s Antarctica. I would absolutely love to go there.

The penguins, icebergs, enormous empty landscapes, more penguins and the chance to experience somewhere that still feels genuinely wild and unlike anywhere else on Earth. And did I mention the penguins?

There is, however, one small issue with Antarctica. You have to get there and back.

My fairly basic knowledge of Antarctic history tells me that the second part hasn’t always gone particularly well.

I’ve watched enough documentaries about Scott to know that I’m probably not built for Antarctic exploration.

I get cold taking the rubbish out, so I’m fairly certain I’d be the first to go full Captain Oates, grab my jacket and tell the others, “I am just going outside and may be some time”, and never be seen again.

Thankfully, things have moved on a bit since 1912. So, Antarctica stays firmly on the list. I want the icebergs, the vastness, the complete silence and, most importantly, the penguins.

I’d also love to attend a Formula 1 race, and for me this one is all about McLaren.

I’ve always loved the Bruce McLaren story. A kid from Auckland who started racing an old Austin 7, headed overseas and ended up putting his own name on a racing team that, more than 60 years later, is still one of the biggest names in motorsport.

I just love that. There’s something wonderfully Kiwi about having absolutely no business being on the biggest stage in the world, turning up anyway and becoming part of its history.

I’d love to be sitting in the grandstand when those papaya McLarens come screaming past.

The noise, the speed and that McLaren name flashing past at 300km/h.

I’m fairly certain at that point I’d somehow get a bit of dust in my eye.

And naturally, I’d bring all my newly acquired Formula 1 knowledge back to the daily commute.

Yelling “BOX, BOX, BOX” before pulling into the service station, demanding to know why my puncture repair took longer than three seconds and blaming my tyres when I’m late for work.

I may even start spraying a bottle of Lindauer around the driveway every time I successfully reverse into the garage.

And finally, one of the forgotten wonders of the natural world, the Hamilton Gardens.

Yes, Hamilton Gardens.

I know what you’re thinking. Rockefeller Centre, the Northern Lights, the Hollyford Track, Antarctica, Formula 1 and then Hamilton Gardens.

One of these things is not like the others.

But I grew up in Hamilton, I’ve been to the gardens plenty of times, and I reckon they deserve their place.

Where else can you wander through an Italian Renaissance garden, head into ancient Egypt, nip through Tudor England, pop into Japan and still be back in time for lunch?

It’s basically international travel without the jet lag, Customs queues or having to remove your belt at airport security.

I always loved the New Zealand Garden too. Among all these incredibly elaborate gardens inspired by great cultures and civilisations from around the world, there was ours.

A washing line, an old lawnmower, a pair of jandals and cricket wickets.

Add a scoop of Duck Island hokey pokey, and you are at peak New Zealand.

Looking back at my list, though, maybe I’ve accidentally highlighted the problem with bucket lists.

We tend to fill them with the big overseas stuff. Great cities, great adventures, great wonders of the world, usually requiring a great deal of money and an even greater amount of time sitting on a plane.

But maybe we spend so much time looking for great somewhere else that we forget how much great we have right here.

We have Great Walks. Great gardens. Great beaches, great lakes, great small towns and great little hidden gems that people travel halfway around the world to experience, while we keep driving past them because, well, we can always do them next weekend.

Maybe that old TV campaign had it right all along. Don’t leave town ‘til you’ve seen the country.

So see you at Hamilton Gardens.

Although I still want to see the penguins.

Pastures Past: World War II petrol shortages put the brakes on horse transport

New Zealand Herald September 12, 2026

In 1945, the Wanganui Chronicle reported that World War II fuel rationing caused 'a good deal of extra trouble and expense' for horse owners and trainers. Photo / 123rf

Kem Ormond takes a look at the world of farming back in the day. In this week’s Pastures Past, she’s found newspaper articles on how petrol shortages affected horse transport.

During World War II, petrol shortages affected almost every aspect of daily life in New Zealand, including the country’s popular racing industry.

Strict controls were introduced on the use of petrol, making travel increasingly difficult for owners and trainers wanting to take their horses to race meetings.

Horse floats, which relied on precious fuel to transport thoroughbreds around the country, came under particular scrutiny.

Eventually, a 30-mile limit was imposed on their operation, forcing many owners and trainers to seek permits, use rail transport or make alternative arrangements to get horses to race meetings.

Below is a selection of his historical stories from the New Zealand Herald (1940), the Whanganui Chronicle (1945) and the Te Awamutu Courier (1946).

Territory restricted

Long-distance travel

Special permits necessary

New Zealand Herald, February 2, 1940

Horse floats having been brought within the petrol restrictions will operate within a limited distance of Auckland in visiting future race meetings.

Without special permits, they will not be permitted to travel south of Opotiki, so that such centres as Gisborne, Wairoa, Hastings, Wellington, and New Plymouth will fall within prohibited territory.

Instructions to this effect have been issued by the No. 1 Transport Licensing Authority, Mr. E. J. Phelan, in connection with a co-ordination plan to cover road and railway services to conserve petrol.

Temporary permits to visit points beyond the boundaries of the Auckland district will be issued from the authority’s office.

In the meantime, a new scale of charges has been drafted and sent to operators for their comment.

Mr. Phelan has stipulated that two floats will not be permitted to travel from any one area where one can accommodate all the horses to be transported to a race meeting.

He has also advised that trainers owning horse floats and conveying horses other than their own will be required to obtain a licence to operate on the road.

Referring to conditions governing the present licensing of transport vehicles, Mr. Phelan pointed out yesterday that many auxiliary operators were operating without licences, which they were required to have under the regulations.

He said the only justification for the continuation of such services was in cases where an application had been made for licences, and operators were awaiting a hearing of their claims.

Removal of restrictions urged

Wanganui Chronicle, August 24, 1945

(P. A.) Wellington, Aug. 23.

In the House of Representatives this afternoon, Mr. W. A. Sheat (Opp. Patea) gave notice to ask the Minister of Transport when the present 30-mile limit on the operation of horse floats was likely to be lifted.

Mr. Sheat said if the present restrictions were removed owners of horse floats would be able to make much better use of their vehicles with their existing petrol licences.

Owners and trainers had had to put up with a good deal of extra trouble and expense while war conditions necessitated the present severe restrictions, he added, and would appreciate an early relaxation of the restrictions.

Needs of Te Awamutu

Application to authority

Te Awamutu Courier, July 24, 1946

A petition by owners and trainers that the authority give consideration to the granting of an application for a horse float license at Te Awamutu was submitted to the No. 1 Transport Licensing Authority, Mr. E. J. L. Phelan, at a sitting in Hamilton on Monday.

The applicant was a returned serviceman, Mr. Colin Alfred Self (Mr Page).

In the past the owners and trainers in the Te Awamutu district had not received adequate service, said Mr. Page.

It was considered there was work for two horse floats located in Te Awamutu.

The applicant said he was satisfied he could make a good living at Te Awamutu.

Several trainers had told him that transport of one horse per year cost £100.

A number of trainers had promised to support him.

Edward Joseph Murtagh, trainer of Te Awamutu, said that he and other trainers had been inconvenienced at times by the lack of sufficient floats.

Hamilton floats had attended to their needs, but on occasions they had been too busy, and it was necessary for the horses to be sent by rail.

The Authority reserved its decision.

He said he would grant an application by James Keith Robson to operate a float from Te Awamutu.

- Source: Papers Past

No, it wasn’t a rogue poll. Chris Hipkins and Labour’s trend is down – Heather du Plessis-Allan

New Zealand Herald September 12, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Chris Hipkins looked flat this week.

Even when he plastered on a smile, it was hollow. There was no twinkle in his eye.

It was especially noticeable the day after the Taxpayers’ Union Curia poll landed.

That poll put Labour on 25.9%. That is a full percentage point lower than the already-low result the party recorded at the last election.

Labour insists the poll is wrong. Its internal polling puts it in the early 30s. But even that is down on the high 30s Labour started the year on.

Which means, either way, it is a trend. Down.

It shouldn’t surprise Labour that this is happening. It was predicted.

The high-30s was always a mirage. The only reason Labour was that high in the polls was because Hipkins wasn’t saying anything. Which meant Labour was a blank canvas that voters could paint their own version on to.

If voters wanted to believe that Labour would bring down the cost of groceries, they could. Labour wasn’t saying anything to dispel that fiction.

If voters wanted to believe Labour would suddenly develop a case of financial competence a la the late Michael Cullen. They could.

But the minute Labour was forced to start delivering a few policies here and there, the beautiful, projected image got broken up by static.

And it got much, much worse when Labour’s mates really got going on their own policies. A Treaty commissioner from the Māori Party who could stop Parliament from passing laws. Forcing supermarket owners to sell their businesses to the Government from the Greens.

Because Labour wasn’t telling voters what its Government would do, their likely coalition partners did it for them.

Possibly, National’s nine taxes claim stuck a bit too.

If Labour MPs were honest with themselves, they knew a long time ago it was very unlikely they would win this election.

The clue is that no one has rolled Hipkins. No one thought it was worth wasting their one chance at being Prime Minister on the 2026 election.

Really, Labour should ask itself how it has managed to put itself on trend to lose an election that everything says it should win. The economy is still a grind. The right track-wrong track polls show a plurality of Kiwis think this country is not getting better. The coalition has fought with itself more than any other in the past 30 years. The National Party has experienced three attempts to roll the Prime Minister.

How a party is not soaring in the polls against that backdrop is actually quite an achievement in being bad.

It begs the question: is 25.9% the bottom or can this trend take Labour even lower?

The odds don’t look good. Labour might be able to rescue the situation with a whopper of a policy announcement. But Labour doesn’t seem to have any money to spend on it and definitely doesn’t know how to come up with great policies that cost nothing.

It won’t win many voters with personnel. Too many of its key MPs were in the last Labour government which means they remind us of Covid restrictions and huge amounts of money blown on nonsense.

Hipkins is probably not going to campaign them to victory. He was awkward in crowds last time around and apparently preferred playing online word games with Toni.

He might land some zingers in the debates which might make some nice viral moments on social media. But those clips will do a lot of heavy lifting when everything else is looking stale and uninspired.

All of which Hipkins probably knows because he’s been around politics long enough to know it. Which may explain why he’s looked so flat this week.

Warner Bros axed this Looney Tunes movie. But fans refused to accept defeat

Sydney Morning Herald September 13, 2026

The story of how Coyote vs Acme came back from the dead is crazier than a Looney Tunes cartoon.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Will Forte could not have been prouder of Coyote vs Acme. The live-action animation hybrid, in which a disgruntled Wile E. Coyote and his lawyer (played by Forte) face off against John Cena in a chaotic courtroom battle, was one of the most entertaining – and heartwarming – projects he’d worked on. His wife, after watching it for the first time, even told him it was hands-down the best thing he’d ever done.

So it’s safe to say that its inexplicable axing in 2023 sent Forte into a head-spin.

“This was a movie that I wanted so badly to share with my kids, but [I realised] I was never going to get to. It was confusing, frustrating and heartbreaking. I was just pissed,” said the American actor and comedian, who is known for his stint on Saturday Night Live and, more recently, Tina Fey’s The Four Seasons.

Coyote vs Acme, Dave Green’s absurd comedy in the vein of Who Framed Roger Rabbit, was ready to hit screens when it was suddenly shelved by Warner Bros in November 2023. Despite ongoing praise from its producers, overwhelmingly positive test screenings and a $US70 million budget, the studio decided it would be better off as a $US30 million tax write-off. Its fate mirrored that of Batgirl and Scoob! Holiday Haunt, both of which were cancelled by Warner Bros the year prior.

“With the relaunch of Warner Bros Pictures Animation in June, the studio has shifted its global strategy to focus on theatrical releases,” a WB Motion Picture Group spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “With this new direction, we have made the difficult decision not to move forward with Coyote vs Acme. We have tremendous respect for the filmmakers, casts and crew, and are grateful for their contributions to the film.”

3:57

Will Forte loved this movie with all his heart. Then Warner Bros axed it

After years of waiting in limbo, Coyote vs Acme is finally hitting screens.

The decision was driven by a desire to offset corporate losses, a strategy spearheaded by the studio’s new head, David Zaslav. But for those who worked on the film, as well as the Looney Tunes fans feverishly anticipating its release, it was a punch to the gut.

“We heard that Warner Bros was going to shelve it, but they still said we could come see the movie that next Tuesday. So, for the five or six days before that screening, I thought, ‘This is probably going to suck. If they’re going to shelve it, it can’t be good. Maybe these producers are just too deep in it to see that’. Then I showed up [to the screening] and I just loved it with all my heart. I was so proud of it, which was heartbreaking. I got so mad for a long time,” Forte says.

1:46

Coyote vs Acme trailer

The live-action animation Looney Tunes hybrid lands in Australian cinemas on September 17.

The film’s cancellation was especially disappointing given how broad he expected its appeal to be. Based on a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs Acme tells Wile E. Coyote’s story. Fed up by the countless Acme products that have malfunctioned – costing him his lifelong dream of capturing the Road Runner – he decides to sue the major corporation with the help of Kevin Avery (Forte), a down-and-out billboard lawyer. This results in the unlikely pair going head-to-head with Acme’s chief executive, Foghorn Leghorn, as well as his ruthless lawyer Buddy Crane (Cena).

For Looney Tunes fans, it delivers a healthy dose of nostalgia, reconnecting audiences with “old buddies”. Forte himself says the cartoons helped to form his comedic mind from a young age, subconsciously inspiring him to weave some of its madcap absurdity into his own comedy. That said, you don’t need to be a fan to enjoy this film. It has “a bit of everything”, Forte says, from legal drama to slapstick comedy.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

1:21

Eric Bauza's many voices

As a voice actor for the Looney Tunes cartoons, Bauza brings iconic characters like Daffy Duck and Bugs Bunny to life.

“It’s just this weird thing of: The movie’s testing really well, and it’s your IP [intellectual property]. If you’re not going to take a chance on that, what are you going to take a chance on?”

Beyond the upset and disappointment, however, lay a painfully ironic parallel. Coyote vs Acme is largely Wile E. Coyote’s story. It’s an underdog tale, or as Forte puts it, a tale about “the little guy against the big corporation”. Everyone, from the cast and crew to the fans, immediately noticed the connection between Coyote’s journey and the film itself. If anything, it just made the movie even more resonant, Forte says, not only to himself but to every other Looney Tunes lover.

As soon as the film was scrapped, fans and industry heads went to battle on social media, launching relentless campaigns in a bid to pressure Warner Bros into selling the project to another studio.

“Disappointed, and somewhat mystified by the Coyote vs Acme news,” the film’s composer Steven Price wrote on X. “Dave Green made (and completed) an excellent movie, and a lot of people – not least the brilliant musicians and colleagues who worked with me on the score – poured their hearts into it … that’s (f---) all folks!”

Writer-director BenDavid Grabinski, who received an off-screen additional literary credit for the film, lamented Warner Bros’ decision, writing on X that Coyote vs Acme was “the best of its kind” since Who Framed Roger Rabbit.

“The leads are super likable. It’s beautifully shot. The animation is great. The ending makes everyone f---ing cry,” he wrote. “I thought the goal of this business was to make hit movies?”

Looney Tunes fans even released an online petition urging Warner Bros to release Coyote vs Acme, attracting 23,483 supporters. It was in this response that Forte discovered a silver lining. “It was a good lesson in the power of people,” he says. “Fans of the movie did not give up. They had hope when I didn’t.”

It was their “constant noise-making”, he says, that eventually caught the attention of another studio: Ketchup Entertainment.

In late March 2025, Ketchup – a far smaller studio than Warner Bros, but one that has released hits such as Michael Mann’s Ferrari (2023) – acquired the rights to Coyote vs Acme in a deal reportedly worth about $US50 million. And now, nearly three years since it was axed, it’s finally set to appear on Australian screens on September 17.

Ketchup has become something of a saving grace for Looney Tunes, having also recently released The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie, another film jettisoned by Warner Bros. This movie, which is entirely animated, managed to gross $US8.2 million in domestic ticket sales after just three weeks in cinemas.

In a slightly twisted way, Forte says he’s actually grateful to Warner Bros for cancelling Coyote vs Acme.

“It might have all happened for a reason,” he says. “As much as I think they made a mistake not putting it in theatres themselves, I’m thankful that they let somebody else do it. And look, I understand it’s always a crap-shoot. They’re making a business decision … [but] it might be because of that craziness that we went through – that rollercoaster ride that Warner Bros put us through – that might make more people hear about the movie.”

It certainly was a tough journey, he says. But neither the fans nor those involved in the film gave up on it – just like Coyote refused to give up on catching the Road Runner.

“This is a character who doesn’t know the word ‘quit’. He’s facing insurmountable odds, and he just still goes for it every single time. He fails spectacularly, picks himself back up, gets a little rest, and then goes out again. It’s a good lesson for people – I wouldn’t say use that in your desire to kill birds or people, but you know, just in that attitude towards positive goals.”

Wile E. was never Forte’s favourite Looney Tunes character – he preferred Elmer Fudd and Bugs Bunny (aka “the Fonzie of Looney Tunes”) – but the coyote is definitely up there now. Forte developed a deep connection with this wildly resilient character, even before post-production brought him to life and he was just a tennis ball on a stick. Coyote is an underdog who found hope among the madness – just as Forte did with this film.

Coyote vs Acme is in cinemas on September 17.

Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it?

Sydney Morning Herald September 13, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When US President Donald Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of “gambling with World War III”, in a furious exchange in the White House in March last year, it was easy, perhaps, to write the statement off as overblown rhetoric. That’s just Trump, trying to strongarm Zelensky into giving up stolen land to Vladimir Putin, in exchange for peace.

But in the 18 months since that explosive episode in the Oval Office, the world’s mood has shifted.

Mastheads from around the globe – from Japan to the United States and Britain – have begun asking if we are perhaps already in World War III, and just don’t know it. (Or, as The Hill put it on August 11: “World War III is already here, and Trump must rise to the challenge”.) Dialogue, the invite-only social club co-founded by billionaire tech investor Peter Thiel, was reportedly planning to hold a session on “Prepping for WWIII” sometime last month until this year’s conference was cancelled.

“It’s a fair question, and a number of people are asking it,” says Professor Robert Pape, a University of Chicago political science expert, of whether we’re in third world war now, and just don’t know it.

“Because we have two major wars that are impacting big parts of the world happening at the same time [in Iran and Ukraine],” says Pape, whose popular substack, The Escalation Trap, has been monitoring the Iran war. And watchers of history, he says, know how unexpected events can suddenly spark a massive escalation, and unforeseen devastation, within existing wars.

We might spy Iran holding the Strait of Hormuz hostage – causing the price of oil, fertiliser and other goods to skyrocket around the world – while the US threatens “D-Day”-like sanctions on Iran and bond markets dive, and think back, worryingly, to earlier times. The impact of hyperinflation on the Weimar Republic in Germany and the rise of the Nazis, for example, or the bloodless, economic warfare that led Japan to bomb an American naval fleet in Pearl Harbour on December 7, 1941.

That event changed the course of World War Two, drawing in the United States, and leading, eventually, to then-president Harry S Truman’s fateful decision to unleash the nuclear bomb.

Japan shared no fealty to the Nazi ideology, the motivating force behind Hitler’s reign of terror that saw him direct Germany’s forces to invade country after country across Europe. Rather, Japan decided to bomb Hawaii, only after the US, Britain and the Netherlands had imposed a total oil and raw material embargo on it.

“So they thought, ‘our survival and our standing as a great power requires going to war with another great power’,” says James Der Derian, director of the University of Sydney’s Centre for International Security Studies.

“So, who’s Japan in this instance?” he says, of our current geopolitical climate. “I’d be stressed to say China. But if China feels like its economy is being threatened by failure to have sustained and predictable flow of not just oil and fertiliser, but other things related to oil, and 20 per cent [of that] coming out of the Hormuz Strait, would they become more involved? So far they don’t have that projection of power. But they certainly do have, increasingly, ways of influencing behaviour in this part of the world.”

So far, China seems to have been meeting its energy needs and a notable feature of the economic sanctions announced by Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, last month, was the caution the US exercised towards Chinese interests, declining to target Chinese banks as part of the sanctions regime.

When the war in Iran began in February, Trump declared the conflict would be over in a matter of weeks. That has not come to pass. So we watch, as it drags on, with a new front opening up in the Red Sea, in early August, when the Houthi Rebels, an Iranian ally, began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia. This threatens yet another oil export pipeline. In the last few days they took control of a strategic island, giving them control of the sea.

All the while, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s persistent refusal to cave to Trump’s demands to withdraw Israeli troops from Gaza and Lebanon, in a bid to broker the peace with Hamas and Hezbollah, further prolongs the conflict.

The good news? This does not mean we are in – or on the precipice of – World War III. So says Graham Allison, who served as American president Bill Clinton’s assistant secretary of defence for policy and plans, and was a special adviser to the secretary of defence under then-president Ronald Reagan.

The category “world war”, he says, refers to a global conflict with extraordinarily devastating consequences: like the 25 million victims in World War I, and the approximately 60 million dead in World War II.

“So I reserve ‘World War III’ for the catastrophe that is catastrophic beyond imagination,” says Allison, a Harvard University professor. For many historians, this has meant the dangling fear of another nuclear conflict. Or at the very least, two great powers engaging in battlefield warfare, in which other, smaller nations, are then forced to choose a side.

Nevertheless, in 2017 Allison wrote that the world was lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II, culminating in his book Destined For War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’ Trap?

Does he still feel that we’re lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II?

“Yes,” he says, over the phone from Massachusetts.

He refers to the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, who argued that when a rising power threatens to displace an established ruling power, the stress and mutual fear this brings often makes violent conflict inevitable. (Thucydides had observed during the Peloponnesian War that “It was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable”.)

“I think if Thucydides were assessing the situation [now], he would say the two rivals are pretty much right on script,” says Allison, referring to China, the power on the rise, and the US, the established power that is waning.

“The rising power is continuing to rise and to feel its oats, and to become more assertive, and continue to complain about the international order ... saying, ‘I need more say and more sway’,” he says, referring to Chinese encroachments in the South-China Sea, and military threats in and around Taiwan, a sovereign territory that Chinese leader Xi Jinping says is an inseparable and integral part of China.

“And the colossal ruling power, the US, you can see all of the insecurities that come from them thinking, ‘Wait a minute. What’s happening?’” He refers to Trump’s decision to impose a 145 per cent tariff on China last year, saying: “So, I was quite worried that things could get out of control in an economic confrontation.”

Allison’s nerves calmed after Trump backed down on his tariffs. (This, only after Xi responded by cutting the US off from critical minerals, without which the American economy and military industry cannot function.)

But he plays out the scenario that could have resulted, had Trump not dropped his tariffs on China.

“Well, let’s imagine now, a month later, and the American economy is grinding to a halt,” says Allison. “The fellow that runs Ford Motor Company calls and said, ‘I’m closing the production line for these trucks next week’, if this continues. And the people making Tomahawk missiles and F35s said, ‘We can’t continue producing these’.

“So now, what would the US do? … [Likely Trump might think] ‘I’m going to try to cause pain to you’. And as I do that, could one thing lead to another and with a little bit of miscalculation you get to a war? Well, the US and Japan did, in 1941. So that’s one path.”

Given the structural factors at play, he estimates the chance of China and the US becoming embroiled in a full-fledged war at 75 per cent.

“That still leaves 25 per cent for human agency,” he says.

A war? Imminently? “No, over the [next] decade or more,” he says. “Not tomorrow. But it could happen anytime because something crazy could happen in Taiwan tomorrow.”

The US skidded close to such a crazy moment two years ago, he recalls, when two senators co-sponsored a bill requesting that the US recognise Taiwan as a non-NATO ally.

“And I said, ‘This is crazy’,” says Allison, of the bill, backed by Democrat Bob Menendez, and the late Lindsey Graham, a Republican, which would also have provided billions of dollars in security aid to Taiwan. “I actually said to Senator Menendez, ‘I love your bill, I’m going to subscribe to it entirely. You should simply add to it, Fast track to war with China’.” The bill was later scotched.

But a fight over Taiwan – a scenario that could see the US military firing on Chinese ships or planes, with other, smaller countries, joining each side – is just one other possible trigger for another World War, in the current geopolitical climate, according to experts.

“An act of terrorism [is another],” says the University of Sydney’s James Der Derian. “It would take a mass casualty attack.”

So far, he says, both Russian President Vladimir Putin, in Ukraine, and Trump, in Iran, have been “fairly restrained”.

The US, for instance, has avoided an attack on the oil infrastructure on Kharg Island – a likely trigger for an escalation in conflict, given that it is the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp’s economic lifeline, processing about 90 per cent of Iran’s crude oil exports.

And Putin has reduced his threats to launch tactical nuclear weapons against Ukraine, in the years since late2022, when the CIA put the odds of him conducting such a strike at 50-50.

But were Iran, or another power, to hit a US warship, and were American soldiers killed by a drone, it could trigger a wider war, or a catastrophic war that involved multiple major powers, says Der Derian.

So, too, could an accident, or an incident that causes a cascade of events that leaders – whether they’re in Iran, Ukraine, Russia, the United States, Israel, China, or elsewhere – are unlikely to anticipate.

“I always tell people to go back and look at 1914, which is the most incredible story in the world,” says Allison, of the unlikely killing that sparked World War I. “How could an assassination of an archduke [Franz Ferdinand, the heir presumptive to the Austria-Hungarian empire] by a terrorist in Sarajevo, which was an event so inconsequential that it didn’t even make the front pages, within five weeks, spark a fire that produced a conflagration that burned down essentially the whole of Europe?”

But what of the risk, now, of nuclear warfare?

The closest the world has come to World War III is often cited as the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. Back then, only four powers possessed nuclear weapons. It was the psychologically and politically stable American president John F. Kennedy, who had his finger on the proverbial nuclear button.

Now, nine powers have nuclear weapons. And the unreliability of the United States has led countries like South Korea and even Japan to begin debating the need to acquire their own nuclear weapons, leading to global fears over another burgeoning arms race.

And Trump, a famously tempestuous leader, is commander-in-chief of the US armed forces. Is he a risk factor for the start of nuclear war?

“I would say that answer is yes and no,” says Allison, who advised Reagan during the years when the Cold War was still underway.

“The bad news, is that he seems so erratic, and emotional and unpredictable that there’s hardly any statement you can make about which you’d say ‘He couldn’t say that. He couldn’t do that.’ The answer is, ‘Excuse me, I think he might, ok?’ Trump even, as he explains it, he likes chaos because in a chaotic situation, you can often push and get a little more of your way. So is he a risk factor? Yes.”

But Trump’s disposition also leads to two positives, in terms of risk, says Allison.

One, he is terrified of the prospect of nuclear warfare.

And second, Trump is far from a hawk on China; to the contrary, he reveres Xi as a leader. “And he appreciates that China is a big strong country that the US is going to have to live with,” he says, an understanding that minimises the chance of escalation via the so-called Thucydides trap.

At an event in Sydney last week, former prime minister Paul Keating argued that Trump’s engagement with Russia and, in particular, China was all about avoiding World War III. “That’s a big objective,” he told the audience.

“This is why he’s friendly with Xi Jinping ... Trump does not want a military exchange with the Chinese, above all else.”

Der Derian also finds reason for hope, noting that it’s been much smaller players during heart-stopping moments in previous conflicts who have made unexpectedly clear-eyed decisions. Which saved the world from possible nuclear armageddon.

“Sometimes it’s just dumb luck,” says Der Derian, noting the event of October 27, 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Deep in the ocean near Cuba, a US warship spotted a Soviet submarine, and dropped a non-lethal charge in the water nearby, in a bid to force the Soviet submarine to the surface.

Inside the Soviet sub, not knowing if the war had begun or not, the captain and political officer wanted to launch its nuclear-tipped torpedo against the US fleet, in retaliation.

“But the Soviet officer” – Vasili Arkhipov – “refused to launch, even though he thought he was under attack,” says Der Derian.

And, he says, it may now be that civilians around the world might prove to be the necessary sanest minds in the geopolitical space.

“You know, I can’t remember who said it, but every end is a beginning,” says Der Derian. “I think we’re coming out of the end of a crisis. I do feel that in general people can tolerate only so much disruption, chaos, disorder before they get rid of the leaders who they feel are responsible for it.”

How KPop Demon Hunters’ Ejae ‘failed’ Korea’s strict teen music machine, and became a star

Sydney Morning Herald September 13, 2026

Born Kim Eun-jae, the 34-year-old has gone from unknown songwriter to global phenomenon, thanks to hit tracks like Golden.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In 2020, early in her career, South Korean-American musician Kim Eun-jae, known as Ejae, joined the small songwriting team for a new animated film project, KPop Demon Hunters. She ended up co-writing some of the film’s biggest hits, including Golden, Your Idol, How It’s Done, and providing the singing voice for its protagonist Rumi.

The film, released in June 2025, became, quite simply, a global phenomenon: I tell her that Golden has been played in our house and in our car every day for a year, thanks to my five-year-old’s obsession with it. “I’m sorry,” Ejae says, giving a small smile. But no wonder she’s smiling; Ejae’s life has been a whirlwind of fame, adoration, accolades and red carpets ever since the film came out.

Today, we’re in Paris on the set of Ejae’s photo shoot. Yesterday she was sitting in the front row at the Dior couture show (she is an ambassador for the brand). She attended the Golden Globes in January, the Grammys in February (taking home awards for Golden at both) and the Met Gala in May. She sang at the opening of the World Cup in June (a song she co-wrote for the tournament, naturally) and performed at this year’s BAFTAs, Brit awards, Coachella and the Oscars, where she scooped the best original song award and discovered that Beyoncé and Jay-Z are mega-fans.

“I was at their after party and Jay-Z came up to me and said, ‘Hi, my name’s Shawn,’” says Ejae, 34. “I was beyond starstruck. Beyoncé is my idol and she said, ‘You have an incredible voice.’ I asked her, ‘Do you know Golden?’ She was like, ‘Yeah, my girls sing it.’” Ejae pauses, wide-eyed, and adds: “And her daughter’s name is Rumi.”

Blending comedy, action, fantasy and music, KPop Demon Hunters, an American animation drenched in Korean characters and pop culture, is about a girl band called Huntrix – Rumi, Zoey and Mira – who sell out stadiums while secretly fighting demons that feed on human souls.

Rumi, Zoey and Mira are voiced by actors, but their singing voices come from Ejae, South Korean-American singer Rei Ami (Zoey) and American singer Audrey Nuna (Mira). The trio have become best friends, having performed together countless times.

Ejae describes Golden as the film’s Let It Go, a pivotal moment in the Disney film Frozen and another song that went viral. Golden is a certified pop banger about self-empowerment, self-belief and the power of female friendship. If you’re a parent of a young child, you will not have been to a kids’ party in the past year at which Golden wasn’t blasted out over the bouncy castle.

Six weeks after the release of KPop Demon Hunters, Netflix announced that it had become the platform’s “most watched original animated film of all time”. Five months later, it became the most watched original title in Netflix history and has gone on to rack up more than 628 million views. Google search data revealed that Rumi was the highest-trending Halloween costume idea in 2025, about the same time the soundtrack album was certified platinum in America, and Golden has topped the charts in more than 30 countries. Unsurprisingly, a sequel and a tour have been announced.

“I know [this kind of success] happens, I just didn’t think it would happen to me,” Ejae says. “I had no inkling at all that KPop Demon Hunters would be as big as it became. I did think it might be, because the story is so cool, but you never know. In the past year, I’ve lived five lives. It doesn’t stop. Who does this all in one year?”

Ejae wrote on Instagram in April that “being an Asian-American woman in the music industry is not easy”. I ask what she meant by that. “I don’t see the representation,” she replies. “I’m not going to lie, there’s definitely some level of racism. Definitely stereotyping. Especially women. I am genuinely curious why. But if you have one person who looks like you in that industry, it feels easier to get into that industry, right?”

Kim Eun-jae was born in Seoul. Her mother is Korean, her father Korean-American. The family (she has an older brother) lived in New Jersey, but her mum wanted to give birth in Korea. Then, when Ejae was six months old, the family moved back to America. Her parents divorced when Ejae was eight and her mother moved the kids back to South Korea. “My mum had custody of us and raised us as a single mum, so she wanted to be near her parents,” she explains.

In South Korea, Ejae attended an American school and at the age of 11 started after-school and weekend lessons at SM Entertainment, an influential K-pop record label and entertainment agency that has produced artists such as the girl groups Aespa and Red Velvet.

“They teach you how to be a pop star,” Ejae says. “Singing, different kinds of dancing like jazz, contemporary, hip-hop and ballet to improve your posture, public speaking and interview training. Every month they would take you to do a photo shoot so you could learn how to pose. We did a ton of languages. We learnt Chinese because they knew China would be a huge audience.”

But there were darker aspects too. “They didn’t like us to ‘kimchi squat’.” She gets off her stool to show me. “Because it made your knees ugly; it ruined your knees. We couldn’t chew gum because it would make our jaws bigger. We would have to smile in front of the mirror with a ChapStick here” – she demonstrates a pout as if a small tube of lipstick could rest between your upper lip and your nose – “because it makes your muscles grow and your face shape [better]. We couldn’t have ear piercings. It was very much no sodas, no greasy food, keeping yourself unbloated and fit.

I wouldn’t say it was healthy. Let’s just be real. It’s very ambitious for a teenager.”

Still, she was there for 11 years. Did she enjoy it? “I don’t know if ‘enjoy’ is the right word. Did I work my ass off? Yes. Did I learn a lot? Absolutely. Was it difficult? Yes.

“But did I think it was worth it? Yeah, because my dream was to be in music and it is a system that will help you become a global star. Even today, when I’m posing in front of the camera I don’t feel awkward because I had it ingrained in me as a kid. I’m not shy in front of the camera. I’m shy about performing because I’m a perfectionist.”

Aged 21, while she was studying at music college in New York and still signed to SM, Ejae discovered SoundCloud and became “obsessed with making beats – I got all this equipment.” Two years later she was dropped from SM. “That was depressing,” she says. “We didn’t match artistically. My voice was too low. They liked more feminine, clean vocals.”

Figuring out her next move, she started meeting producers. One invited her to a studio, played her an instrumental track and asked her to try writing lyrics for it. “I’d never written a proper song. They said, ‘Write about whatever you want.’ So I wrote about my boyfriend at the time because we’d had a huge fight that day.”

The song became Hello and was picked up by the South Korean singer Hani. Ejae then met Andrew Choi, a singer, songwriter and fellow SM veteran who became her mentor and later voiced Jinu, the male lead in KPop Demon Hunters.

In 2019, another song she’d co-written, Psycho, was picked up by Red Velvet and topped the Billboard world digital song chart. “That’s when I was like, OK, maybe I do have a skill set for this, let me take this really seriously.”

Months later she was invited to work on KPop Demon Hunters. She sang the demos she’d written for the film and the directors asked her to sing as Rumi. “I never thought I would be an artist,” she says. “I didn’t have thick enough skin. I was very sensitive in my 20s; I can’t handle criticism.”

So what does Ejae’s future hold? She doesn’t yet know if she’ll be involved in the upcoming sequel or tour (“It would be fun, though”). In the meantime, she’s working on an album, “figuring out what my own pop sound is”, and writing for other artists.

In November, she’ll marry her fiancé, Sam Kim, a former music producer she met in 2017 during a songwriting session. He now works in coding and is quietly here with her on set, ever the supportive boyfriend. They live in Brooklyn.

“We got this wedding date really last minute and it’s only a couple of months away, so we need to chop-chop. I don’t know who’s doing my dress and apparently it takes a year to make a wedding dress, so [Dior’s] Jonathan Anderson is out. He has collections to work on; he is a busy man!”

Have there been any downsides to her life-changing year? “The only thing is that I can’t go to onsens [hot springs] any more because you’re fully naked going in.” She shakes her head. “It’s still crazy to me. I was a nobody and suddenly I’m a something.”
