Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 21:17:08 GMT

May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded

Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA

May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.

Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.

The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as “elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.

Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually, Venice doesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.

In an emotional acceptance speech, El-Toukhy thanked Gyllenhaal for addressing the underrepresentation of female film-makers at the start of the festival. Woman Unknown was the only film in competition to be solely directed by a woman.

“This film has been incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” El-Toukhy said. “And what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known. And especially tonight, I feel like I succeeded in doing just that.”

The runner-up grand jury prize went to the Korean director Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, a simmering tale of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband, which drew rave reviews.

The special jury prize, Venice’s equivalent of a bronze medal, went to Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA, about Israel’s AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza.

The film, which was produced by the Guardian, is based on testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders who are interviewed anonymously at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv. It takes its title from an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.

“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the Israeli politicians and journalists who are now attacking this film and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said when accepting his prize. “So much is being done not to look at reality.”

The day after NAZA’s premiere, the Israeli military “categorically denied” the allegations made in the film.

The Russian director Ilya Khrzhanovsky won the Silver Lion for best director for the visually stunning DAU, a biopic of the Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau, who was pressured into working on the Soviet Union’s nuclear weapons programme.

The inclusion of Khrzhanovsky’s film in the Venice lineup was criticised by the Ukrainian government in the run-up to the festival, over its lead actor Teodor Currentzis’s refusal to condemn the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and for having received funding from a Russian businessman who was later sanctioned by the US and Ukraine.

DAU was filmed in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011, before the start of the conflict. At a press conference on the Lido, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”

John Malkovich took home the Volpi Cup for best actor, for his role as an erratic veteran CIA agent whose cancer diagnosis leads him to question the morality of his profession, in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine.

The 72-year-old US actor was not present in Venice and accepted his award via a video link. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice film festival,” Malkovich said.

Golden Lion for best film: Woman Unknown, directed by May el-Toukhy

Grand jury prize: Possible Love, directed by Lee Chang-dong

Silver Lion for best director: Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAU

Special jury prize: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor

Best screenplay: Un bon petit soldat (A Good Little Soldier), Stéphane Brizé, Coralie Amédéo, Olivier Gorce

Volpi Cup for best actress: Mathilde Arcel in Woman Unknown

Volpi Cup for best actor: John Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine

Marcello Mastroianni award for best young actor: Malou Khebizi in 15/18 A Place to Heal

Armani Beauty audience award: Eu contez (I Matter), directed by Alina Șerban

Luigi De Laurentiis award for debut film: La maison du vent (House of the Wind), directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu

Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick save

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 21:14:24 GMT

As the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.

Two minutes after David Raya had, rather majestically, saved Le Fée’s second half penalty, Guimarães delighted both his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs. Yet no one should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty and Reinildo’s sending-off, this was the toughest of tests for Mikel Arteta’s team. If Sunderland can keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris’s players will surely enjoy more good days than bad.

That penalty miss aside, chapeaux off to Le Fée, who has deservedly made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from longlist to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.

Arsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.

There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery following more stellar work from Christos Tzolis.

Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20-yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.

Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the excellent Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.

Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing or winning his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever combative centre-forward, Brian Brobbey.

If a packed Stadium of Light enjoyed that little subplot, the roof was nearly lifted off by the roar of approval that greeted Reinildo’s full blooded early challenge on Martin Ødegaard.

One constant was Arteta’s excursions outside his technical area and eventually the referee, John Brooks, responded by jogging over to the touchline and waving a yellow card in the Arsenal manager’s face. While that booking was hardly unmerited, it seemed a shame that Brooks was turning a blind eye to some persistent shirt pulling from both sides at corners.

With the match even at the interval, Arteta replaced Myles Lewis-Skelly and the hobbling Ben White with Bruno Guimarães and Jurriën Timber. The Brazilian’s past as Newcastle’s captain ensured Guimaraes’s every touch was booed, while Sunderland started the new half strongly with Brobbey continuing to bully Konsa.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

A penalty-area encounter with Ballard at a throw proved no more welcome and when Konsa grappled the defender to the ground, Brooks had no hesitation in pointing to the spot. Up stepped Le Fée but there was a fairly lengthy delay and Sunderland’s normally ultra-reliable penalty taker looked uncharacteristically nervous. He attempted to squeeze his kick just inside David Raya’s left upright but the goalkeeper guessed correctly and tipped the ball, quite brilliantly, on to the woodwork and away.

Then, two minutes later and very much against the run of play, Arsenal broke from another Sunderland throw and Guimarães curled a sumptuous shot beyond Roefs from the edge of the area.

As the scorer celebrated Arteta made a point of congratulating Raya, while Le Bris instructed Wilson Isidor to prepare to replace Nilsson Angulo. Sunderland duly shifted to 4-4-2 and a temperature that had already risen perilously closing to boiling point when Xhaka was booked for a powerful sliding challenge on Guimarães continued climbing.

With no option but to take risks, Le Bris sent on Malick Fofana, newly signed from Lyon in place of Thomas Meunier, and the Belgian’s first advance into Arsenal’s penalty area prompted rare defensive chaos among the visitors.

Although it took Roefs, who saved superbly from Saka, and Ballard, with a header off the line, to keep Le Bris’s side in the game, while Timber had a headed “goal” disallowed for offside, Arteta had reason to look slightly nervous. Sure enough, Mukiele volleyed a Le Fée corner just over the bar and, with Xhaka now reigning supreme in central midfield, an equaliser beckoned.

Arsenal, though, are not champions for nothing and when Reinildo felled Saka in the area deep in stoppage time, another penalty was awarded. Sunderland’s left-back, who had already been booked, was shown another yellow and then a red card and trudged off. Roefs touched but could not hold Saka’s kick from 12 yards.

Keely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Audrey Werro takes Ultimate gold

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 20:50:26 GMT

Swiss wins $150,000 with dominant display in 800m

Georgia Hunter Bell second to Kazimierska in 1500m

This season has witnessed an extraordinary arms race between three of the greatest female 800m runners in history. But, as so often over the summer months, it concluded with the sight of Audrey Werro going nuclear.

There were some in the press seats who wondered whether the brilliant 22-year-old Swiss might be tired and vulnerable, whether Britain’s Olympic champion, Keely Hodgkinson, or the fast-rising Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol could take advantage. But at these Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Werro proved again she was 2026’s ultimate performer as she took the $150,000 first prize with another dominant display.

Werro’s formula is simple but devastatingly effective. Run the first 200m in a shade over 27sec to take the lead, control the race like a puppet master, and then apply the squeeze in the last 300m. As things stand, no one has an answer.

She applied it perfectly here, to win in 1min 55.88sec, with Hodgkinson second in 1:56.26 and Broeders-Bol a further half a second back in third.

Werro’s statistics during the outdoor season are extraordinary. Since losing to Hodgkinson at the world indoor championships, Werro has won all 14 events she has entered, run four of the 10 fastest times in history, and took gold at the European championships. Indeed, the only time she has failed to cross the line first was when she was tripped up in the semi-finals in Birmingham.

After this latest win she described her season as “really crazy” and suggested she would use her first prize to improve her training. God help her rivals if that is truly the case.

The scary thing for Hodgkinson and Broeders-Bol? Werro is 22, and only started full-time training this year after finishing her studies. Jarmila Kratochvilova’s 43-year-old world record is already within striking distance. Would anyone be surprised if she found the 0.43 needed to topple it in 2027?

However, it would be foolish to write off Hodgkinson, who confirmed that she had torn a hamstring during the European championships, which meant she was unable to do the speed work needed to compete with Werro.

“I think, on the outside, people might think I’d be disappointed with that, but I’m actually quite proud of how I approached that,” said Hodgkinson. “I didn’t even know I was going to be here. It was very much touch and go. I was really going at it with rehab.

“It’s been a bit of a frustrating season, but I think overall I’ve finished second in the world, and I can’t really be too hard on myself with that,” she added. “And congrats to Audrey, as well. Incredible season, absolutely incredible, dominant. Yeah, I look forward to racing her again next season.”

That comment was a measure of Hodgkinson’s class after a frustrating year, which started with a world indoor 800m record and a world indoor title. But she has not been able to show the same form after badly scarring her knees in a fall in Eugene in July, and then tearing her hamstring last month.

“I felt good,” said Hodgkinson. “I think with the injury I had to prepare a bit like Tokyo last year. I had to just take my foot off speed and focus more on strength.”

Earlier in the evening Hodgkinson’s training partner Georgia Hunter Bell also finished second behind Klaudia Kazimierska after a thrilling 1500m.

When Kazimierska kicked for home with 200m remaining, Hunter Bell was the only athlete to immediately respond. It led to a thrilling duel along the final straight, with the Pole having just enough to win in 3:57.55, with Hunter Bell 0.15sec back in second.

It left Hunter Bell $75,000 richer and she was delighted with her performance, after what she felt was a flat display in the Diamond League final last weekend. “I thought it was a great race,” she said. “I’m really happy with that. I felt really comfortable the whole race. I chose to go on the rail because last week I ran 15 extra meters by running wide, and that really took the sting out of my kick at the end.”

When it comes to the cash, Hunter Bell has certainly earned it this year, having won gold at the world indoors, Commonwealth Games and European championships. “I mean, the money is interesting,” she said. “I’m not really thinking about that in the home straight. I’m just thinking about trying to get to the line first.

“But I’ve run 20 races this year. I’ve shown up to absolutely everything that I can, and done myself proud. I had 14 wins, three out of four majors won, one runner-up. I’m not going to sniff at 75k.”

One of the performances of the night came in the women’s 100m as the world champion, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, ran a scorching 10.62sec to take victory. It was the fastest time in the world this year, too quick for the Olympic 100m gold medallist, Julien Alfred, who was second in 10.74, with another US star, Sha’Carri Richardson, third in 10.76. Britain’s Amy Hunt was last in 11.09.

Tove Lo: ‘The rumour I hear the most is that I’m either pregnant or in rehab. I want both of those to not be true’

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 20:00:45 GMT

The Swedish electro-pop singer-songwriter on eloping to Vegas, checking cupboards for murderers and her spooky party trick

What’s been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

The one that comes to mind is a fan in Austin who I met on one of my first tours there. He ran up to me and said, “SIGN MY ARM!” I signed his arm and then when he came back to the show the next night he had it tattooed – there was plastic over it. I remember saying, “I would have done a better job if I knew you were going to get it tattooed.” Then we took a picture of us, with me pointing at the tattoo.

The next year when I was playing at Austin City Limits, the sound broke down and I was talking to the crowd for quite a while, and I saw him – he had a T-shirt on with the photo of me and him pointing at his tattoo. He’d made a T-shirt for me as well, so he threw it up on stage … I still have that T-shirt in my closet.

Is there a rumour you’ve heard or read about yourself that you wish were true?

The one that pops up the most is that I’m either pregnant or that I’ve gone to rehab, so right now I want both of those to not be true.

What’s the most impulsive thing you’ve ever done?

Probably get married. We eloped to Vegas and took a group of our closest friends with us and had a party weekend. We went to the Little White Chapel and just did it, I think within two weeks of us talking about getting married.

Your latest single is called DNH, meaning “drunk and horny”. When was the last time you were drunk and horny?

Last weekend. I was at this party in downtown LA called Midnight Lovers – they throw parties in an outside venue under a bridge – and a DJ that I love called Azzecca did a really great set. We were dancing, hanging out and then went back to my friend’s house for an after party. We got in the hot tub when we got home. It was a very typical LA night for me and my crew. It was fun and sexy.

What’s the first thing you do when you get to a hotel?

If it’s late, I check under the bed and in all the closets and the bathroom to make sure that no one’s in there ready to murder me – and then I will pour a drink and take a bath.

If you could be any animal, what would you be?

I would be a lynx, the Nordic wildcat. It’s what Lo means in Swedish. It’s the animal that I’ve always gone back to, my favourite animal since I was kid [shows a tattoo of a lynx on her hand].

How many lynx tattoos do you have?

I have this one right here of Sunshine Kitty [the name of her fourth album] with Super Ted. The rest of my tattoos are hearts, bunnies, vaginas and aliens.

What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened to you on stage?

Having food poisoning and needing to run off stage to puke. I was playing a festival in Bali and I got sick like five minutes before. I was thinking, I’ve done the initial spew so I probably have an hour until I need to puke again, so let’s go! I got through the whole set, ran off to spew, ran on again and did the last two songs. Afterwards I was like, “Get me to bed.”

Would you rather die at the bottom of the ocean or out in space?

Out in space. I don’t know why. Maybe because it feels like I’ll be floating and slowly suffocating, whereas drowning for some reason feels really painful. I think I will just be mesmerised that I’m even out there.

Do you believe in extraterrestrial life?

I do. I don’t know if we have yet figured out their shape or form. But I don’t think that we’re the only ones out there. I think there’s already proof that we’re not, we just haven’t found anything that we can communicate with.

Do you have a party trick?

I’ve kind of stopped doing it but I can go down into a bridge pose from standing, then walk like the girl from The Exorcist. But if I’m a little too drunk and I fail and land flat on my head, it gets dramatic. If I’m walking down a hallway and I can hear someone coming, I go into the Exorcist pose and start walking at them. It looks pretty impressive and spooky.

Tove Lo’s album Estrus is out on 18 September. The Estrus tour is coming to Brisbane, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth, 1-7 March 2027

The moment I knew: I had planned to break up with him – then he snuck out of school to buy me hot chips

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 20:00:43 GMT

Maleah Pearce wanted to end her relationship with high school ‘bad boy’ Dylan before they grew too attached. Then one lunchtime, he brought her a surprise

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

Dylan and I first started dating in high school when we were 16. He was a “bad boy” who got drunk at parties and occasionally spoke to other people with his fists.

One night, I was sitting at my computer, chatting with friends on MSN and Facebook and Dylan’s name popped up. I enjoyed playing online checkers with people from school, so I invited him to a game. During the game we chatted online, which led to flirting. The winner got to choose what they wanted. I lost and what did Dylan ask for? To date me. We agreed to one date at the movies and to declare to the school we were boyfriend and girlfriend. I thought this was hilarious, though I planned to break up with him after a few days.

The date went better than I thought – he offered to invite friends so that I wasn’t alone. He paid for my ticket, bought me Malteasers, and when I realised I’d left my glasses in the car, he ran back to the car park in skinny jeans and sandals to retrieve them.

At school, I remember the first time he tried to touch me, on my lower back. When his hand made contact with my shirt I immediately told him he was not allowed to touch me without my permission. And he didn’t. I liked this about him and felt more comfortable around him.

Days turned into weeks, and I still hadn’t broken up with Dylan. I liked that he had a strong relationship with his mother, worked two part-time jobs while at school, was eager to go to university and had great plans for his future. He also did a lot of pull-ups and had nice biceps.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

On another date, we watched Toy Story 3 at the cinemas. Dylan pointed to the little girl character, Bonnie, and said, “That’s what our daughter would look like if we had one.” I was surprised that a teenage boy would think of this.

He said he wanted a long-term relationship, someone he could be with for ever, and said he would like that with me. I wasn’t too sure about that yet. I had a lot of plans of my own. I wanted to go to university and go into scriptwriting or become a novelist – both difficult career paths. Dylan wanted to be an engineer. His future was very assured, while mine felt unknown. I decided to end the relationship before we grew too attached.

Then one day at school, during lunchtime, I sat in a group with my friends and said I felt like some hot chips from KFC. Dylan overheard, and snuck out of the school grounds and walked all the way to the shops. I remember him jumping back over the school fence in his school uniform, clutching a brown paper KFC bag. I had no idea he was going to do it and was very surprised when he brought it to me – grinning, red-faced, hair a mess. He was put in detention. Dylan lost an afternoon, but he won my heart. And the chips were delicious.

From then on, this teenage boy would do anything for me. He drove me anywhere I wanted to go, stopped going to parties, never drank alcohol again and went to therapy to deal with his reckless spirit. I never asked him to do these things, but he said he did them for me. Although he did continue to ditch school and bring me KFC – which was traitorous, since he was doing weekend shifts at Red Rooster.

At 18, when we were at uni, Dylan and I moved in together. In our early 20s, we married. In 2020, our little girl was born – we named her Bonnie.

Dylan is so supportive of me. When I told him that I was going to work on becoming an author, the next day he renovated our spare room to become my office and surprised me with my dream computer. His way of saying “I love you” is by asking, “This weekend, should we buy some more books?” and “Do you want me to read what you’ve written today?”

And of course, on date nights, Dylan and I always go out for KFC.

Maleah Pearce writes under the pen name Penny Sunday. Kill To Love by Penny Sunday is available now through Hachette Australia (AU$24.99)

Ben Shelton faces date with destiny against Zverev in US Open final

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 19:32:57 GMT

World No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat German for the first time

As Ben Shelton lapped up the explosion of joy and adoration from a full Arthur Ashe Stadium after reaching a grand slam final for the first time, one of his first thoughts was of his paternal grandmother, Regina, who died this year. Shelton credited his grandmother with ensuring that his father, Bryan, made it as a top professional, becoming one of a small group of Black men on the tour. “My dad lost his mom earlier this year and she’s the reason he was able to play tennis,” he said. “Without her, there’s no Ben Shelton standing here today. So this one is for her.”

Shelton stands on the verge of history. On Sunday, he will attempt to become the first Black American man to win the US Open singles title since Arthur Ashe in 1968, a feat he will attempt inside the stadium named after Ashe. Shelton would also be the first Black man to win any grand slam singles title since Yannick Noah at Roland Garros in 1983, and the third overall. He is also aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003.

The final step, however, will be the most difficult. Tennis is a game of match-ups and Shelton has had an especially difficult time against Alexander Zverev, the Roland Garros champion and the top seed in the absence of Jannik Sinner. After winning the first set they played, at Cincinnati in 2024, Shelton has lost 10 sets in a row to Zverev, compiling a 0-5 record against the German on hard courts, grass and clay.

Zverev is well suited for left-handed opponents due to the strength of his two-handed backhand, which allows him to counter the effects of their swinging serve out wide from the left advantage side as well as their crosscourt forehand from the same position.

There are plenty of reasons, however, for Shelton to be hopeful that things will be different in New York. He will remind himself of the fact that they have never faced each other in a grand slam tournament, where the American so often elevates his game, and particularly that the theme of this tournament has been breaking new ground in difficult match-ups.

“Problem-solving has been the name of the game here,” he said. “I was 0-1 against Stef [Stefanos Tsitsipas], 0-3 against Carlos [Alcaraz], Foe [Frances Tiafoe] beat me the last time we played on this court. It’s been a lot of uphill battle, so I think I’m fully ready for the challenge to problem-solve.”

His father and coach, Bryan, stressed how well his son, who is 7-2 in finals, competes with a title on the line: “He’s got an amazing record on Sundays. Don’t want to jinx him here, but if you look at his record throughout his career, he’s played well on Sundays.

“So that’s where he wants to be. He feels like he’s going to play his best tennis at the end of the week, or end of the two weeks. So glad he has a chance at the US Open.”

One of the most striking aspects of Shelton’s emergence has been his relentless improvement. His path took him through the college route where he started as an unremarkable prospect. When he first emerged on the ATP Tour, the strengths he showed with his enormous serve, athleticism and the variation he could play with were counterbalanced by glaring weaknesses in his backhand, return and consistency from the baseline. They were all still present on his explosive first full season on the tour in 2023, which he began with a run to the quarter-finals of the Australian Open on his first trip outside the United States. He reached the semi-finals of the US Open that year, yet despite progressing only one round further this year, Shelton is a different player now.

after newsletter promotion

He has made such drastic improvements to his backhand, return of serve and consistency, which is what has allowed him to perform at such a high level during this tournament. Against Alcaraz, he returned well and was the far more stable player from the baseline. In his win over Tiafoe, he saved one of the best backhand days of his career for one of the biggest matches.

“I still feel so many categories that I think I have a long way to go, but I’ve made improvements and changes in some of the most important categories to be able to compete at the top,” he said. “Return of serve, stability from the baseline, even my serve, the way that I go about putting together my service games has improved, and my ability to focus for long periods of time are all areas that have come together and have helped me play at the level I’m playing. But the pursuit and hunger to get better, to find ways that I can improve, it’s just a part of who I am and something that will never change.”

Late on Friday night, as Shelton left the court and only just began to digest his achievement, a smile spread widely across his father’s face. “To do it here at the US Open and be playing on the final day, this kid, it’s kind of surreal,” he said. “I didn’t think he was going to even get into this sport and then to be where he’s at right now, I mean, it’s just hard to believe, hard to believe and just super, super grateful.”

Tottenham waiting for first league goal of season after draw against Everton

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 18:47:01 GMT

Is it too early for a Tottenham crisis? To which the answer is surely that it is never too early for a Tottenham crisis. After four Premier League games, they have yet to score. This kind of run has never happened in their history at the beginning of a league season.

At least they mustered a couple of shots on target this time, having failed to do so last weekend in the 0-0 draw at Nottingham Forest. The first – from Mateus Fernandes – at the start of the second half was greeted by ironic cheers from the South Stand. It has certainly not been what the club expected when they spent £300m on overhauling the squad in the summer.

Spurs were anxious, they lacked certainties – apart from the one about how they were never going to score. They were fortunate that Everton, who remain defiantly unbeaten, did not do so at the other end. David Moyes’s team had big chances in the second half through Thierno Barry, Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and the former Spurs winger, Brennan Johnson. Everton defended superbly, albeit they were helped by Tottenham’s bluntness, and were full value for the draw. They probably deserved to win.

Spurs have won only one league game at home this year – in do-or-die circumstances against Everton on the final day of last season. Going back to November 2024, their record in the competition here reads: P35 W5 D10 L20. As Everton savoured the result with their fans at full time, the Spurs crowd turned to a familiar soundtrack: a burst of booing.

It was difficult not to remember the game here last season when Spurs won 1-0 to stay up. Defeat and they would have been relegated. It was an extraordinarily nervy occasion for them, all the way to the last knockings of stoppage time. The pessimistic edge about the home support has not gone away. Far from it. You could hear it before kick-off. ‘Good luck? Yeah, we’ll need it.’ That sort of thing. A major part of the mission was to try to tear down the psychological barriers. They failed.

There was hope, too. It always bubbles somewhere in the background. And Spurs did start well, pressing on to the front foot, moving the ball quickly. Rodrigo Bentancur imposed himself. Savio was a ball of pace and tricks. There was a statistic beforehand that rated Tottenham as the worst team in the league for the quality of chances created. What could they do with their possession against an Everton defence that knows how to stifle? It was the question that pounded.

Everton travelled with confidence after good results in their opening fixtures. Their squad is alarmingly thin. But they have enough at this point of the season and the fallout from that disastrous transfer deadline day appears to have bonded the squad. Everton were the second worst team on the chance quality index but they were always likely to be measured by how well they defended.

Spurs pushed for the first half of the first period, albeit the pickings in front of goal were slim. Jan Paul van Hecke banged a half volley high from a tight angle at the far post after an Andy Robertson free-kick and that would go down as their only chance of the opening 45 minutes. There was a stumble from Fernandes inside the area after a nice ball up through the lines from Van Hecke which summed things up for them. The anxiety transmitted itself to the crowd and bounced back.

James Garner worked Antonin Kinsky with a free-kick at the end of the first half, which went down as the first shot on target. When Fernandes mustered his from distance in the 47th minute, it was met with that sarcasm.

Everton were more proactive after the restart. They fed off the Spurs nerves. They threatened to get in behind. Tyrique George did beat Archie Gray, who stood in for the injured Pedro Porro at right-back; Roberto De Zerbi was also without Destiny Udogie through injury at left-back. George’s cross picked out Barry at the far post and his header hit Kinsky before flying off target. The goalkeeper knew little about it. George also had a blast that hit Bentancur.

Tottenham came to be undermined by terrible errors on the ball. There were so many passes that were woefully off target, including one from Kinsky that he sent straight to Dewsbury-Hall on the edge of his area. Kinsky made amends with a smart block. Dewsbury-Hall cursed the passing up of a golden opportunity.

Everton were the likelier team to score. Spurs battled the internal demons. There were cross words between some of their players, Omar Marmoush overtaken by frustration at one point. Johnson blew his chance on 75 minutes, lifting high after a Dewsbury-Hall tee-up.

Spurs had one flicker at the very end after Jordan Pickford sent a poor clearance straight to James Maddison, who had come on as a substitute. Spurs moved it to another replacement, Lucas Bergvall, and his low drive worked Pickford. It was a comfortable save. Everton were exactly that.

Solheim Cup: Hull and Woad flop for Europe as Kupcho pulls USA level

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 18:25:50 GMT

Scores level at 8-8 after dramatic day two

Anna Nordqvist pairing of star duo fails to pay off

It has been the great anomaly of this Solheim Cup. Europe keeping perfect pace with the United States is an impressive achievement even without factoring in the meagre points contribution from Charley Hull and Lottie Woad. European hopes of reclaiming the trophy lost to the United States two years ago surely depend heavily on their star turns finding singles form.

The heroics of Jennifer Kupcho in fading light dashed Europe’s ambitions of taking a lead. It is 8-8 as things stand. A 12-match shootout remains.

Anna Nordqvist’s deployment of Hull and Woad as a pairing on Saturday morning has to be considered odd. The duo had claimed half a point from two previous outings. Hull does not look particularly suited to foursomes. Woad is a Solheim Cup debutant. Nordqvist, it appeared, focused heavily on the status of both players inside the world’s top 10. The tactic backfired; Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin thumped the English pair, 6&5. Undeterred, Nordqvist sent Hull and Woad back out. This time it was Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee who emerged victorious.

“I don’t think people understand these are the best players in the world,” said Nordqvist when asked whether Saturday afternoon selection was wise. “I think they played [against] the strongest pairings in each session. Lottie herself made six birdies yesterday in the afternoon. So they’re playing solid and I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a little bit of blue on that board this afternoon.”

The Swede’s hopes proved in vain. Troubles on the greens undermined the performance of Hull and Woad as the Americans prevailed on the final green. The Europeans gave the regular impression they would rather be elsewhere. A high point came on the 17th, where Woad’s brave putt from 15ft kept the match alive. At the final tee, Hull pulled a fairway wood into water.

Nordqvist’s decision-making created history, with Hull and Woad the first to play four sessions together in the same Solheim Cup. Nordqvist’s faith has failed to find reward. In fairness, in Noh the Europeans in question faced the player of this event. She has been exceptional.

Hull and Woad said they knew they would play every session, which raises questions over how nimble their captain is. “It was pretty frustrating,” said Hull of the fourball loss. Woad added: “It doesn’t matter who wins the points. I would happily lose my matches if we win.”

This is indeed a team business. After back-to-back tied sessions, Europe forged ahead on Saturday morning. The superb Maja Stark and Linn Grant saw off Allisen Corpuz and the world No 1, Nelly Korda. Angela Stanford, the US captain, stood down Korda after lunch.

Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit enjoyed a successful reunion as they defeated the US pair of Kupcho and Rose Zhang. The European rookies Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud were again outstanding as they claimed a point from Auston Kim and Andrea Lee. Alison Lee and Coughlin returned the sole US reward of the foursomes.

Coughlin will be the only US player to feature in all five sessions. Stanford explained that was not determined before the event. Coughlin and Megan Khang tasted fourball defeat to Stark and Grant. “Maja played out of her mind,” Coughlin said.

Noh and Andrea Lee confirmed victory over Hull and Woad on the last green. Kim and Zhang were 3&2 winners over Maguire and Nadaud. In seeking to tie the fourball session, Europe needed Carlota Ciganda and Céline Boutier to hold off Kupcho and Lindy Duncan.

Europe were two up after 14. A three from Duncan on the 15th narrowed the deficit, but the Europeans looked like they would do enough to cling on. Enter Kupcho, who converted in extraordinary circumstances from 90ft and off the green at the 17th. She followed it up with a birdie from 30ft at the last. From moments like these, Solheim Cups are won. No wonder Ciganda and Boutier looked distraught.

A background cause for concern for the US arrived from Angel Yin. The 27-year-old had been a serious doubt to feature due to illness that significantly disrupted her season. That Yin did not play on Saturday was no great shock, but the sight of her pounding balls for a lengthy time on the driving range as competitive action unfolded elsewhere implied she is struggling for form.

Yin and the US need six points from the 12 remaining to hold on to the trophy. Six and a half is the European requirement. Momentum is suddenly with the visitors.

Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 17:41:46 GMT

Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings

Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration.

Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.

They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.

One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.

A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.

Donna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.

Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.

“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.

“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”

In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.

Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.

A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.

In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.

Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.

The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.

The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.

Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.

MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.

Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.

Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.

Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”

The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.

The incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.

Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.

Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.

The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.

Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.

The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.

Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.

“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”

England survive sluggish start to overwhelm Australia in second half

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 16:06:25 GMT

WXV: England 48-15 Australia

May Campbell kickstarts flurry of seven tries

England had to execute something they have not had to do in John Mitchell’s reign against Australia on Saturday, win after being down at half-time. It was the first time in almost six years the Red Roses had been trailing after the first 40. But whatever was said in the changing room shook the team to life as they scored 43 second-half points to keep their winning streak going.

Australia gave the Red Roses quite the scare in the first half. The Wallaroos were not just clinical when in attack, but they were thorough and physical in defence to disrupt England’s front-foot ball. The visitors played some of their best rugby since last year’s World Cup, when they were knocked out in the quarter-finals, before falling apart in the second half. England were uncharacteristically poor at times with several knock-ons and other handling errors hampering their attack.

This was the first game with the smaller ball. In WXV matches this autumn, teams are playing with a size 4.5 ball instead of the usual size five. World Rugby has introduced the trial to see if it has a positive impact after similar trials in youth competitions and in sevens. At a windy Salford, Australia dealt with the change better but the Wallaroos captain, Siokapesi Palu Sekona, said she and her teammates “had already played with the ball in our Super [Rugby] season so we haven’t had to adjust much”.

The England captain, Meg Jones – who was sporting a black eye – said: “I think we are fed up of speaking about it. I’m a craftsman and I’ll never blame my tools.”

The England fly-half, Holly Aitchison, won her 50th cap less than 40 miles from her home town club of Firwood Waterloo. She led the team out and her teammates congratulated her as they lined up for the anthems. Just like the last time the two nations played, at last year’s World Cup, Australia scored the first points with a penalty from Samantha Wood’s boot.

Australia then deployed ferocious defence but all of their good work looked to have been undone after Meg Jones appeared to score from a charged-down kick, however Tatyana Heard was offside.

A deliberate knock-on from Wood meant the visitors were down to 14 and while England were sloppy with the ball they went over through Abi Burton. The Wallaroos had a try ruled out before Faliki Pohiva scored and another impressive defensive set saw them hold a thoroughly deserved 10-5 half-time lead.

England were sharper in the second half and showed their teeth in attack with a tirade of tries beginning with a score by May Campbell. Just as the scrum was the Red Roses’ winning north star in the 2025 World Cup final and Women’s Six Nations grand slam decider this year, it gave them much needed momentum – particularly after the front row was changed – and it generated a try for Jones. Credit must go to the captain too, with a bit of individual skill sealing the score.

The Red Roses scoring tap was firmly on and the debutant Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya added tries. The replacement scrum-half, Lucy Packer, made an acrobatic finish and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald finished out the tries.

Australia were completely outplayed in the second half and their director of women’s high performance, Tim Walsh, said even when his team are at their best “we are probably not good enough”.

“If we are going to win, we want to win [a home World Cup in 2029] so that is a good benchmark to work our way back from.”

Frustrated Liverpool lack any spark as Fulham claim deserved first point

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 16:06:00 GMT

Álvaro Arbeloa was often the obstacle to Andoni Iraola’s international ambitions back in the days when both were vying for a right-back role with Spain. On his return to Anfield, and under the watchful eye of former manager Rafael Benítez, Arbeloa thwarted Iraola once again to claim his first Premier League point as Fulham head coach against an ineffective Liverpool.

Fulham belied their lowly position and run of three league defeats to take a merited point from a Liverpool team that was a pale imitation of the one that beat Atlético Madrid in the Champions League on Wednesday. Iraola fielded a front four that cost almost £400m but the most impressive forward on display was the Fulham academy graduate Josh King. The draw was Liverpool’s third in four league games under their new head coach and the seventh in 12 Premier League matches at Anfield in 2026. Progress can be painfully slow at times.

“It is the first game we’ve had problems creating chances and making the difference offensively,” Iraola said. “It is easy for me to say the players were tired (after Atlético). There was a lack of freshness and, we cannot hide it, it was the worst turnaround in terms of 60-70 hours. But this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt. Sometimes you need a set play or a moment of brilliance to win these kind of games but we were not as good offensively as other games.”

Liverpool were sluggish and sloppy – Florian Wirtz and Kostas Tsimikas put simple passes straight out of play in the first half, setting the tone for a disjointed performance – while Fulham bypassed the central midfield pairing of Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch repeatedly. The visitors’ confidence and composure on the ball, along with their defensive organisation, was hugely impressive considering the start to the season under the former Real Madrid interim coach and Liverpool defender. With more conviction in front of goal, Arbeloa’s side could have capitalised on Liverpool’s malaise.

Bradley Barcola created an early, difficult chance for Alexander Isak that the striker swept wide of the far post. Victor Muñoz went closer still with a glancing header from a Szoboszlai corner. Bernd Leno, the Fulham goalkeeper, reacted superbly to claw the ball away. But that was the sum total of Liverpool’s first-half enterprise.

Fulham were gifted a glorious opportunity when Alisson played a ridiculous pass to Gravenberch, who was under pressure from Sander Berge. Berge’s challenge fell to King, who was sent flying by the Liverpool goalkeeper but the referee, Thomas Bramall, played a good advantage as Gonzalo García received the loose ball. García had time to pick his spot but Jérémy Jacquet blocked his shot in front of the goalline.

The visitors prospered down their left and Oscar Bobb missed another good opening when, unmarked and 18 yards out, he miscontrolled Alex Iwobi’s pinpoint delivery. Jacquet came to Liverpool’s rescue once again seconds later when preventing García breaking through with an excellent challenge.

Liverpool were deserving of a few home truths during the break – chiefly, you would have been lambasted for this last season under Arne Slot – and performed with more intensity in the second half. But not with any more threat. The introductions of Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Milos Kerkez brought modest improvement but Fulham continued to contain the hosts comfortably. The new signing David Affengruber had a fine debut and Calvin Bassey was commanding against Isak.

Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 16:05:32 GMT

Donald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.

The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.

“I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, ​but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”

The unification of Northern Ireland with the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”

The intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham said a referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.

Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement.

Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.

“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.”

Colum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.”

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”

Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy.

Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace of the Irish president, Catherine Connolly.

Before her election to the ceremonial post last year, Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policies in Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies.

Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”.

Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was gathering in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests.

Addressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration.

He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK.”

Thousands of protesters marched through central Dublin and held a rally outside parliament. Speakers accused Trump of facilitating genocide in Gaza and led chants of “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”

Others in the crowd accused the president of misogyny, sexual assault, racism and xenophobia. “Donald Trump is utterly immoral and he’s wrecking the world,” said Anne McGuinness, 70, who held a banner that said “unwelcome”.

Emily Hamilton, whose daughter held a banner saying “Get rid of the evil orange”, said the Irish government should have shunned him. “We can’t stop him going to Doonbeg but we should not be welcoming him.”

Mick Brennan, 70, said he and his wife Helen do not normally attend protests but made an exception for the US president. “We can’t stand that Trump fella, from his toes to his nose.”

A smaller protest was held at Doonbeg. Trump is to stay overnight at his resort and present the Irish Open trophy to the winner on Sunday before returning to Washington.

‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 15:46:01 GMT

In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems

The CEO of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic issued a new appeal on Saturday for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps.

In a post on social media, Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he laid out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.

The move comes after a former Anthropic researcher warned on Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.

“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian that the company had “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and it was building “models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry”.

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, posted on social media. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”

Other tech figures echoed this, including Elon Musk, who simply posted, “Dario is right.” The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin also called the post “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.

Earlier this year, Amodei published a lengthy essay titled The Adolescence of Technology that addressed some of fears surrounding the accelerating technology.

In his latest essay, he said that “carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity.

“But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious … A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he wrote.

But, Amodei continued, “over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added in bold type.

Amodei also wrote that over the summer he’d seen AI “advancing drastically faster”, a dynamic called recursive self-improvement.

“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he said.

The executive also addressed the recent Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.

Amodei wrote that simply dismissing the Hugging Face incursions because the OpenAI swarms appeared to have no malicious intent was not sufficient.

“It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote.

Clément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face, wrote in response to Amodei’s Saturday letter that “it’s now clear that alignment is critical and won’t be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Delangue said Hugging Face had asked to be part of Anthropic’s “embedded evaluators” program.

He added: “Let’s make AI safer by making it more transparent!”

The three-step plan Amodei proposes includes building AI “at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety” by “ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this”.

The second step he proposes is to require industry-wide coordination, and the third is to ensure global coordination. “The steps do not need to be taken strictly in order, and some of them may be much harder to achieve than others,” he wrote.

Amodei said he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life”. But he warned that “the measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.”

Everybody Wants to F*ck Me review – Taron Egerton is hounded in sharp-toothed dating nightmare

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 15:27:17 GMT

Toronto film festival: It’s Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list in this hugely entertaining mix of dark comedy and stalker thriller with a brilliant alternating turn from Taron Egerton

Everyone knows an Adam. He’s not like those other guys, the ones who won’t take no for an answer and speak lasciviously about women to their mates. He’s doing the work, listening to and uplifting female voices, working at an all-female gallery while being constantly aware of his cis white male privilege. He has a Mubi tote bag, reads Edna O’Brien’s Country Girl in Hackney cafes, has a poster of Cléo from 5 to 7 in his apartment and has even named his dog after his favourite Haim sister. He is … a nice guy.

In first-time writer-director Jonathan Schey’s canny debut Everybody Wants to Fuck Me, Adam is also a fraud.

He’s played by Taron Egerton, someone who has recently been finding his footing as an adult actor, whether as more conventional lead of Netflix’s excellent B-movie thriller Carry-On or as the less expected gonzo villain of Netflix’s mid B-movie thriller Apex. But freed from streaming shackles (he’s also led two Apple dramas, one of which I genuinely don’t think anyone knows exists), he’s able to show just how much more he can do in edgier, stranger territory and how far he’s willing to go without blinking. Turns out, pretty far.

In a swiftly revealing cold open, we see Adam in a note-perfect meet-cute with Mia McKenna-Bruce’s unsuspecting Londoner. They dance to Troye Sivan (ally!), discuss their love for Before Sunset and, despite him not obviously pushing for it, they have sex back at his place. But the morning after, despite telling her he’s “obsessed” mid-thrust and despite making leaf art in her flat white, something is off. Maybe it’s the fact that she’s put her artisanal mug on the nightstand without a coaster or maybe it’s just because he’s in a “bojangled headspace” or maybe it’s because he does this all the time.

His exhausted gay best friend Emma (Rooster’s Charly Clive, incredibly charming) accuses him of “romantic terrorism”, but rolling her eyes and gently jabbing him is part of their learned shtick as is her allowing him to cut their night out short when he spots an attractive woman at the theatre bar. Adam tries his luck with Sofia (Jessica Henwick), who sees through his performance, poking fun at his dating profile and his many, many matches left on read. But still, she seems interested and invites him back to her place …

Something happens that night, the specifics of which we’re unsure of, like Adam. After a quick smoke, he’s knocked unconscious and he wakes to find Sofia gone. He chalks it up to yet another one-night stand but something has shifted not in him but in the world around him. Adam was never exactly struggling for female attention but there’s a new, more aggressive intensity to it with women staring at him on the tube and colleagues laughing a little too hard at his mediocre jokes. For a while, Adam makes the most of it, his door revolving that much more than usual but the sweetness begins to sour as he realises there’s something more sinister going on when even his dog Alana starts giving him the eye.

There are elements here of last year’s Toronto breakout Obsession but we’re more firmly in the recently familiar, and increasingly exhausting, land of the “social thriller”, although wisely with more (genuinely funny) comedy than this often overly self-serious subgenre has entertained for a while. The post-Get Out surge has been far more miss than hit and while this is a smarter and sharper addition (a crude sell would be Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list of 2017), it does still grapple with some recurring issues, especially as the last-act explanation rears its head. To Schey’s credit, he does a better job than most (the bar has been set low by the maddening stupidity of both Blink Twice and Don’t Worry Darling) and finds the right balance of serious to silly, but the film is reliant on a poorly thought through convenience that pushed me a little too far out. Schey also leans on a last-scene trope that ranks among my least favourite ways to end a movie, right next to a character asking another “what now?” as credits fade.

But he mostly gets a lot right, both as writer and director, a not-to-be-sniffed-at achievement for a first-timer given how many tend to only convince while wearing one of those hats. The target here is so easy to so many of us (last year even saw a performative male contest in Washington Square Park), but Schey works at making Adam a real person rather than a meme to be simply ridiculed. He doesn’t turn Adam into a full-throated bad guy but also manages to avoid softening who he really is, and even as we follow his descent right alongside him, Schey skirts falling back on uneasy “you can’t say anything any more!” frustration especially during a cleverly telling spiral speech (Adam complains how “exhausting” it is to be nice). So much is also down to Egerton, who delivers a fearless, full-on performance, scarily believable as both the guy who would politely and ethically get you into bed and also the one who would coldly suggest you leave the morning after, and he shows himself to be a more specifically funny and understated comedy actor than he’s been given credit for.

It comes from Margot Robbie’s LuckyChap production company, also behind the not dissimilar Promising Young Woman, but it rights so many of that film’s many wrongs, from an increase in emotional maturity to an improved aesthetic (this takes place in real, breathing, stylishly captured London, not a bright and tinny approximation of a 2000s Sundance indie) but most prominently in its willingness to bear and use its teeth to draw blood. If that film was a tease then this one isn’t scared to go all the way.

Everybody Wants to Fuck Me is premiering at the Toronto film festival and will be released at a later date

Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 15:09:05 GMT

Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’

Analysis: donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

The cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from fellow billionaire Ben Delo.

The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on money received from individual donors.

Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the payments, which come as the party is facing intense scrutiny regarding its funding. Reform said it planned to use the money to hire about 400 campaign managers in target constituencies and was now on an “election footing”.

The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.

Harborne’s donation was announced on Saturday afternoon. The Guardian understands the money has already been received by Reform.

Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.

Rachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping” on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.

The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.

Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.

“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.

Duncan Hames, of Transparency International UK, said the donations made “an irrefutable case” for a cap, adding: “At this rate just two people could end up buying our democracy before the next election.”

The campaign group Spotlight on Corruption said the donations could have a “huge and damaging impact” and accused the government of “ignoring the very high risk of the Americanisation of our politics”.

Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field”.

Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.

“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.

“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”

Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.

The Guardian asked Reform exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. A spokesperson said: “All donations to Reform UK comply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law. Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”

Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.

Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer and former chair of the House of Commons public accounts committee, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.

“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”

Many senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.

“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.

However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.

Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.

“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”

Reached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.

“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”

Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.

“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”

Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to the Palestine Red Crescent.

The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man, apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.

Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.

The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.

On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.

The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.

After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.

It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.

Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.

East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.

On 4 September, two Palestinian teenagers were shot dead in al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.

The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.

According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.
