Girl Group review – Rebel Wilson’s dreadful music comedy is a spice-free wannabe

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 13:20:23 GMT

Toronto film festival: the actor turned writer-director’s ode to girl groups is a shoddily made and embarrassingly unfunny catastrophe

There were plentiful on-paper delights for certain music fans of a certain generation promised at Toronto’s splashy Friday-night premiere of pop comedy Girl Group. Posed as a tribute to the Spice Girls and the fizzy boom of girl power-fuelled music that came in their wake, its cast includes OG member Mel C, All Saints’ Shaznay Lewis, and Pussycat Dolls’ Ashley Roberts and Nicole Scherzinger while its soundtrack includes Glee-like covers of Destiny’s Child, En Vogue and Fifth Harmony, a feast for those who have recently felt famished. At a time when such music is still sadly rather thin on the ground, save for the manufactured kids pop of Katseye and the often effective yet more boutiquey throwback R&B of Flo, it seemed to be a reminder of how thrilling it all used to be back when such girl-pop supremacy felt impossibly never-ending, a form of nostalgia-bait that many of us could fully get behind.

But there are not enough pandering nods to the past that will get even the most dedicated pop girlie through the five-alarm catastrophe that unfolded for those of us who bravely decided to stay awake (someone in front of me wisely chose the release of sleep within the first 30 minutes). Hailing from Live Nation Studios, also behind the Weeknd’s roundly ridiculed vanity project Hurry Up Tomorrow, but lit and shot like a pharmaceutical commercial, it barely even feels like a real movie let alone one that should be premiering at such a prestigious festival. It’s the clumsy handiwork of Rebel Wilson, a once in-demand comedy star who has been trying to chase her career highs in the years since. In a theoretically admirable move, she’s moved behind the camera to take control and reintroduce the kind of broad comedies she used to be a part of before they faded from the mainstream. Her directorial debut, a cheap and cheerful adaptation of Australian stage musical The Deb, was ultimately best known for being the subject of a nasty and prolonged court case, but it showed us how Wilson saw herself as a film-maker and which of her films she was most eager to relive *coughs* Pitch Perfect *ends cough*. Girl Group sees her return once again to that territory – female friendship, musical numbers, unfriendly competition – but with even lesser results.

That’s partly down to Wilson now taking sole writing credit, and her scribbled-together script indulges her very worst impulses – tiresomely one-note bawdy jokes, unearned sugary sentiment, depressing attempts to relive former glories – and her strained journey to give us a new easy comfort film ends up feeling far too much like hard work. She plays Tassie, a former member of hit group Gurlfriends (made up of the aforementioned pop stars along with a game but above-this Sheridan Smith) who decided to leave in their prime, arrogantly assuming she could make it on her own. She fails miserably and years later, as the group reforms for a reunion tour, she’s shocked to discover, via a sleepwalking-on-Ambien Jennifer Coolidge, that she’s been replaced by Scherzinger’s ruthless super-fan. In a comedy so lacking in successful jokes that one starts to briefly, existentially panic, the one underused bit that does work is Scherzinger’s surprising willingness to poke fun at her monstrous persona. At the funeral of the girls’ school music teacher (played by a clearly lost Sally Hawkins), Scherzinger’s aggressive interloper decides to out-sing her fellow groupmates before she weeps in harmonised song. I smiled. Briefly.

Wilson’s aggrieved ex-star gets into a car crash after drinking in a laughably unconvincing idea of LA (the entire film was gauzily shot in the UK although it could be inside Sora for all I could tell) and is sentenced to community service, which lands her at a youth centre, which then leads her to a wannabe girl group, which then coincides with her finding out about some big competition and whatever.

It’s all too distractingly plasticky and haphazardly assembled to be taken seriously even as a throwaway plane comedy, which is about as high as it aims. Everything looks so grimly synthetic that one wonders if Wilson’s character died in the crash and we’re stuck in a version of hell that emulates the cheapest imaginable version of heaven. The bright spots only emerge when covers are being performed, and nothing original here has any power (Wilson performing Look at Me suggests the character is loosely based on Geri Halliwell, which feels unfair to Geri Halliwell). Like in The Deb, which at least benefited from a non-fabricated sense of location, Wilson tries to comment on the generational gap, this time critiquing an uneasy millennial obsession with overly sexualising young women, but it’s an idea that’s cheekily pointed at rather than explored with any depth. She has nothing of interest to say about anything and instead is content with lamely tracing over a formula set out previously by others, often in front of her (as well as Pitch Perfect, she cribs from a Bridesmaids set piece with a character needing an inopportune toilet break). The humour is base and consistently uninventive with Wilson assuming the mere mention of a tampon or a blowjob will have them rolling in the aisles. She also relies on a similarly simplistic score soundboard, hopelessly pressing the most obvious button for whatever mood is required. Imagine all of the care, detail and wit of the brilliant Girls5eva replaced with conference room lighting and dick jokes.

What Wilson doesn’t seem to understand is that her best movies – Bridesmaids and How to Be Single – cleverly weaved in anything more serious and emotional into the more raucous comedy without anyone seeing the joins. Here she so shamelessly switches gear that it’s hard to believe her intentions or buy her claims of authenticity. As an ode to the girl groups of our youth, it’s devoid of genuine affection (it was originally set to be a K-pop comedy until Wilson paid attention to the backlash), as evidence of what Live Nation Studios has in-store I would recommend a clear-eyed focus on the day job, and as proof of Wilson’s career to come, it’s a bleak simulacrum of what came before and a flashing red sign of what she’s just not able to do without better support. Like an overly confident yet entirely off-key tribute band, she just can’t reach those high notes.

Girl Group is premiering at the Toronto film festival and is seeking distribution

Michael Barrymore becomes unlikely TikTok star with nearly 5m followers

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 13:00:34 GMT

Former primetime TV host films himself eating dog biscuits, doing ‘munchie runs’ and addressing pool death case

Filming from the driver’s seat of his car, with his pet whippet, Lara, in the background, Michael Barrymore shows an array of dog treats he has collected to test to the camera. There’s a twist, though: it won’t be the dog doing the testing.

In a series of quick edits, the fallen star of primetime 1990s television grimaces his way through cheese biscuits and pork sausages. The lamb spaghetti is particularly challenging, though he claims to quite like the chicken sausage slices.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The dog treat video is part of a steady stream of content being produced by Barrymore on his TikTok account, where the 74-year-old has become an unlikely hit. The platform is used most heavily by the under-30s, many of whom would have no memory of his former career as one of Britain’s leading light entertainers.

Particularly popular are Barrymore’s “munchie runs” to supermarkets, sweet shops and takeaways, where he snacks his way through an alarming array of treats, energy drinks and fast food.

It is all a long way from his ITV heyday hosting Strike It Lucky and Barrymore, a career he abruptly lost in 2001 after the death of Stuart Lubbock, a 31-year-old father of two who died shortly after being found unconscious in Barrymore’s swimming pool.

Despite investigations and several arrests, no one has ever been charged in relation to Lubbock’s death. The case remains unresolved. Barrymore has always denied any involvement, but his TV career did not recover.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

However, TikTok and its all-powerful algorithm have allowed him to build a vast new audience over the past four years. He is on course to amass close to 5m followers by the end of 2026.

More than 6m have watched him scoff a trending pistachio nut cake after driving across the south-west, where he now lives, to find one. In another viral hit, he devours an M&S Colin the Caterpillar cake with his bare hands.

His success has become a case study in the media’s digital revolution, which is causing angst among traditional broadcasters. It has allowed Barrymore to bypass TV gatekeepers who shunned him after Lubbock’s death.

“Barrymore reflects an interesting aspect of modern online celebrity culture whereby you can become popular, or in his case regain popularity, even if you do not appear on mainstream TV,” said Scott Bryan, the TV critic and chronicler.

“Twenty years ago, appearing on TV was essential, and it was the end of his career when ITV dropped him. These days, those who don’t think he should be in the public eye simply don’t follow him on social media.”

Professional short-form video editors have noted there is more to Barrymore’s TikTok success than his snacking antics. His videos often adopt trending music or memes and his output is prolific – both crucial ingredients to feeding the algorithm.

A social media expert at a major British media company said: “I would be shocked if he’s doing this entirely on his own. He feels like he’s got support.”

In an email exchange, Barrymore confirmed he had his “own social media expert” but not a team.

Barrymore did attempt a more traditional comeback route after Lubbock’s death, with appearances on Celebrity Big Brother in 2006 and Dancing on Ice in 2019. Yet the outings did not revive his TV career.

According to calculations based on his public view counts, Barrymore’s TikTok and YouTube channels are providing him with an income, though not one comparable to his former earnings as the de facto face of light evening entertainment.

“I have always done what I do for the love of it,” Barrymore said. “I certainly do make a living from social media, which is increasing substantially year by year.”

Much of his content simply follows him around his daily activities, usually cooking, snacking or travelling. He delights in being recognised by cashiers pricing up his latest haul of treats. Some shop workers have complained about being filmed by him via his smart glasses.

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

Matt Navarra, a social media consultant, said: “Barrymore is simultaneously evidence that everything about the media has changed and almost nothing about entertainment has changed.

“His whole career was built around spontaneity, comic timing, talking to ordinary people, reacting quickly and creating chaotic moments. Those are fantastic short-form video creator skills.

“We haven’t really got rid of gatekeepers. We’ve swapped human gatekeepers for algorithmic ones.”

While it may appear to open up a comeback avenue for other 90s stars who have fallen out of favour, it is not so easy in practice. Fellow entertainer Jim Davidson’s Ustreme channel is also on TikTok but does not have Barrymore’s reach.

Barrymore said: “The majority of the followers are from today’s generation and don’t know me from television – this isn’t what I ‘think’, this is facts coming from the analytics of TikTok and YouTube.”

The domestic banality of his videos contributes to their success. Holly Beddingfield, a creative strategist and founder of the Capsule pop culture newsletter, said: “We increasingly see gen Z audiences push back against perfection in favour of authenticity.

“It makes sense, then, that someone like Michael would resonate. It’s similar to the success of [British social media personality] Big John – he is just a guy who people see as a sort of funny uncle or dad.”

Even on TikTok, however, Barrymore cannot escape discussion of Lubbock’s death. He has repeatedly addressed the case in videos, taking issue with various claims circulating online.

Barrymore has insisted his social media success meant he would now not go back to broadcast TV.

“It would be like taking a step backwards,” he said. “It would, I think, struggle to get the 20m to 30m views I currently get a week.”

Meanwhile, Essex police continue to appeal for information from those who attended the party at Barrymore’s house on the night of Lubbock’s death.

“Nine people were at that party,” said a spokesperson. “We know that not everyone was responsible for what happened, but someone was. Anyone with information about Stuart’s death can always contact us, whether directly or anonymously through Crimestoppers.”

Joe Root makes most of no-ball luck as England win despite Pakistan scare

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 12:28:20 GMT

England lose two wickets in first over but take series 3-0

Root, reprieved on 23, finishes with unbeaten 62

It was a run chase that began in alarming fashion for England as Mohammad Abbas hitched up his strides, glided in to the crease and sent Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay trudging back to the pavilion at either end of a magical first over.

Pakistan’s players suddenly believed, their supporters inside Edgbaston likewise. After Razaullah’s firework display with the bat the previous evening, it was hard not to wonder whether their penchant for the unexpected – that seemingly innate ability to flip the script from nowhere – was rearing its head once more.

But, albeit with a couple more heart-in-mouth moments, England had enough about them to reel in their target of 130 to complete an eight-wicket victory and their first series clean sweep for two years. Joe Root, 62 not out, and Jordan Cox unbeaten on 59, finished things off by 1.07pm.

“We had a little bit of pushback yesterday, which was, in a strange way, quite a good thing for the group,” said Root, in a nod to Razaullah’s incendiary 81. “But for us to come through it and be so convincing in the way that we’ve finished the series off, and throughout the whole three games really, has been really pleasing.”

Root had walked out at the end of the first over with the scorecard in disarray at two for two. Abbas had nicked off Duckett first ball to continue a rather sorry Test match for England’s opener, and then pinned Gay lbw for a duck that dented some of the credit built up by the left-hander’s 60 in the first innings.

Alongside Cox, whose start to Test cricket has been an assured one, Root immediately got down to business, batting on leg stump in an attempt to minimise the threat of lbw, and the scorecard soon started to tick over. On a pitch with no demons by this stage, all it needed was a couple of calm heads.

Razaullah was unable to roll over his personal momentum after being handed the new ball – an early hand injury did not help – while no frontline spinner meant Abbas, bowling with the wicketkeeper stood up, was the only way that Babar Azam could make things claustrophobic out in the middle. There were two more chances created along the way and neither came to fruition.

The first came when Root was on 20 and an expansive cover-drive cannoned into his leg-stump. Mohammad Ali was haring off in celebration, only to turn around and see the umpire’s arm outstretched for a front foot no-ball, his 17th such offence in this series, but the first to rob him of a wicket.

England would have been 36 for three and Root’s response was emphatic, drilling Ali through the covers for four. Abbas then saw an edge off Root’s bat fly between first and second slip on 34 without either man going for it – much to his disgust.

The pressure eased, as this thinned-out, day-four crowd essentially watched a 90-minute net, a couple of tidy half-centuries, and the winning runs coming off a mis-field. Root has resumed the England captaincy with a pretty comfortable 3-0 series victory while knowing that tougher challenges are to come.

Sign up to The Spin

after newsletter promotion

For Pakistan it was a chance to finally breathe after a helter-skelter tour that saw seven players sent home at 2-0 down, a head coach removed, and a cast of new faces for this third Test. For Razaullah, just 21, it may be the start of something special, even if it was not enough to secure the player of the match award.

That instead went to Dan Lawrence, who made 65 with the bat, picked up a couple of wickets with his slightly eccentric off-spin, and two catches that included a one-handed blinder to remove Shan Masood, Pakistan’s top-scorer in their resurgent second innings. Lawrence made three half-centuries in the series and has seven in his career to date. The key now is to bank that first hundred.

“If I keep playing the way that I am, I’m sure that three figures will come,” said Lawrence, whose frustration at getting out on day two was palpable. “I’m desperate to get multiple hundreds for England. Contributing in all three games has really helped my confidence. Hopefully I get the nod to carry on playing.”

With 21 wickets at just shy of nine runs apiece, Ollie Robinson was England’s player of the series. For Pakistan it was Abbas, another master of the wobble seam. The 36-year-old probed to the very end, an island of calm in what at times has been a maelstrom of a tour for the visitors.

Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 12:00:34 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves

Earlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize on Instagram. In a sponsored ad, Schuman, who has more than 500,000 Instagram followers, is holding up a vial of GLP-1 drugs, advertising the telehealth company Gala. There was just one problem: Schuman had never heard of Gala and had nothing to do with the ad.

The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, and TikTok posts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.

“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.

Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.

As generative AI makes it easier to create text, code and media, it has also supercharged the creation of deepfakes, the synthetic photos and videos that can be nearly indistinguishable from reality. Influencers are some of the easiest people to impersonate due to the sheer amount of videos and images AI can learn from. The vulnerability represents a new workplace threat: influencers aren’t just competing for brand deals with other creators, but also fighting to preserve the credibility of their own likeness – the very asset that generates their income.

“Their brand is their business,” said Alice Marwick, the director of research at the Data & Society Research Institute, who published a recent paper on the rise of AI impersonation scams. “If their brand takes a hit, so does everything in their business life.”

On social media, impersonation schemes run a large spectrum, from deepfaked Elon Musk promoting a fraudulent cryptocurrency, to brands quietly scraping an influencer’s image to manufacture ads. Global consumers may have lost as much as $3.7bn due to deepfake scams in 2026, according to an investigation from the VPN-maker Surfshark’s research team. The investigation found that social media impersonations on social media accounted for about half of all losses.

Celebrities and influencers are often the easiest to impersonate because they “have hundreds of hours of footage and thousands of pictures of them online. So you can feed that into a model and produce a fairly convincing deepfake,” said Marwick. Taylor Swift, Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Gwyneth Paltrow and Tom Hanks have all been deepfaked by AI to promote various products online.

But big celebrities aren’t alone. On Instagram, beauty influencer Arielle Lorre was deepfaked to promote a skincare brand. Fashion creator Jessi Caparella discovered altered images of herself on Pinterest redirecting traffic to affiliate clothing links. And deepfaked videos of OnlyFans creator Elaina St James were used to trick fans into sending money to fraudulent accounts. While the financial impact of these impersonation schemes is hard to pinpoint, creators say that deepfakes dilute their value, cost them the trust of their followers, and can be time-consuming to fight: even when one deepfake post is reported and removed, another one pops up in its place.

With AI, “impersonation is much easier and much more convincing … [so] scams can be operated at a much larger scale,” said Marwick. “It’s often really believable. And with every new frontier model, they get better and better.”

One reason for the rise of deepfakes may be a growing use of AI-generated marketing content in general. AI-generated or “virtual” influencers accounted for $1.37bn, or about 4% of all brand spending in 2026, according to research from marketing consultancy Digital Applied. Virtual influencers may not have the same authenticity as real people, but they are much cheaper, always available, and infinitely customizable, which makes them attractive for some brand campaigns.

While the ad industry has always blurred the line between real and fake with airbrushing, CGI and other digital editing tools, the rise of AI has allowed brands to generate content from nothing with minimal production costs. And for some brands, that means crossing the line into deepfakes.

Influencers are doing whatever they can to fight the issue. Molly Tranchin, a fashion influencer known as FashionVeggie with more than 500,000 followers on Instagram, recently filed a lawsuit against the underwear brand Eby. According to the lawsuit, Tranchin had a contract to create three marketing videos for Eby in exchange for a fee. Eby was entitled to one round of “reasonable edits” for Tranchin to revise. The lawsuit claims that instead of posting the videos Tranchin submitted – in which she posed “modestly covering her chest and breasts with her arms” – the brand instead posted a deepfake video of Tranchin in a different pose, “exposing her breasts and nipples through one of Eby’s sheer bras”.

Tranchin has since dropped the lawsuit over a lack of jurisdiction and plans to refile it in a different court, according to court documents filed last month.

Eby spokesperson Clara Spahr said the company couldn’t comment on the pending litigation but will address the claims through the legal process.

Tranchin, whose lawsuit is ongoing, has the benefit of knowing exactly who to hold accountable for the deepfakes. Other creators are not as lucky.

When Schuman discovered the deepfaked ads using her likeness, she and her manager immediately reported them to Meta. She said many of her followers, who brought these ads to her attention, also reported them. But it took weeks of badgering before Meta removed the GLP-1 ad. The makeup ad still remains in circulation on Instagram, despite many attempts from Schuman to get it taken down.

Both Meta and TikTok explicitly prohibit using artificial intelligence or digital manipulation to replicate a person’s identity. But the reality is that these platforms’ personalization algorithms may inadvertently grease the wheels for these schemes.

Meta, for example, allows advertisers to use hyper-targeted audience slicing, meaning bad actors can quietly launch fraudulent ads, create new accounts if one gets flagged, and scale their reach rapidly. In response to complaints about rampant scams on its platforms, Meta introduced new tools this year, including stronger advertiser verification policies and an AI detection tool to prevent “celeb-bait”, or the impersonation of celebrities. But experts say these tools do not go far enough, and that the company lacks incentive to clean up its own ad ecosystem. Meta did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

“The reality is that platforms make a lot of money off scams,” Marwick said.

Meta made about $16bn from ads promoting scams or banned goods, accounting for about 10% of its revenue in 2024, according to a 2025 investigation from Reuters. That investigation also quoted an internal presentation from Meta’s safety team, which estimated that its platforms were “involved in a third of all successful scams in the US”.

Not only do deepfakes hurt brand deals for individual influencers, but they also challenge the entire influencer marketing ecosystem. They disrupt the already delicate premise that a real person trusts a product or brand, and therefore their followers should do the same.

Schuman said she is deciding whether or not she needs to retain legal counsel to help her fight off the deepfakes as they keep popping up. Besides reporting the offending posts and threatening legal action, influencers don’t have much recourse.

“That’s money and time lost,” Schuman said about hiring a lawyer. But the alternative is a hit to her reputation. “So it’s a lose-lose from all ways of looking at it.”

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 12:00:34 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

These days, there’s a bewildering array of mature cheddar out there, but the good stuff can be hard to find. Which blocks have that tangy farmhouse flavour and which are better left on the supermarket shelf?

The best vegan cheese, tasted and rated

As a West Country lad from the Somerset borders, I believe cheddar should come from Cheddar. The village boasts England’s largest limestone gorge, at three miles long and almost 400ft deep, and the stable low temperatures, high humidity and unique microbiome of its caves are perfect for maturing this famous cheese.

But good cheddar can be hard to find, not least because it’s a British kitchen staple that’s often sold as a loss-leader and produced by industrial creameries. The resulting generic block of cheese is pleasant enough, but if you want something with a complex flavour profile, crunchy calcium lactate crystals and a creamy texture, you’re going to have to put in some legwork.

Today’s test group are all labelled mature and mostly carry a strength rating of four, though I’ve awarded my own strength scoring as they vary greatly and there’s a huge range in quality, texture and flavour. Every big supermarket tends to have a wall of different cheddars, so try as many as you can to find your fit.

★★★☆☆

A large, utilitarian block of creamy cheddar made at Taw Valley Creamery in Devon. Rich and sharp, with a clear, lactic-sour twang. Full of umami, with a buttery texture and some crystallisation. Strength rating of four.

★★★☆☆

A protected designation of origin cheese made in Somerset using traditional methods and British milk. Produced by Barber’s dairy, the oldest cheddar maker in the world, this wonderfully savoury cheese is rich and nutty with a crumbly yet creamy texture. Strength: four.

★★★★☆

A small but punchy and crystalline block of mature cheddar made by Godminster in Somerset. There’s a real depth of flavour and sweet umami notes, and it’s also tangy and crunchy with calcium crystals. Strength rating five, and my best splurge.

★★★☆☆

A creamy block that’s sharp and lively on the nose, with a pungent undertone and very creamy mouthfeel. Good flavour development, too – all buttery, savoury and umami-rich. Lives up to its strength rating of four.

★★★☆☆

A classic, crumbly yet buttery block studded with calcium crystals, and also made by Barber’s. Matured for up to 12 months, this has an intensely flavoured, tangy, salty and cow-y flavour. Strength: four.

★★☆☆☆

A large, family-friendly, sweet and creamy block of Cornish cheddar made by Davidstow Creamery. Mild but still flavourful, with lactic sweetness and a little tang. Strength: two.

★★☆☆☆

A creamy block from Britain’s largest cheese factory. Made with 100% Cornish milk and matured for at least 12 months. Not too strong (strength three) with a milky, lactic sharpness and a rounded sweetness. Some crystallisation.

★★☆☆☆

A family-friendly, creamy and smooth Cornish cheddar made by Davidstow Creamery with West Country milk. Sweet, acidic, grassy and with a smooth, buttery texture. Strength: three.

★☆☆☆☆

A sweet, slightly rubbery cheddar made with British milk. It has a slightly chemical aroma (packaging leakage, perhaps?), and is very creamy, more like a younger cheddar, but with a lactic sweet milk and hay umaminess. Strength: three.

★☆☆☆☆

A small block of creamy cheddar with little provenance other than that it’s made at an “award-winning” British creamery, albeit without naming it. A touch sour, very buttery and soft. Strength: three.

From socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 12:00:33 GMT

Those who have encountered the interim president paint her in starkly different ways, but all agree she is likely to remain in power

It was April 2002 and Delcy Rodríguez was a woman on a mission.

Venezuela’s then president, Hugo Chávez, had been temporarily toppled by a bungled coup and Rodríguez, a junior diplomat who had been studying at Birkbeck, University of London, decided to act.

Rodríguez, then 32, set about trying to convince two reporters from the BBC programme Newsnight to accompany her to Venezuela’s capital to tell the world about what had happened.

“She desperately wanted to get the story of Chávez and the coup out there on a big platform,” says one of those journalists, Meirion Jones, who engaged Rodríguez as their fixer and flew to Caracas with her.

As the trio travelled around the South American city trying to land an interview with Chávez – who by then had reclaimed the presidency after being briefly detained – Jones had no inkling that his Venezuelan field producer and interpreter might one day become president herself.

“She looked like she was still a student really … it was just impossible to imagine at that point that she would become president of Venezuela,” Jones says.

Yet that is precisely what Rodríguez, now 57, has become, albeit in extraordinary circumstances precipitated by Donald Trump’s decision to abduct Chávez’s authoritarian heir, Nicolás Maduro.

When US special forces snatched the unpopular Maduro on 3 January this year, he was widely expected to be replaced with María Corina Machado, the Nobel-winning opposition leader whose movement beat him in the stolen 2024 election.

Instead, Trump discarded Machado and backed Maduro’s vice-president, Rodríguez, who became Venezuela’s interim leader two days after the downfall of her boss.

Eight months later, Rodríguez is still in power – despite leading a country many now consider a US protectorate – and looks likely to remain there for the foreseeable future, with scant sign of fresh presidential elections being called.

“We are very happy with the president-elect that we have right now,” Trump said of the un-elected Rodríguez after announcing what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.

Imdat Oner, a former Turkish diplomat in Caracas, believes the deal has strengthened Rodríguez and dealt a big blow to those hoping for democratic change. “Delcy is winning … I see Delcy Rodríguez staying in the presidency for at least four or five more years,” he says.

The Delcy Rodríguez that Jones flew with to Caracas more than two decades ago was a well-connected but politically insignificant figure known fundamentally because of her father.

Jorge Antonio Rodríguez was a Marxist activist who died in police custody in 1976, when his daughter was seven, reputedly after being tortured while detained over the kidnapping of a US businessman.

“All the Chavistas knew who her father had been – but they didn’t really know who she was,” says Jones, who is now a freelance investigative journalist. “[But during our time in Caracas] she’d made herself known to all these people … and I think by the end of the trip she was starting to think: ‘Maybe there is an opening for me in politics in Venezuela.’”

Soon after, Rodríguez returned to Venezuela, landing jobs with its state oil company, PDVSA, and foreign ministry. By 2006, she had become Chávez’s chief of staff, although she fell out of favour after clashing with Venezuela’s then ambassador to Russia during a visit to Moscow.

That row interrupted Rodríguez’s rise but she was rehabilitated by Maduro when he became president after Chávez’s 2013 death. In the years that followed, as her country nosedived into hunger and authoritarianism, Rodríguez enjoyed a rapid ascent.

She served as foreign minister before taking charge of the country’s economy as petroleum minister, finance minister and Maduro’s vice-president. Her brother, a psychiatrist turned politician, Jorge Rodríguez, established himself as the head of the national assembly.

After Maduro’s capture, the siblings formed a powerful triumvirate, alongside the feared interior minister, Diosdado Cabello.

“Delcy is not Delcy. Delcy’s Delcy and her brother. They do everything in tandem … they don’t do anything without each other’s approval or consent,” says Andrés Izarra, Chávez’s communication minister who went into exile after falling out with Maduro.

Those who have encountered Rodríguez during her unlikely 25-year rise, from being a leftwing student in the UK to the pinnacle of power in Venezuela, paint her in dramatically different ways.

Admirers describe a pragmatic, witty and intelligent workaholic who they credit with helping Venezuela escape years of hyperinflation and believe can fulfil promises to revive the country’s decaying oil industry and economy.

“Venezuela under Delcy is going to have the best possible kind of technocratic care – and that’s what is needed right now … she’s going to get that oil moving,” says Greg Palast, the other journalist who flew to Caracas with Rodríguez for the BBC in 2002.

Palast believes Venezuela is “way better off” under Rodríguez than the incompetent Maduro, calling her a clever strategist who plays politics “on a four-dimensional chessboard”.

Detractors paint Rodríguez as a belligerent, power-hungry chameleon whose political leanings can change on a dime and who, as a key member of Maduro’s regime, was herself responsible for Venezuela’s slide into poverty and dictatorship.

“They’re evil, they are crazy and they are smart … they’re evil geniuses,” a prominent opposition politician, who asked not to be named, says of the Rodríguez siblings.

Izarra says his former friend is “very machiavellian” and has a taste for luxury.

Tom Shannon, a retired US diplomat who has worked with Venezuela since the 1990s, describes the multilingual Rodríguez as a “very smart, very articulate, very determined” and profoundly ideological person.

Shannon recalls being “intercepted” by Rodríguez – then foreign minister – after flying to Caracas to meet Maduro during Barack Obama’s second term.

Their conversation was wide-ranging. “But I remember very distinctly, at one point I raised the issue of human rights – our interest in especially seeing the release of certain people from prison,” Shannon says.

“She … turned to me, with a look almost of contempt, not for me, but for the subject I was raising and she said: ‘You might not know my story, but my father was a revolutionary member of an armed revolutionary movement in Venezuela who was arrested [and] tortured during interrogation and killed by the Venezuelan security services when I was a girl.’

“And she said: ‘This interrogation and the killing of my father took place during a time when, from your point of view, Venezuela was a democratic country governed by the rule of law. But I can tell you, the security services weren’t.”

Shannon adds: “It was very striking … it was evident to me that she saw her father as kind of a revolutionary north star, kind of a martyr point of reference – and I believe that’s still the case.”

He thinks Rodríguez’s objective in her new partnership with Washington is political survival “and to make sure that a revanchist, conservative, elitist, democratic opposition does not return to power”.

Speaking in the White House, Trump heaped praise on his unlikely Venezuelan partner. “Delcy is doing a very, very good job – very highly respected,” he told reporters.

Trump claimed Venezuela had only just escaped a “very nasty” regime and was not ready for elections. “You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.

Such comments will have been music to Rodríguez’s ears. “Delcy wants to survive,” says Oner. “And she knows that if she gives enough to the Trump administration, the Trump administration will allow her to stay in power.”

Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 12:00:33 GMT

Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe

I think I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takes like men shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story.

Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrous announcement on Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters.

Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman.

“That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino on Thursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Maybe – it doesn’t mean you’re going home with her, but it keeps you interested. It keeps you intrigued and wanting more. That’s what this is about.”

Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you to look up the story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing.

But back to this definitely-not-a-bribe $5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand man Elon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember the Doge dividends floated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in a Truth Social post last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. However, it has been estimated by the Joint Economic Committee – Minority that the average American family will pay more than $2,500 in tariff costs this year.

I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. But let’s just play along for a minute and pretend that Trump isn’t a fabulist. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. Isn’t it a bit reckless to be giving all this money away, a total that exceeds $1tn, when the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn for the first time? As Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement, that debt “doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers”, it is shouldered by everyone. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.”

Don’t worry about all that, says the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News on Thursday. The Trump administration is going to earn that money from various moneymaking endeavours like the Trump Platinum Card, which allows wealthy people to pay up to $5m to extend their US visas. JD Vance, meanwhile, has suggested that the money might come from US tariff revenues, even though economists have pointed out the $125bn in tariff revenues wouldn’t come close to covering the costs.

The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters. When the ABC reporter Rachel Scott asked him about the rationale behind the $5,000 checks on Thursday night, he said it was a reward to Americans for putting up with Joe Biden. After Scott tried to ask a follow-up question, Trump lunged at her and said: “Your network … you’re the worst.” Which is very on-brand for the president. He can’t seem to handle being asked tough questions by anyone, but gets particularly nasty when those questions are posed by a woman.

While Trump doesn’t want to get into the details of his dividend, the proposal reflects how the president is looking at some very unconventional ways to sway the midterms. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has already gutted election security programs and attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him.

A ProPublica analysis found almost 200 women died after an ectopic pregnancy from 2020 to 2025. That’s compared to about 100 in the previous six years. To nobody’s surprise, mortality is worse in states with strict abortion bans. “While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies,” ProPublica notes.

Sudan’s civil war, which started in 2023, has created the world’s worst displacement crisis. Now, many of the women who fled to Egypt are being sexually exploited.

The Pentagon published a guidance document on 2 September outlining a new mandatory testosterone screening process to create a “High-T military”. However, the very next day it was withdrawn from the public domain for reasons that remain unclear. Maybe someone in the Pentagon came to their senses.

Naza, a highly-feted new film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, reveals the secret systems used in mass killings of civilians in Gaza. “Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,” the Guardian writes. “[O]ne said their mission was to ‘thwart peace’.”

The short answer is because they are misogynists who cynically weaponize women’s rights to advance their agenda. But do read Zoe Williams, who has a longer and more eloquent answer, following on from the attack on a female protester at the Reform UK conference.

They seem to think showing photos of a buff podcaster in his underwear demonstrates that the left are scary “radicals”.

Phoebe Bridgers’ unshaven legs at her Venice film festival debut sparked a flurry of headlines. But, says Leah Harper, Bridgers’ “au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations”.

Bonino got involved in politics after she had an abortion (then illegal) at age 26 and said she decided that “never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation”. She handed herself in to the police as an act of protest, leading a campaign to eventually legalize abortion in 1978.

Diana famously wore the fitted black dress on the same night that Charles admitted to his infidelity on TV in 1994. It will be auctioned off in December.

Jamaican delegation defends legal route of petition to King Charles for slavery reparations

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 11:00:34 GMT

Petition to king, who remains Jamaica’s head of state, is formally lodged in landmark visit to UK by officials

A palpable surge of emotion swept through Brixton’s New Park Road Baptist church as the packed congregation rose to sing Bob Marley’s Redemption Song.

The service on Sunday marked the anniversary of the 1781 Zong massacre, when more than 100 enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so the ship’s owners could claim insurance for “lost cargo”.

And the song – a lament for the horrors of transatlantic slavery and a tribute to the resilience of those who fought for freedom – set the tone for a landmark visit to the UK by Jamaican officials to petition King Charles over reparations for slavery.

The petition, backed by leaders of other Caribbean nations, asks the monarch to request legal advice from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.

It asks Charles, who is still Jamaica’s head of state, to seek guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.

Led by the culture minister, Olivia Grange, the Jamaican delegation included lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparations.

The delegation met diaspora communities, UK politicians, church leaders and institutions – including the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts.

Grange also held talks with the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, though sources say these were not focused on reparations.

Jamaica’s petition has ignited a fierce debate about the legality of transatlantic slavery and political implications. The former privy council member Lord Sumption dismissed the legal strategy as “nonsense” and argued that the issue was “not a question of law at all” but one of morals and politics. Jamaican experts have defended the legality of the petition.

Speaking at a briefing for UK parliamentarians, Edward Fitzgerald KC insisted Jamaica was acting in accordance with a little‑used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833 which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts.

Harj Narulla, a member of the UK team of counsels, told the Guardian it was an “obvious jurisdictional route”.

“It was quite clear you can’t do a judicial review, for example, of some government decision … The issue is with the state itself, with the United Kingdom, which is the state responsible for slavery in Jamaica,” he said.

Ulele Burnham, another member of the UK legal team, added: “The petition argues that the atrocities, the forced uprooting, the violent subjugation for profit was of course immoral, everyone knows that. But the petition’s very focus is to show that it was also clearly inconsistent with the law of the time. Non-Europeans did not suddenly become human when slavery ended. They always were. And even in those days, humans had some rights in English and international law.”

In Jamaica, though the pursuit of reparations is supported by the two main parties, members of the opposition People’s National party raised concerns that the delegation had not managed to secure a meeting with the king. Grange said a meeting with Charles “was not part of the plan”.

“Before we came to London, we had consulted with both the Palace and the privy council to confirm the correct legal process for filing the petition. Both confirmed the correct process was to file it by post and email, which is what we did,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro‑Addy, the chair of the all‑party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said Jamaica was well within its rights to petition the monarch. “Due to colonialism, which obviously initially had its root in enslavement, there are certain responsibilities that [the UK] has. We don’t get the privilege of still having Jamaica as part of the realm … without them also in turn having the right to petition King Charles. They are enacting their rights under English law and they have the right to ask those questions,” she said.

In December 2024, Jamaica’s government tabled a bill in parliament to remove the king as the country’s head of state. The bill has not progressed to becoming a law.

Pointing to recent global momentum – including 123 nations voting for a UN resolution describing chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity – Ribeiro‑Addy said it was time for Britain to confront its past and the decisions that continue to shape the present.

She described headlines quoting huge reparation figures (which were not mentioned in the Jamaican petition) as a distraction. “What seems to happen a lot when we talk about reparations is people want to distract people with figures,” she said. “They divorce themselves from the reality of what we are talking about. No one is saying that reparative justice will never include any sort of payment. But that is never the starting point. And we have to remember that this country refuses to even apologise. This country refuses to do the things that it can do, which don’t cost any money at all.

“The enslavement of peoples of African descent … meant that anybody who was not white was considered less than … almost being classified as not quite human. And that is a serious issue. If we are ever going to challenge racism properly, we have to get down to its very root.”

As the delegation lodged the petition on Monday, a spokesperson for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.

Ribeiro‑Addy said it would be an insult to African and Caribbean countries if Britain refuses to discuss reparations at the upcoming Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua, which the king is scheduled to attend.

“We’re meant to no longer be a group of countries under an empire. We were meant to be a group of countries with a shared history and who are treated as equals,” she said. “The idea that all of the countries bar one want to have a discussion and so the discussion is stopped has to be wrong … if we do things like that, I think we will soon see the crumbling of the Commonwealth. And that would be a huge shame.”

‘I said, if you want to fire me, just fire me. And so he did’: my showdown with Donald Trump

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 11:00:32 GMT

What’s it like to be shown the door by the US president? A former national security adviser, an Apprentice contestant and more share their stories

Plus: The truth about my 11 days in the White House, by Anthony Scaramucci

Gene Folkes, 62, based in Manhattan, was a contestant on season 10 of The Apprentice, which aired in 2010. A former air force recruiter until 1991, he retrained as an investment banker, then launched his own business before appearing on the reality show. He was fired by Trump in episode 5. He now runs the technology consulting firm OshunX and hosts a podcast, Folkes Unfettered.

I didn’t audition to be on The Apprentice. I received the call out of the blue: “Would you be interested in doing this show?” I didn’t know a lot about it. However, like any young business person, you look for people who you consider titans. There’s this mythology around Trump. He was one of the people I wanted to emulate.

The first morning, wardrobe comes into your room at 3.30am. You meet the other contestants for the first time, then within an hour you’re on your first task. You learn really quickly that you’re playing a game and the rules can change at any moment.

The first time we met, Trump was outside his building on Wall Street. He is an imposing figure. When he walks into a place he owns the room and there’s not a lot of air for anyone else to breathe. I thought, “OK, he’s presenting as exactly who I believed him to be.” There was a sense of admiration and aspiration. It was only when you dug deeper that you realised the emperor had no clothes.

In the corporate world, there are certain things you just don’t do without consequences. And they were so natural for him. The first time we met him in the boardroom, Trump asked us if we thought the women were attractive. He would make these innuendoes – things that were sort of hard to pin down – but you felt kind of icky afterwards.

The first round was split men v women. I put myself forward to be the project manager for the men’s team. Task one was to design a modern office space. We won that task, and my prize was a one-on-one with Trump. His desk in Trump Tower was rather small and somewhat messy. Initially, I felt he knows how to connect with people. There was charisma, there was charm; he evokes a certain amount of confidence. You can really get drawn into all things Donald, but as I sat back and started really listening to him, I thought, “Oh, I don’t think this is the person that I have tried to model myself after.”

I didn’t feel empathy from him: I was more product than person. I think about it a lot now, because I believe that anyone who wants to lead a nation has to have a certain amount of empathy. If you don’t, then how can you relate to someone who’s a single mom or dad who’s struggling to put food on the table?

A producer told me the series was mine to lose. The week I got fired, I didn’t feel like it was coming. We had to put on a fashion show for Rockport. When you’re an air force recruiter, like I had been, all you do is publicly speak, so my project manager selected me to be master of ceremonies. I wear glasses. In that episode I decided to wear my contacts. They weren’t bifocals, and I remember saying, “I need to go back and get my glasses.” We never got to it. We got on to the test and I couldn’t read a freaking thing on the script.

When we went to the boardroom and we lost, they brought in three of us. Trump really took me off guard. The narrative shifted from, “Hey, I couldn’t see, and I wasn’t going to admit that I couldn’t see, because I didn’t want to start making excuses”, to one where I became illiterate: I couldn’t read; I couldn’t speak. It was very coded language that I was familiar with. It dawned on me: oh my God, he is framing me as a dumb person of colour. I’m sitting here with a degree in finance and he’s talking to me like I’m a moron. At that point I pushed back and said, “No one gets to talk about my speaking abilities. I don’t know what the bleep you’re talking about, but that’s not me.”

His face was red. He was visibly angry. One of the things he did when pushed back on was escalate. It was like he didn’t hear anything you said. He was animated but in a controlled way. He was playing to camera. He knew the audience was salivating for his line.

I finally said, “You know what? If you want to fire me, just fire me.” And so he did.

I did not feel anger. I felt relief. At that point you realise you’re playing in a system that’s rigged. And the person in power controls the narrative, controls the outcome. This was a game, but my real-life consequences were: what is my life going to look like after the programme, for my relationships, business dealings, opportunities?

When I watched the series, I got on the phone with NBC to say, “Holy crap, that’s where you guys want to go with that? That I was uneducated, ignorant?” There was no sense of empathy or compassion from the network or him.

Afterwards I did not want to leave the house. I could not get out of bed some mornings. I really became almost a recluse for three months. It took me years to get comfortable talking about it. I was depressed.

When I got a hold of myself, I began to do what I normally do: I started fighting. I wrote a blog where I gave my opinion on Trump considering running for the presidency. NBC asked me to take it down, which I refused to do.

I remember someone saying to me, “You’re hurting the Trump brand, you’re hurting the NBC brand and you’re hurting the Apprentice brand”, and I remember saying, “But you’re hurting the Gene Folkes brand, and I didn’t sign off for this crap.”

In the 15 years since I was on The Apprentice, media, entertainment, politics and news have started converging. Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology.

When I served in the military, there were certain leaders you would follow to death. You knew they loved and cared about you. They were able to manage their emotions. They realised that the goal of the team outweighed their individual personality. Trump is the opposite. He’s all personality; there is no team.

Good leaders want to be challenged. And what I learned from The Apprentice, and what I’m seeing now in politics, is consistent: don’t challenge him.

As told to Kate Lloyd

NBC declined to comment.

John Bolton, 77, based in Washington DC, is an attorney and former ambassador to the United Nations who was national security adviser from 2018 until 2019, under Trump. His exit from government was announced by the president over Twitter on 10 September 2019: “I informed John Bolton last night that his services are no longer needed at the White House. I disagreed strongly with many of his suggestions, as did others in the administration, and therefore I asked John for his resignation, which was given to me this morning.” Bolton says things played out differently.

For me, there was no one straw that broke the camel’s back, and I think that’s true in many resignation situations. It was an accumulation of factors. I had had a resignation letter drafted, and kept one copy in my desk drawer in the office and one copy at home, knowing I could print it out whenever I needed to.

It was basically a one-sentence resignation, which was the way I wanted to do it. And it finally came to that in September 2019.

The last conversation really was on 9 September. He was complaining about this and complaining about that, having heard, obviously from people inside the administration, of something I had done that they didn’t like. And I said to him, “Well, look, if you feel that way, I’ll resign.” And he was leaving the Oval Office to go and give a speech. [Trump told Bolton they would talk about his resignation offer the following morning.]

I went back to my office and I just thought, I am going to resign; I’m not going to talk to him. So I did a few other things that evening and then I went home, and came in early the next morning. There were a couple of meetings I wanted to finish up, particularly the freeing up of the security assistance to Ukraine. I got that done and I gave the letter to my secretary and said, “I’m going home. I’ll call you when I’m there.” I wanted to get out of the blast zone. So I told her to hand it to Trump’s secretary and then be prepared that she would probably be leaving soon thereafter.

The only mistake I made was that I should have tweeted right then that I had resigned, because when Trump saw it he went through the roof. I did get one tweet out saying I had resigned, and then they closed my Twitter account. I had to fight later to get it back.

I believe in pre-emptive strikes, and I had failed to follow my own advice. I should have fired first, but I was pursuing old-fashioned norms.

I tell this story in my book: before the Singapore meeting with Kim Jong-un, the first in the series on the North Korean nuclear programme, there was a chance that Trump was going to cancel, which I thought was exactly the right thing to do. I thought the whole thing was going to be a terrible waste of time. He was going off to a dinner, I think, with state governors, and as he was leaving, I said, “We can send out something saying we’re not coming if you want to do that.” And he said, “Let me think about it.” He said, “When I was dating, I always liked to be the one to break up with the girl. I never wanted the girl to break up with me.”

I didn’t keep that much stuff in the White House office. A lot of things – pre-government files of clippings and things – I thought my secretary would be able to walk out with because they clearly weren’t government property. But we had to fight over that, too. There were several other of my staff who were also let go within 24, 48 hours. Some of their stuff was taken as well.

I don’t think I get called naive very often. I thought I knew what I was getting into, largely because I thought that the weight of the decisions Trump would have to make in the national security area, the gravity of the responsibility, would discipline him. It turned out I was completely wrong about that. Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did in my 17 months was struggle to keep the train on the track. Things like long-range planning? Forget it. By and large, there just wasn’t time to do it.

I firmly believed that Trump would be no different from his predecessors. And, to me, it just exemplifies that it really is an aberration in American politics – I’d say almost in world history – to have somebody who performs the way he does. People would just ignore the [national security council policymaking] process and go directly to Trump. It was the phenomenon of the last person in the room gets his attention.

There was this occasion when the Iranians shot down an American drone over the Persian Gulf, in what we believed was international airspace. We sized up what we were going to do, came up with retaliation, the president ordered it, then literally as planes were in the air, he changed his mind. So that leads people to say, why are we doing this? Why do we even bother?

Look, everybody’s got an ego. Politicians notoriously have bigger egos than most. But I’ve never seen a politician where the ego wasn’t subsumed to at least some extent by bigger considerations. With him, it’s not subsumed by anything. That was part of the mistake I made. I just had never seen a personality like that before.

As told to Julian Borger

Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, 45, lives in Maryland. A Democrat, she was appointed to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), an independent agency of the US government, by Donald Trump in 2018. The FTC’s work includes fighting illegal business practices, safeguarding online privacy and promoting competition to keep prices down for consumers. Slaughter was fired last year and fought a protracted legal battle, arguing that Trump did not have the right to remove an agency commissioner without cause. This culminated in the supreme court case Trump v Slaughter, which decided in favour of the president’s at-will removal power, overturning a 91-year-old precedent.

It was an incredible privilege and honour to work for the FTC. In the time I was there we blocked the largest grocery store merger in history, which would have raised grocery prices even further. We sued big tech platforms for violating children’s privacy, for subscription traps that charged people more money than they should have been paying. We investigated things like the price of insulin and the role of pharmacy benefit managers in keeping drug prices unnaturally high.

Right after the inauguration in January 2025, the president removed commissioners at a different independent board, the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board. But he didn’t fire me or my colleague, commissioner Alvaro Bedoya. We went through a period from mid-January through mid-March thinking, is he going to fire us today? He didn’t fire us today. Does that mean he’s not going to fire us? We don’t know.

We decided early on that we couldn’t and wouldn’t operate in a way that was inconsistent with our oaths of office or our principles in order to avoid getting fired. We were just going to do the jobs we had as well as we could, and we couldn’t control how the president was going to react.

On 18 March 2025, I worked a full day in the office then went to our local public elementary school, where I was volunteering in the evenings with the drama club production of Beauty and the Beast. I was the parent lead for this production. But, much more importantly, my second kid was playing Belle. She was in fifth grade. This was the culmination of all of her hopes and dreams in her 10-year-old life.

I was sitting outside the dusty elementary school gym, children were running around pretending to be plates and spoons, inviting my daughter to come be their guest, and I checked my work phone and I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. I can’t remember what it was titled – “Message from the president” or something like that.

I thought, well, that can’t be good. I opened it, and it was a very long email, purportedly on behalf of the president, clearly not written by the president – many legal citations, no words in caps – the culmination of which was, your continued service on the FTC is inconsistent with my priorities, therefore you are terminated effective immediately.

I took a deep breath and said some expletives in my head. I looked at the other parent volunteers sitting next to me and said, “I think I might have just gotten fired. Is it OK if I step outside to deal with this?” They said, “No, go home, go take care of what you need to do.” I said, “Oh no, I am not leaving Beauty and the Beast.”

The rest of that evening is a blur in my mind. I talked to my husband, who was in California. I talked to my staff. I talked to a million reporters. We hastily organised a press conference that I participated in from the parking lot, holding a phone in front of my face, under the floodlights with a brick background behind me.

I didn’t want my daughter to hear about this from other parents or other kids. I pulled her aside after they got through the run-through and said, “I have to tell you something. It’s going to sound scary but we are going to be OK and I don’t want you to be worried about it.” She said, “OK, what?” I said, “I got fired this evening.”

I could see her little face well up. She said, “Are you going to have to stop working on the show?” I said, “No, I’m not going to let that happen”, and she said, “OK.” That was the key information she needed. You can try to take my job but you cannot take drama club from me.

Alvaro [who was also fired] and I knew pretty quickly that we wanted to challenge our dismissals in court, because if we failed to do so it would be like acceding to this blatant violation of the law and destruction of these institutions, but the timing and structure of doing that were all questions we had to sort through.

I was doing that until about midnight when my doorbell rang, which I thought was odd. I went to the door and there was a pizza delivery guy there. I said, “I didn’t order any pizza.” He showed me an order form with my name, my personal email address, my cellphone number, my home address. I said, “Well, I didn’t order it and I’m not gonna pay for it, so, sorry.”

I called my husband and I was, like, this weird thing happened. Isn’t that funny? He goes, “No, it is not funny. That’s a thing that online trolls do to people, especially people who the president doesn’t like, in order to scare them.” I didn’t like that I was home with my four kids in the middle of the night when this happened. I talked to Alvaro, who also got a pizza. His take was, thank God, I’m starving, I haven’t eaten all evening!

I don’t feel angry on my own behalf. It is very much not about me. I don’t feel any personal animus. I do feel a lot of anger on behalf of institutions of government, of public servants throughout the government. I have a lot of anger for those reasons.

Donald Trump doesn’t think about me at all. I don’t think he knew that he fired me; I don’t have any evidence he actually knew and was involved in it. The president cares a lot about a ballroom and gold plating the White House and building monuments to himself. I don’t think he’s thinking about conservative legal theory. I also don’t think he is thinking about the American people.

Last summer, in my interregnum period, I knew that I needed a project, so I signed up for the New York City marathon and ran it for charity. I had never run a marathon and I always thought it was impossible, and it felt like a metaphor for the professional experience I was going through. It was hard. It didn’t go as well as I had hoped or trained for, but I finished anyway. And that was also the metaphor for me: we do the hard things because they’re the right things to do, and that is the reward – even if it doesn’t turn out exactly the way you envision.

Barbara Res, 76, based in New Jersey, met Donald Trump in 1978, when she was working as an assistant superintendent for the contractor HRH, building the Grand Hyatt hotel in New York. Two years later, he hired her to lead construction on Trump Tower. She eventually became senior vice-president and executive vice-president of the Trump Organization. She quit after a final stint as a consultant, when the redevelopment of the Ambassador hotel site in Los Angeles fell apart amid a prolonged condemnation battle with the Los Angeles school district and a collapsing real-estate market. Res says a last‑minute change in leadership, made by Trump against her advice, undermined negotiations that she believed could have allowed the project to finish with a small profit. She has written two books about her experiences over those years. She retrained as a lawyer and is now semi-retired.

I worked for Donald for close to 18 years. I left on friendly terms. If I saw him at a function, we’d nod to each other. But in 2016 I wrote an op-ed in the New York Daily News about my experiences with him. He came out blazing guns against me at rallies and on Twitter. He released emails I had written to him five years earlier when I was looking for a job. A tabloid newspaper wrote that he had “got rid” of me and that I had begged him for a job. Both lies. His supporters tweeted things about me like “glad Trump fired her”. I wasn’t fired.

I’d impressed him when I was working for HRH. In meetings the project managers and superintendents would talk about different problems on the job, and the architect would often blame the contractor or the subcontractors. I’d say, “That’s bullshit.” He loved that.

At a meeting at his apartment, Donald asked me to be in charge of the construction of Trump Tower. I remember it was in a nice building on Fifth Avenue. Everything inside was white: the carpet, the upholstery, the walls, the ceiling. Donald went through a spiel about what he was building. I was to be the last word on site, he said. “You’ll be like a Donna Trump.” He offered me almost twice the salary I was getting.

I liked being there. Trump Tower was a big deal and I had the best crew in the world. There were times when Donald was actually like a human being. We used to go into his office and sit and talk. He’d tell jokes. He was pretty funny. Now, I’m not saying he was a nice guy. Not at all. Any time anyone really disagreed with him, he would yell at them. He always needed someone to blame. If he screamed at me in front of the team it didn’t matter, because they were all getting screamed at. If he’d screamed at me in front of an architect or an investor, I would have walked out the door.

When he wanted to do something that we thought was wrong or illegal, you couldn’t just say that. He couldn’t handle it. So we found ways of working around it – making him think that a substitute idea we’d come up with was his. I used to put him in a good mood by saying, “Hey Donald, did you see Ivana this morning? What an incredible outfit she’s wearing. She’s so gorgeous.” We were able to keep him somewhat under control. Nobody does that now.

I was offered a partnership elsewhere and left. Donald threw a massive party for me. He got me a Cartier bracelet, signed, “Towers of thanks, love Donald.” A few years later, I got back in touch with him for some advice and he hired me again, this time to be in charge of all construction, then construction and development, for the Trump Organization.

When I went back in 1987, he was surrounded by yes‑sayers. His book Trump: The Art of the Deal absolutely changed him in terms of his picture of himself. Even though he always said he was the smartest, now he thought he was a real big-time player. Everybody knew everything about him: how great he was, how brilliant he was.

The second time I left was around 1990, when I was running Trump’s big West Side project on the riverfront. Neighbourhood groups and some big-name opponents – including Christopher Reeve – were fighting it hard. And a friend of Donald’s came to him and said, “You’ve got to meet with these people, and you’ve got to make a deal with them.” He wanted to build 14m sq ft. He made a deal to build just 7.5m. In that deal, the opposition group put their person in charge of the project. They wanted a semi‑famous lawyer who worked in development and didn’t have construction experience. I quit primarily because they brought in this other person.

I told Donald I had to leave. My son has to have surgery, I said. The surgery was a big deal, but I wouldn’t quit over that. I told him it to soften the blow.

I stayed on as a consultant on two other projects. One of those was the Ambassador hotel. One of our partners was going under. He wanted to be in charge of everything. My assistant and I told Donald this would blow up the project, which it eventually did. Donald allowed him to take over against our advice. Afterwards, at a big meeting with the realtor and the partners, Donald came down on me. I told him, “I told you not to let this guy get involved.”

He started screaming. His face was contorting. That was the only time he’d ever done that in front of external people. I was enraged. I looked at him and I said, “You know, Donald, there are medicines that can help you control that.”

He got crazy about that.

After the people left, I went back up to Donald’s office and said, “Look, I can’t do this, I’m leaving.” And he said, “Why?” I didn’t say, “Because you made a fool out of me in front of the partners.” I said, “I’m looking after my son, I’m still having problems” – which was not true. “They’re just going to start school now, and I think I really should find something that won’t take me to California every week.”

Donald talked about running for president when I was at the Trump Organization. I thought at the time that he was a very good manager, given the right people, and that he could be a decent president. I didn’t know then that he had zero knowledge of government.

The Apprentice thing I’ve always thought of as a big joke. In my experience, he didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people. He didn’t want to look bad. If someone was going to get fired, he wasn’t doing it.

In my case, we had a woman who was working on some lobbying efforts we were doing. She had gotten pregnant. He found out and said, “Fire her.” I said, “You can’t, that’s against the law.” He got angry at me. “Fire her now!” I did it. It was terrible. I told her I would support her if she wanted to go after him because I knew that it was illegal to fire her.

Here’s another story I remember: when we needed an apartment manager at Trump Tower, he found a guy and hired him to work under me. He was terrible. We didn’t like him; he had a bad attitude. I told Donald, “We’re going to fire him.” He said, “Go ahead.” We fired him, and he went across the street to where Donald’s office was at the time. Donald was convinced by him. He told us, “Give him another chance.” And that happened twice. It took three times to fire this guy.

I think all the firing he has done in government shows a big shift in his attitude. But he has to blame someone. And how do you prove someone is at fault better than firing them? Even if they didn’t do anything wrong.

As told to Kate Lloyd

Tower of Lies: What My Eighteen Years of Working With Donald Trump Reveals About Him by Barbara Res (Graymalkin Media, £14.99) is available now.

The Trump Organization did not respond to a request to comment.
