Iran Finds Escalation Is Fruitful Path to Leverage in War With U. S.

The New York Times September 12, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Iran and its allies now hold sway over two key oil shipping routes, and Tehran is setting the stage for a diplomatic win that could enhance its stature.

By Yeganeh Torbati

The routes to export oil out of the Middle East are diminishing. The price of energy is soaring. And Iran’s neighbors could be about to endorse some measure of its authority over the Strait of Hormuz.

In the past week, Iran and its allies have used military escalation to upend any minimal sense of stability in the region, most dramatically in Yemen. That is shifting the momentum in Iran’s war with the United States to its advantage.

The shift may not be decisive. The Islamic republic remains under immense economic pressure, with the ongoing U. S. naval blockade of its southern ports and escalating rounds of sanctions cutting it off from the world.

And yet, a series of attacks in recent days by Iran and its allies have expanded the scope of the conflict. That, analysts said, may have given Tehran greater leverage, at least at this moment.

The Iranian-allied Houthis of Yemen captured a Red Sea island on Friday, giving them a perch to disrupt shipping in another critical waterway for shipping oil out of the Middle East.

“The Houthi success in Yemen has swung the pendulum back in Iran’s favor,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group. Iran, he said, had managed to shift “the status quo without bringing back a return to full-scale war, which the regime likely doesn’t want at this time.”

While Iran backs the Houthis with weapons, cash and logistics, analysts say the Shiite militant group is neither a direct conduit for Iranian interests in Yemen nor fully independent of Tehran’s influence.

The price of oil briefly jumped to about $110 per barrel on Friday, roughly 50 percent above prewar levels. That gives Iran further leverage, as high energy prices pose a political risk for President Trump as his party heads into elections in the fall.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, has become increasingly reliant on the Red Sea, since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz early in the war. But the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships in July, firing on passing vessels in the Red Sea and attacking oil facilities in the kingdom.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia plunged last month to their lowest level in at least 13 years. Compounding its problems, a pipeline that carries oil to the kingdom’s Red Sea ports was temporarily shut down on Friday after a drone attack from inside Iraqi territory, the Saudi energy ministry said.

While it was unclear who was behind the attack, Saudi Arabia has in the past accused Iran-backed militias in Iraq of attacking its energy infrastructure, and Mr. Trump said on Saturday that Iran was “probably” responsible.

Since the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February, the longstanding U. S. security guarantee for its Gulf allies has looked less assured, with those countries coming under missile and drone attacks from Iranian forces.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia urged Mr. Trump to take military action against the Houthis, but the president said he was not willing to do so, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations. Mr. Trump said Saturday that the Houthis had conveyed to his administration that they do not want a fight with the United States.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains far below what it was before the war, though a limited number of ships had been getting through with the help of U. S. naval escorts.

That meant Iran was losing some leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, said Behnam Ben Taleblu, an expert on Iran at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that is hawkish on Iran. “The regime is now clawing it back elsewhere,” he said, with its allies staging attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“Iran’s military strategy is both escalatory and predictable,” Mr. Taleblu said. “It’s all about cross-domain escalation for an increasingly risk-tolerant Tehran.”

Iran has also been stepping up attacks against U. S. warships patrolling the Persian Gulf. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s top national security official, said that Iran had tested what he called its first anti-ship missile against a U. S. ship. The U. S. military responded to Iranian attacks on its warships by destroying several Iranian crude oil carriers.

Iran’s attacks were highly risky, Mr. Taleblu said.

“These high and fast-flying systems can be fired from further inland and, if they strike a U. S. vessel, could cause a significant loss of life,” he said.

Iran’s actions in the region complicated the BRICS summit of emerging economies in New Delhi this weekend, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India urging Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, to safeguard “freedom of navigation and commerce.” India’s own fuel imports are threatened by the ongoing conflict.

Mr. Pezeshkian used his speech at one of the summit’s events to criticize American power.

“Who said it should decide for the entire world, that others have no rights, and that whatever they want everyone else has to obey?” he said. “This is something we will not accept.”

In what could be a potentially powerfully symbolic image of how Tehran’s asymmetric military strategy has resulted in concrete wins, Iran and Oman are set to meet on Monday with other Persian Gulf states to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman said on Friday.

Omani officials did not respond on Friday to a request for comment about the meeting. For weeks, Iranian and Omani officials have been discussing a shared agreement for managing the strait, though Iran has insisted that even such an agreement would not mean that the strait is fully reopen for shipping traffic.

It was still unclear what may come out of the meeting, if it takes place at all. Bahrain, a Gulf country that has been attacked by Iran and hosts a major U. S. military base, said on Saturday that it would not take part. Other Gulf countries do not appear to have immediately commented publicly.

The meeting, if it goes ahead, is “a reflection of the profound disappointment across the Gulf with Washington and with U. S. policy in the region,” Danny Citrinowicz, a retired Israeli intelligence officer who specializes in Iran, said on social media.

They were being forced to choose, Mr. Citrinowicz said, “between an open-ended confrontation with no clear political endgame, one that is destabilizing the region and inflicting enormous economic costs,” and some degree of recognition of Iran’s authority over the strait in hopes of restoring stability.

Iran’s diplomacy with the Gulf countries is “a textbook case of a knife in the back and a handshake in the front,” Mr. Taleblu said. “Tehran spent months attacking these nations directly and indirectly and creating the conditions that led to a major loss of revenue and inability to export oil.”

Now, he said, it is trying to “lock in a more favorable posture of deference to Tehran from elements of the American order in the region.”

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.

A. I. Slopware Is Everywhere Now. Nobody Is Using It.

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Paul Ford

Mr. Ford is a technologist, an essayist and a contributing Opinion writer.

The number of mobile apps available on Apple’s App Store was up 30 percent last year, according to one estimate. But downloads were up only 3 percent.

It isn’t just apps. Software in general — everything made of code — is suddenly available in huge, heaping quantities. Thanks to artificial intelligence, you can now, in plain language, tell a computer to write code, in plain language, and it will often do an excellent job. These capabilities get better nearly every week.

But when was the last time you ended up marveling at a new app or game on your phone? Whither the applications like Slack that take industries by storm, or games like Candy Crush that dominate our subway commutes? Is it just all app slop from here on? Did A. I. kill the “killer app”?

That would be a natural conclusion to draw, but I think that we’re headed for a very different kind of digital revolution. We shouldn’t expect a spate of A. I.-made software to replace all our existing tools. After all, people don’t like to switch to new software unless they must. A. I.’s real strength may be to make many new things that play a more moderate, specific role: reducing sources of small friction that otherwise stack up in our lives.

Most big corporate efforts to use A. I. to increase productivity fail — perhaps as many as 95 percent, according to an M. I. T. study published last year. A boss sits a team down — let’s say it’s a financial services firm, or a consulting firm — and asks them to use A. I. to improve the sales process or track relationships, and after a lot of trial and error, it doesn’t work out. This finding is quite awkward, given the projected multibillion-dollar valuations of A. I. companies, but nothing I’ve learned from talking to dozens of people in the industry disproves it. People are hopeful that a bold A. I.-powered future is right around the corner. They are tantalized. They often use A. I. tools all the time individually. But companies’ internal efforts don’t work.

I don’t blame the coders for this, or even the bosses. I blame the big A. I. companies, who are in such a hurry that they often release new versions of their models and tools without manuals or even clear YouTube tutorials. When projects fail, the implication is that humans just need to stop everything else they’re doing and prompt the models harder.

But that’s a hard trick for an old industry to learn. The tech industry loves to act as if it just sprang out of Zeus’ forehead, but it’s actually a septuagenarian, and surprisingly set in its ways. It will take years before A. I. tools can fully supersede traditional approaches to making software. As dramatic as everyone would like this revolution to be, it’s barely begun.

Venture capital money that drives tech innovation is being poured almost exclusively into A. I. Products that aren’t A. I.-first (such as an old-school game or a task organizer) seem like a risky investment. Why invest in a culture that will soon be gone? If A. I. makes software cheap and abundant, and digital products are easy to clone, then it will be hard to compete. Software used to be the ultimate “moat” — but now it’s starting to look like a commodity. That’s another reason the App Store is now flooded with unimaginative apps instead of thrilling new efforts.

Which gets to something fundamental about A. I. coding, and A. I. in general: It’s very good at reproducing things that look and feel like what came before. It can make a PowerPoint presentation, or even, with time and coaching from a human, a flimsy version of PowerPoint itself. But making something new, something no one has seen before, takes much more time — sometimes just as long as it took before A. I.

Where A. I. excels, I think, is in letting you get access to aspects of computing that were previously out of reach. You can use A. I. to develop complex business models, machine learning systems or advanced software that runs in a web browser. These were all utterly normal things before large language models showed up, but they required specific skills and tended to be the domain of very highly paid software developers. A. I. lets you learn these things as you go, and you’re less likely to give up along the way.

The way I know this is true is that I see a lot of new software that only modestly improves certain things. Librarians are using A. I. to build better, more accessible historical archives; novelists are “writing” subsets of code and contributing to open-source projects; underfunded health care start-ups are whipping together custom tools to help people deal with insurance companies. None of this stuff ends up on the homepage of the biggest tech news outlets, and most of it probably will not make anyone a dime. It’s extremely normal software, not revolutionary or transformative. I think we’re witnessing a cultural throat-clearing — people scribbling in their notebooks, getting ideas out.

For a while, I must admit, it looked as if software developer roles like mine were done for. How could we fight against tireless robots? But our industry is slowly realizing that making truly cutting-edge software still requires humans to think and work together, to maximize their skill sets and to practice their respective crafts. A. I. can write very good software, but it also makes it easy to do someone else’s job badly, which is part of why all those projects fail. Now that everyone can code, it’s become clearer why many shouldn’t.

The reason they shouldn’t is not spiritual but financial: Craft makes money, and A. I. tends to wreck your sense of craft. For months, we’ve seen report after report of companies encouraging all technical employees to use A. I. as much as possible to write more code — “tokenmaxxing”— even if costs skyrocketed. Now managers are hitting the brakes hard. The call to stop burning money? That’s a sense of discipline re-emerging.

Some of the most interesting conversations I’ve had about A. I. are with organizations like food banks and small museums who’ve wanted to build simple custom apps for their patrons and donors, clean up their data or create smarter marketing tools, but never had the money. Often they have real qualms about A. I. and its social costs, and sometimes they decide not to use the technology at all. But many want to deliver good things to their constituents, and that seems more possible now because of A. I.

The future may not be a few huge apps running on a few huge platforms, generating tons of revenue; it could instead be tons of little ones, purpose-built for the church, mutual aid group, company department or softball league. I’d enjoy a future in which the answer to “where’s the great software A. I. was supposed to bring us?” is: “everywhere.”

Paul Ford is a contributing writer in Opinion. He is a founder and the president of Aboard, an A. I.-powered software acceleration platform, and a co-host of “The Aboard Podcast.”

Saudi Arabia’s Oil ‘Lifeline’ Was Attacked. Here’s What to Know.

The New York Times September 12, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

A drone attack from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close its East-West pipeline, the kingdom said, threatening a key workaround to Iran’s Persian Gulf blockade.

By Ismaeel Naar and Aaron Boxerman

Ismaeel Naar reported from Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Aaron Boxerman from Tel Aviv.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest oil producers, on Friday said it had shut down a vital oil pipeline as a precautionary measure following a drone attack from Iraqi territory.

The infrastructure, known as the East-West pipeline, is key to Saudi Arabia’s ability to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz — the Persian Gulf waterway that Iran blockaded after the U. S.-Israeli attack in late February, throttling global oil exports.

The targeting of the East-West pipeline showed that even alternatives to the strait can be disrupted if Iran and its proxies expand their attacks, exposing another vulnerability in efforts to restore the flow of oil to world markets and bring down energy prices.

Here is what you need to know about the pipeline.

Built in the 1980s — when the Iran-Iraq war was similarly squeezing oil exports from the Persian Gulf — the 1,201-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline crosses the Arabian Peninsula to the Saudi port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.

Earlier this summer, Yasir O. Al-Rumayyan, the chairman of Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil company, said engineers had expanded the pipeline’s capacity to carry up to seven million barrels per day, nearly 30 percent more than before the war.

“We had a similar situation back in the ’80s where the Strait of Hormuz was threatened to be blockaded by the Iranian regime,” Mr. Al-Rumayyan said in June. “It was decided since then that we will have a pipeline from east to west and if it wasn’t for this pipeline, we wouldn’t have a lifeline for us as a Saudi economy.”

Still, Saudi Arabia’s oil exports fell last month to 3.2 million barrels a day, the lowest level in at least 13 years, according to data from Kpler, a maritime information company.

The pipeline has allowed Saudi Arabia to mitigate the impact of the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz by keeping oil flowing out through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern entry to the Red Sea.

But that backup route has come under threat as well.

In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized new territory and tried to cut off the Red Sea to Saudi shipping by declaring a blockade and by firing on Saudi vessels. In the past week, the Houthis have taken over more coastal territory near the strait, including the Perim Island in the Red Sea and the port of Mokha, further threatening Saudi vessels carrying oil from the East-West pipeline down the Red Sea to global markets.

Saudi Arabia can also export its oil north out of the Red Sea though a pipeline near the Suez Canal, in Egypt. But that route through the Mediterranean is costlier and adds weeks to the voyage to Asia, where most of the kingdom’s customers are.

Over the past several weeks, a growing number of oil tankers have also been avoiding the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz with U. S. military guidance. The number is still a fraction of those that transited the waterway before the war, though, according to shipping trackers — meaning the pipeline is still important.

No group has officially claimed the drone attack on the East-West pipeline, although on Saturday, President Trump said Iran was “probably” behind the assault. Iran has not commented on the claim.

Saudi officials have said the drone came from Iraq, which has been a hotbed for well-armed militias under Tehran’s sway that the Iraqi government has struggled to bring under control. On Saturday, the office of Iraq’s prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, said he had agreed to conduct a joint investigation with Iran into drone launches along the Iraqi border.

Josh Holder/The New York Times

Analysts have said that a broadening U. S. economic campaign against Iran was likely to lead it to escalate attacks in the region and try to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.

“Saudi Arabia had the workaround, at least partially, through this East-West pipeline,” said Joey Hood, a former senior State Department official. “Iran saw that and said — we’re getting the economic stranglehold around our necks, so we’ve got to do something.”

“Seeing the Iranians doing such bold and outlandish things seems to signal that the economic strangulation is beginning to work,” he added.

The attack on Friday is the first against the pipeline since it was targeted in April. At the time, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said a drone had hit a pumping station and led to the loss of nearly 700,000 barrels per day of pumping capacity. While the pipeline was quickly brought back online, it exposed a fundamental vulnerability for Saudi Arabia’s oil routes as it seeks to bypass the volatility of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Following that attack, and after months of restraint, Saudi Arabia joined the United States in bombing Iran-linked Iraqi militias in July, targeting logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq.

This time, Saudi Arabia has “chosen not to respond at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government” in preventing future attacks from its territory, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.

But Mr. Hood, the former diplomat, said Iran was likely to continue its attacks, which could ultimately force Gulf states like Saudi Arabia to take a more aggressive stance.

“This conflict is continuing to widen,” he said. “The Gulf countries have shown extraordinary restraint, but I don’t think that lasts forever.”

Lisa Friedman contributed reporting.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Researchers say artificial intelligence is developing faster than the systems put in place to monitor and control it.

Credit... Jun Cen

Supported by

By Sheera Frenkel and Dylan Freedman

Sheera Frenkel reported from San Francisco and Dylan Freedman from Washington.

More than a dozen top artificial intelligence researchers warned over the last week that the technology that A. I. companies are building is becoming a risk to humanity. The problem, the researchers said, is that the companies are bad at controlling the systems — as hard as they may try.

Coming on the heels of revelations that so-called A. I. agents from OpenAI escaped their testing system and hacked into the computers of another company, the new alarms from inside the A. I. research world added urgency to yearslong fears that companies are putting development speed and money over safety.

The researchers say the problem is twofold. First, companies need to create better safeguards for the newest A. I. models as they are being tested. Right now, because the A. I. works so fast, researchers need A. I. to monitor it. But that doesn’t always work, because the A. I. monitors can appear to be more sympathetic to other A. I. systems than to the humans setting the rules.

That odd combination of A. I. troublemakers and A. I. guards that look the other way points to a second and more difficult issue known as alignment — an industry term that essentially means making sure that A. I. does what is best for humans. Companies have the difficult task of enshrining within A. I. a set of humanlike values so the models make decisions that align with what should be best for people.

Concerns over A. I. safety are escalating at a critical moment for the A. I. industry. Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward what could be two of the largest initial public offerings in history. At the same time, the American public is growing hostile toward A. I. because of the threat of job losses and the construction of the massive data centers that power the technology.

While there is no evidence that rogue A. I. systems have done lasting damage to anything, the researchers believe the speed of their development is outstripping the ability to monitor them.

Among the researchers speaking out over the last week were OpenAI’s chief scientist; a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and its top rival, Anthropic; and Paul Christiano, an inventor of a key method for building A. I. systems who is a new member of OpenAI’s nonprofit board of directors. He wrote on the company’s blog that the speed at which A. I. capabilities were growing could lead to a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.”

A sizable number of A. I. researchers still believe that talk of A. I.’s threat to humanity is overblown and distracting from more tangible concerns like cybersecurity and misinformation. But most agree that the hack by A. I. agents from OpenAI into another company, called Hugging Face, was a wake-up call.

“It is the capabilities of the future that are really scary,” said Jacob Coxon, whose post on social media announcing his resignation from Anthropic prompted dozens of concerned responses from lawmakers and other A. I. company employees. “It is about our current attitudes to safety and what those same attitudes transplanted on to way smarter models would look like, and that is the really scary bit.”

The hack began in May when OpenAI tested several new A. I. models. The company believed the A. I. models were operating in a closed environment known as a sandbox, or an isolated computer setting with no access to the internet. The A. I.’s agents were given difficult problems to solve, including carrying out cyberattacks.

The A. I. agents broke out of their contained environment and escaped into the internet. The agents — an increasingly popular type of A. I. designed to do tasks on its own — also secretly communicated with one another. Referring to themselves as a collective, the agents began investigating ways to cover their tracks, such as falsifying their own chat logs.

They eventually hacked into Hugging Face, an A. I. infrastructure company. Along the way, A. I. agents convinced other A. I. agents that they were doing the right thing and simply accomplishing the task their testers gave them.

Few — if any — of the issues that led to the hack have been solved. Meta and Anthropic disclosed similar but smaller incidents. And OpenAI has since released Astra, its most powerful model, which is harder to monitor than its predecessor.

“The industry writ large is just not at all in position to prevent the next Hugging Face attack,” said Steven Adler, a former safety lead at OpenAI who co-founded Guidelight AI Standards, a nonprofit that assesses the safety practices of A. I. companies. “When we study the controls that companies have in place, across the board they seem to lack basic preventive measures.”

A. I. researchers said there were a lot of mistakes that led to the Hugging Face incident. It is unclear to what degree the company relied on A. I. models to monitor or police the work of the new models being tested.

But many new A. I. models, including the ones in the hack of Hugging Face, are capable of carrying out complex, multistep tasks faster than a human can follow. The only way to track and monitor what they are doing is to rely on A. I. to police A. I.

The system works, until it doesn’t.

A. I. models can appear to collude with one another, said Alexander Meinke, head of research at the nonprofit Apollo Research, which studies A. I. system safety. A. I. systems can be persuaded by other A. I. models to help them cheat on rules created by their testers and evade detection.

One A. I. agent, for example, could persuade another A. I. agent to help it cover its tracks (that’s what happened in the Hugging Face hack), rather than report back to the human beings at the company that something is wrong.

Mr. Meinke said A. I. models needed to be taught: “I will raise the things that humans would have thought are bad when they look at it.” The A. I., likewise, has to be able to determine when something does not rise to the bar where it needs human intervention, he said.

To establish that, A. I. companies need to slow down, the researchers said. They need even more tests where they can observe how A. I. monitors itself. And they need longer testing periods when companies run multiple scenarios as they watch what the A. I. is doing.

The companies also need to figure out the big questions around alignment, or making sure that A. I. does what is best for humans. When humans make a decision, they tend to refer to societal norms and an internal moral compass that help them weigh their actions. Codifying that in a way that A. I. can mimic is a difficult task, researchers said. Without proper specificity, A. I. systems might learn how to break the rules or go off the rails in unexpected ways.

Nate Soares, president of an A. I. safety nonprofit called the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, co-wrote a 2014 paper introducing the idea of alignment. He said companies didn’t understand how difficult it was to “align” smarter A. I. systems. As A. I. becomes increasingly sophisticated — and without proper alignment — it becomes better able to cover its tracks and deceive people monitoring its transcripts.

“A lot of the industry is like, it’ll be fine because we’ll use the A. I. to get the A. I. s in control. That’s like saying we’re going to use the chimpanzees to get humans in control,” he said. “It’s not a viable long-term plan.”

Researchers have also suggested tactics, like stronger sandboxes, that are completely closed off from the internet while the models are being tested, and a kill switch that would allow companies to immediately take A. I. models offline if they took actions that were concerning.

Mr. Coxon said he had been heartened by the response to his public resignation. On Thursday, Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, the Republican chairman of the Senate’s Homeland Security subcommittee on disaster management, said he was starting an investigation that would “probe the existential risk of new A. I. products.”

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)

Sheera Frenkel is a Times reporter based in the San Francisco Bay Area, covering defense and surveillance technology.

Dylan Freedman is the A. I. projects editor for The Times, investigating a range of topics. He has experience as both a reporter and a machine-learning engineer.

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor Say the End of the World Is Now on the Table

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Trump Administration

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

The current political stakes, as Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor see them, could not be higher. In the view of these two influential leftist thinkers, a driving motivation behind far-right politics at the moment is nothing less than the apocalypse. In their alarming new book, “End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World,” Klein, the author of the best sellers “The Shock Doctrine” and “Doppelganger,” and Taylor, an author and documentarian as well as a founder of the Debt Collective, a debtors’ union, argue that a powerful coalition of religious fundamentalists, ethnonationalists and tech oligarchs (Elon Musk chief among them) is actively — and successfully — hastening the destruction of the world as we know it. Why? Because they believe that they’re primed to thrive on the other side of catastrophe, everyone else be damned. This is a sobering, scary vision of contemporary political battles. But as the still hopeful Klein and Taylor explain, they wrote their book because they believe the conclusion is far from foregone.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

Just to start: What is “end-times fascism?”

Naomi Klein: End-times fascism is a fascism that is very much in conversation with planetary-scale existential crises; a fascism that is taking the end of this world for granted. We thought long and hard about the politics of putting any kind of qualifier on a word like “fascism.” And the reason we ended up deciding that it did need that is we thought about how our world has changed since Mussolini declared himself a fascist. Our fascists have weapons that last century’s fascists couldn’t dream of. There was no atomic bomb. Hitler and Mussolini died before the Trinity test. They didn’t understand that fossil fuels were warming the planet. Our world has become more dangerous, and fascism has changed in response and has made peace with the idea of collapse. And now what they’re fighting for is who is going to survive that cataclysm.

How does end-times fascism make itself felt in the world today?

Klein: The first thing I thought of was the SpaceX I. P. O. I think what resonates is like: Hey, don’t the billionaires have bunkers now? Aren’t they somehow prepping? What is this sort of fixation on leaving the Earth behind? I don’t think the idea of space exploration is inherently fascist, but I think the way it is being formulated by Elon Musk is, because it is just accepting that, as he puts it, he’s saving humanity. What is he saving humanity from exactly? Why do we accept that this world needs escape from?

A term like “fascism” can be foggy, and it’s compounded by the fact that over the last 10 or so years, it has been increasingly used. So can you clarify who the fascists are in your formulation?

Astra Taylor: It’s not a dominant political worldview, even on the right, but it is a term we think applies to some of the most powerful people in the world who are leading governments and companies. In the book, we talk about religious end-timers who want to hasten the return of the Messiah, who believe that they will be saved by the grace of their faith. Those are the evangelical Christian Zionists, who are a very potent political force in the United States; that’s Zionists in Israel. These are real groups of people with real power. Then there are the tech end-timers, who believe that it’s worth incinerating this world as long as they can build their virtual one and that we are inevitably heading toward some sort of digital superintelligence, some singularity. And then the third group are the ethnonationalists, who believe that the nation is under existential threat from immigration, from cultural change, and their response is to fortress the nation, to cast out the domestic enemies. These groups are different. There are contradictions, they’re messy and not totally coherent, but they’re responding to this sense that the world is increasingly fraught and dangerous — which it is — and they’re responding by shutting down and trying to defend their group. And they’ve made this very dangerous alliance.

Help me understand the coalition aspect. If someone were to say, “I don’t quite understand what religious nationalists have to do with Elon Musk” — is there an actual, practical, coordinated effort between these people?

Klein: I would say that effort is embodied by the Trump administration. If you look at this awkward, Frankenstein-like coalition that he has cobbled together and that brought him to power, it contains all of these elements. The massive funding coming from Silicon Valley, and Elon Musk in particular. The fact that he appointed Mike Huckabee, a Christian Zionist, to be his ambassador to Israel, and the way he has understood that Christian Zionists are a key part of his base, and the centrality of advancing Messianic Zionist narratives in Israel. And I mean, think about the tech-billionaire class and that moment in Trump’s second inauguration where some of the wealthiest people in the history of the world are lined up. What exactly is going on? The first time Trump was president, many of these same billionaires were criticizing him. They were upset when he left the Paris climate accord. Zuckerberg was condemning him. Bezos was launching an Earth prize. They were positioning themselves as the people who were going to save the planet. One of the things we’re arguing is, as the world changes, our elites are changing, are becoming more fascist, are attracted to ideas that justify the idea that only some people are going to make it. That is not the same story they were telling even five years ago. We need to pay attention to the way the story is changing as our world changes.

But one could say the tech elites are responding to incentives to cozy up to Trump. That it’s better for their businesses. So can you unpack the “fascism” element?

Klein: I don’t think it’s as simple as saying that they’re lining up behind Trump because it’s good for them. They could have done that last time. Very few of them did. They helped him get elected [in 2024]. Certainly Elon Musk and the huge amounts of money that he spent — but not only him. Several people played key roles, including Marc Andreessen; JD Vance was a creature of Silicon Valley, worked with Peter Thiel. But there was a turning point during the campaign when a lot of people who had not supported Trump, who identified as lifelong Democrats, got behind him. We make the case that a lot of it had to do with A. I. and how ravenous A. I. is when it comes to energy. They understood that Trump, as a guy who loves the fossil-fuel industry, would open the floodgates for this A. I. arms race. So that’s an economic incentive. But I would also argue that the business model that they have embraced is a business model that is uniquely antithetical to a shared human existence. They understand the climate crisis and they understand that what we feed A. I. is energy. It’s overwhelmingly being fed with L. N. G. [liquefied natural gas] and coal, and because they understand the climate crisis, they understand that that is going to do exactly what we’re seeing right now: set whole cities on fire, create situations where huge parts of the world are unlivable. So the increasingly brutal views that we’re hearing from people like Elon Musk, where you just seem to be discounting huge swaths of humanity or actively playing a role and destroying USAID at the cost of — I mean, he would say no lives, but perhaps because he doesn’t count African lives. These things go together. You need a story that discounts those lives. That is a fascist story. That is the story that has ideas about whose lives count and whose lives can be discarded. And I think it’s quite active. It’s not just like, Oh, we’re going where the money is. The money is making them fascist.

Taylor: It’s important to note that far-right ideology has a long history in Silicon Valley. It didn’t start at the second inauguration. A figure like Peter Thiel has been cultivating that worldview alongside David Sacks by investing in promoting a certain philosophical paradigm. In 2009, he wrote an article that is pretty famous for good reason, that basically says democracy and freedom are incompatible, staking his claim that if he has to choose between democracy and capitalism, he’d choose the latter. We talk in the book about a conference that Thiel’s venture capital firm hosted just before the election in 2024 that was called Hereticon, “a conference for thought crime.” And the tagline was: “Maybe if you aren’t trying to destroy the world, you aren’t trying hard enough.” We’ve been wrestling with how to talk about what they say because some of it is so nuts that you sound a little kooky quoting them. Elon Musk saying it increasingly looks like “humanity is a biological bootloader for digital superintelligence,” or that we should rejoice in the fact that they’re building the digital beings who will come after humanity.

Klein: Or Sam Altman saying that A. I. takes less energy to train than a human.

Taylor: Or that the world will be covered in data centers.

But how do you disentangle trolling from actual ideological views?

Taylor: My view is they want to be our overlords and our edge lords. And I think we’ve seen that we do have to take some of the trolling seriously. You can be a joke and be really dangerous at the same time.

Klein: The last book I wrote was about a group of people who were dismissed as conspiracy nuts and who shouldn’t be taken too seriously. And then less than a year and a half later, they are running the U. S. government. So I think that there is an impulse when you see lots of really extreme things to be like, Cooler heads will prevail. But then you look at the U. S. secretary of war and what he’s been doing, or who is running Health and Human Services and the effects that it’s already having on communicable diseases and food-borne illnesses. The reason not to be alarmist about alarming rhetoric is that you want people to take it seriously when there is a serious threat. There are enough alarm bells going off right now that I don’t think it’s a good time to self-soothe with ideas that maybe that’s just something they’re saying to get a provocation. The prototype of this is Elon Musk. When he was head of DOGE with his chain saw, he really did slash entire programs that millions of people rely on for health care and nutritional support.

I want to ask an Elon Musk question. He is a defining character of our age, for better or worse. I think, for people who like him, there’s a real grandeur to the idea of SpaceX rockets and colonizing outer space. Or I was talking through the ideas in your book with some folks, and someone said to me, Elon Musk is out there saying more people should have more babies because of population decline. So how does that fit with hastening cataclysm? Does any of that, for you, complicate the idea of what Elon Musk believes in and how he acts? To me it looks incoherent more than anything else.

Klein: I don’t want to do too much work to try to make him coherent. But I do think he has a vision of the future. I think he’s obsessed with the vision of the future that he grew up with in pulpy science fiction and comic books and wants that future. He feels it was promised. We were promised flying cars. Where are my flying cars?

Which Peter Thiel famously said.

Klein: So the idea that he has a vision of a future does not mean he’s not a fascist. I think that he has a vision of a future for a subset of humanity who get to enjoy the implants and upgrades and flying cars and rocket ships. He believes in a kind of V. I. P. bespoke future that is based on this hierarchy of humanity that allows him, on the one hand, to say that people in the so-called West should have more babies, but slash programs that are providing food and medicine to children in Somalia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Those things are happening at the same time.

Taylor: I think what you’re getting at is that there’s something that appeals to people about the idea that we could be interplanetary. We share that. We share the idea that people need something mythic and something to look forward to. We just think it should be something to look forward to here on Earth, and it should be inclusive and sustainable.

Klein: Because you don’t hear him talk about the great future we could have here. There are very few people in politics today, or in the corporate world, who are talking about a vision that feels credible for how we could live together. So we believe it’s the job of a credible left to put forward a vision of the future for how we live together well on this planet — where we aren’t engaged in some project of triaging who gets to live and who gets to die, where we actually figure out how to share our resources and thrive. We want to believe in the future. We have a right to believe in the future. And there’s something treasonous about not believing in the future.

Do you have any concern that using language like “end times” or “fascism” makes it easier for people to perhaps dismiss your arguments?

Klein: This book is a warning, and it’s not about a bunch of fringe characters. We are quoting, in their own words, the wealthiest people in the history of the world, the president of the United States, the prime minister of Israel. We have watched as people with previously quite marginal belief systems have moved to the center of power and gained very powerful roles in government. I mean, you say “end times” is an extreme term. Half of Christians in America believe we’re in the end of times. It might seem like a marginal belief system where you’re sitting, but these are not marginal ideas.

That’s a funky statistic, though. It’s very dependent on how a given Christian interprets “end times.” A Catholic might believe that we’ve been in the end times since Jesus ascended. So half of Christians believing in end times is not necessarily the same as meaning they want to ——

Klein: Accelerate it, yeah. But I just don’t think that these are marginal ideas. These are some of the most powerful stories in our culture. They’re incredibly deeply encoded. Whether we’re religious or not, they’re in us, and there’s a kind of drive to repeat them because the stories are so powerful. So we need mythic stories of our own. It can’t just be, We need universal health care, and we need affordable lives. We also need myth. We need to recover a sense of wonder and awe at this world. That’s why it’s worth looking at it. There’s things that we can learn from what is resonating.

Why does it seem like the left has not been able to harness apocalyptic energy in the way the right has?

Taylor: I think building multiracial democracy is harder than building fascism or authoritarianism. Because we don’t want to just grab the levers of power. You want to share power, and you have to figure out how to live together. So I think our project is just inherently more difficult.

Klein: In answer to your question, as somebody who’s been on the left for a long time, we’ve gotten closer than at any other point. For those of us who were part of the Bernie Sanders campaign — I was living in the U. S. at the time and was part of that campaign as a surrogate for his Green New Deal program, which I felt was the kind of response that both addressed emissions and people’s economic needs. But in politics you don’t get a prize for second place. I do think that this wave that Mamdani has helped lead, and this wave of D. S. A. candidates who are winning in the primaries, speaks to the fact that the left is a lot more serious about fighting fascism; the willingness to call it fascism, to call it genocide, to use the words that describe reality are actually far better at fighting fascism than a supposedly safe centrism that is collapsing around the world.

Where do you see opportunities on the right for pushback against end-times fascists?

Klein: The most awkward alliance is around the big tech companies and the MAGA base. They don’t like the idea of being tracked by their phones, so there are definitely opportunities there. We are seeing it in these local meetings, which is really interesting to me, having done this research around the anti-vaccine, anti-masking, anti-Covid health-measures movement during Covid, which then rolls into a movement for book banning and anti-trans rights. Those were the issues that were making people storm city hall and go to a town hall meeting. Today the thing that is bringing people into their town hall meetings is opposition to the data center down the road.

Taylor: We talk about data centers being icons of this futurelessness. There used to be a kind of bargain: You’d get a factory in the town and that meant there was some pollution and maybe some tax abatements, but there were also jobs that supported your family, even if the wages weren’t the best. And going to Memphis, for example, where Elon Musk now has three supercomputers, and meeting the people there who are fighting against this development because Musk is powering them with gas turbines. Some of them are as big as 30 football fields. And there are basically no jobs. What is the offer?

Are there signs, little flares on the horizon, that would give you clues that the influence of end-times fascists is receding?

Taylor: Minneapolis is a great example. I think that the Trump administration went into that assault thinking that it would be greeted gleefully, at least by its base, and that people would thrill at the video being circulated, celebrating the violence, and actually they overreached. They shot people in the street, and even some of their base were appalled by that. So I think we’re seeing signs that they’re definitely not infallible. Ultimately what we would like to see is some of these people being held accountable. And this goes to the attacks on the I. C. C. [International Criminal Court] and this constant assertion, “Well, we have immunity,” right?

Klein: That’s why it matters when Mamdani says that Netanyahu belongs in The Hague and he should be arrested. For too long we have not put forward our own vision for accountability, a serious one, using these institutions. What would it mean to really hold war criminals accountable and have it apply across the board, not only to people in Africa who commit crimes, or the Philippines, but also the United States and Israel? It would be the beginning of addressing such deep disillusionment, because we are up against a very widespread feeling that there’s nothing you can do. Doing a few things starts to break that spell.

What you just said — could American politicians be held accountable by the I. C. C.? — my first thought is, That’ll never happen. I’m not saying it should or shouldn’t happen. It just seems unlikely.

Taylor: Sometimes things that seem improbable happen because people organize to make them so.

Klein: We didn’t write the book because we think these people are fascinating. We wrote this book because we want people to fight them and beat them. We use this word that neither Astra nor I have ever used before because we’re not nationalist people: We call them “traitors.” Not traitors to a nation, not traitors to a flag or a border, but traitors to creation, traitors to life. And we spent a lot of time looking at where this project is weak. Where it’s strong is money, weapons. We’re dealing with trillionaires; that wealth has merged with the most powerful military in the world. I’m not nostalgic for the last century’s fascists, let’s be clear about that, but they had an offer to their base. They’re like, Let us steal the homes of the Jews and the Slavs and live happily ever after in your Lebensraum Ukraine. The people we’re calling end-times fascists don’t have an offer to their base beyond sadism.

One of the through lines of your book is that end-times fascists are not seeing the beauty of the world and the things that truly make life worthwhile. What are the things that you think, Oh, if only they could see what I see.

Taylor: A big one, and it’s a classic fascist trope, is the fear of the city, the fear of encountering people from different walks of life. We write about how powerful the Mamdani campaign was in re-enchanting the city — not romanticizing it, not saying it’s perfect. Yes, the subways have problems. But also, Wow, you get to ride a subway and who knows what will happen, and it will take you to some amazing place where you can eat something you can’t make at home. Just encountering and not fearing diversity but reveling in it. And absolutely the more-than-human world. Naomi lives somewhere with really good nature, so I feel like she has to take that one.

Klein: Oh, my god, where to start? I live in British Columbia. Honestly I feel the most sadness and rage at a willingness to let it all burn, or to try to escape when I see a dorsal fin of an orca slice through the waters of the Salish Sea, where I’m fortunate enough to live. Or just any of the psychedelia of this part of the natural world: On the very, very dark nights, the water is completely bioluminescent, and you look at your own limbs and they’re made of pure light — no mushrooms required! It is a tragedy for them, and an existential crisis for us, that the people who are closest to the levers of power on this planet are not enraptured by the beauty that is already here and all around us.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Tre Cassetta

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

High Prices Spoil Trump’s New Push to Save G. O. P. Majority

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Gas prices are high, mortgage rates are climbing and inflation remains well above target, complicating the president’s midterm appeal.

By Tony Romm

Reporting from Washington

With less than two months until the midterm elections, President Trump commenced a final push this week to preserve his Republican majority in Congress, arguing that the United States under G. O. P. control had brought prices “way, way down.”

But for many families and businesses, the economy appeared to be on far shakier footing by Friday. Fuel prices soared, mortgage costs climbed and inflation registered uncomfortably high, testing the public’s patience with Mr. Trump’s frequent assurances that the country is on the right track.

The contrast underscored the political and economic stakes for Mr. Trump, who may soon face the wrath of an electorate long spurned by promises in Washington to lower the cost of living. As November draws closer, prices have risen under the president’s leadership, driven largely by an agenda that has included two years of punishing trade brinkmanship and a prolonged war with Iran.

The consequences were evident in the latest gauge of the Consumer Price Index, released on Friday. The report showed that prices rose at an annual pace of 3.4 percent in August, which increased the odds of the Federal Reserve’s raising interest rates next week.

The data came on the same day that a separate, long-running survey from the University of Michigan found that consumer sentiment dropped sharply this month. In that report, Americans expressed new worries that the economy was sputtering, and that inflation would continue to rise.

The unease set the stage for Mr. Trump’s renewed push this week to make the case to voters that he has helped, not hurt, the economy. Over two days of speeches at his party’s midterm convention in Dallas, the president labored to convince Americans that Republicans had achieved “tremendous economic success.”

But Mr. Trump did not limit himself to a brash defense of his record. The president also said he would send a $5,000 check to American citizens if Republicans retained the House and Senate in November, though he has failed to deliver on similar promises in the past.

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us,” Mr. Trump said, soon after adding: “Congratulations. Now all we have to do is win.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

For Mr. Trump, the fight with inflation has proved so pernicious that it has overshadowed even the few bright spots in the economy. Despite nearly two years of policy tumult, the labor market has remained strong, the economy is growing and the country is witnessing a boom around artificial intelligence, one that has generally delighted financial markets.

But those positives have not always been obvious or tangible to voters, who have suffered through years of compounding costs that peaked during the coronavirus pandemic. Those financial strains continued into August, when prices rose faster than hourly wages on a year-over-year basis for the fifth straight month.

“The economy is performing well, but this isn’t buoying consumer attitudes,” Oren Klachkin, the financial market economist for Nationwide, wrote in an analysis of the new inflation data on Friday. “Rather, they’re squarely focused on rising prices and interest rates eating into purchasing power.”

In an interview, Mr. Klachkin added that he did not see inflation “coming down at a meaningful pace any time soon.” He cited a range of risks, including uncertainty around the tariffs in Mr. Trump’s trade war and the war with Iran.

Both of those conflicts worsened this week, a period that was not captured in the latest inflation report. But Americans still felt the consequences. The return to hostilities in Iran, for example, sent the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, to $110 per barrel briefly on Friday.

It was the first time since July that oil prices had reached those levels, and in the United States, it coincided with a continued surge in gas prices. Nationally, gas averaged nearly $4.30 per gallon by Friday, according to AAA — well over a dollar more than a year ago. Still worse was the cost of diesel, which topped $6 per gallon, setting a record that could deeply affect shipping and transportation.

The increase prompted Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, to acknowledge that soaring diesel costs in particular represented a “big, big issue” for the economy. In a Friday appearance on Fox Business, he pointed to geopolitical uncertainty — including in the Middle East — as the root cause.

But there was no sign this week that the war with Iran was close to finished. Even Mr. Trump acknowledged at one point that high oil and gas prices could persist until “right after the election,” though he predicted costs would fall quickly, contrary to warnings from economists.

“They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down. I think for gasoline, we’ll get them below $2 a gallon,” the president told reporters, adding: “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”

The renewed energy shock created more headaches for the Fed and its new chairman, Kevin M. Warsh. As the Fed eyes a rate increase to bring inflation into check, Mr. Trump has redoubled his demands for significant rate cuts. Absent a steep reduction, the president even threatened last week that he could cut off all trade with countries that sell more to the United States than they buy. Rates are now in a range of 3.25 to 3.75 percent.

On Wall Street, the economic headwinds also helped to push up the cost of the government’s own borrowing all week. That came in the form of higher yields, which topped 4.9 percent on 10-year bonds, the highest level seen since 2023.

The rise carried significant implications, particularly for homeowners, since mortgage rates closely track yields on those bonds. The average rate on a 30-year loan reached around 6.8 percent last week, according to Michael Fratantoni, the chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, a 15-month high.

At the start of the year, Mr. Trump had promised an aggressive plan to lower housing costs. Since then, a confluence of factors has sent mortgage rates skyrocketing, and led Mr. Fratantoni to predict on Friday that it could reach “at or above 7 percent” soon.

So, too, did high yields raise the costs for Washington to service its own debts, which recently surpassed $40 trillion under Mr. Trump. But an attempt by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to buy up old bonds this week failed to push down yields, as markets shrugged off the intervention.

Brett Loper, the executive vice president for policy at the Peter G. Peterson Foundation, which supports deficit reduction, attributed the poor reception to the many “tectonic forces at play,” including the fast-growing U. S. debt.

Add to that Mr. Trump’s new sales pitch to voters, promising $5,000 to Americans if Republicans prevail in the midterms — a plan that Mr. Loper estimated could cost $1.2 trillion.

That price tag, on top of existing fiscal woes, would probably “lead to greater inflation and higher interest rates,” he said.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Republicans, Facing Midterm Peril, Try to Brand Democrats as Communists

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Communism, in the president’s hyperbolic telling, is a graver threat to the country than the Pearl Harbor or 9/11 attacks were. Whether this midterm strategy works is an open question.

By Tim Balk

One by one, Republican speakers at President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas this week turned to a far-fetched argument with echoes of the Cold War.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana claimed, “Next year the communists will be in Congress — that’s what’s so frightening.” Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 House Republican, said implausibly that there had been a “Bolshevik Revolution in the Democrat Party.”

And when Mr. Trump, the ringleader of this new Red Scare, took the stage, he returned — again and again and again — to baseless claims that Democrats were running as communists in the midterms.

“It’s going to be a communist country if they win,” he predicted, one of at least 60 times a speaker at the convention mentioned communism or communists.

Although this year’s Democratic primary season brought a surge of left-wing momentum, and a handful of victories by democratic socialists running for Congress in Colorado, Michigan, New York, Pennsylvania and Florida, no credible midterm candidate identifies as a communist. And there is little momentum behind any communist movement in U. S. politics at the federal level.

Still, for months now, Mr. Trump and Republicans, staring down a daunting political environment and the potential loss of one or both houses of Congress, have been trying to cast Democrats as communists, deploying a charge that has little overlap with Democrats’ actual platforms.

Republicans have been grasping for a potent attack line as they confront widespread voter discontent with the president’s war with Iran as well as high gasoline and grocery prices. They believe the left-wing congressional nominees have offered an opening to build an argument that Democrats are outside the mainstream.

“Stalin. Mao. Castro. Democrats,” the Republican National Committee wrote on social media last month. “Different leaders, same goal.”

Whether the attacks make a difference in the midterms is still far from clear. Some Democrats have expressed worry that the rise of democratic socialism in their party could play into Republican efforts to cast them as extremists and that constant mentions of communism could blur the lines for some voters. At the same time, Mr. Trump’s overheated language could weaken the force of the argument.

Mr. Trump and Republicans have pointed to a series of victories by democratic socialists in Democratic primary races — including a suite of June results in deep-blue New York and a stunning Senate upset last month in conservative-leaning Florida — to accuse their opponents of harboring radical beliefs.

Perhaps not since the 1950s or ’60s has an American political party spent so much time talking about communism. In Mr. Trump’s telling, communism poses the gravest danger to the country. It is more severe, he says, than World War I, the Japanese raid on Pearl Harbor in 1941 or the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001.

Communists, he said in a bizarre aside at a July rally in Georgia, even want to destroy an American landmark.

“They tried taking Mount Rushmore down — they want to blow it up,” he claimed, without elaborating.

In some ways, far-left leaders have fed the argument. In 2020, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a leader of the progressive movement and a self-described democratic socialist, praised elements of the Communist Cuban revolution. And Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist who unseated a Democratic congressman in a New York primary in June, once maintained a social-media account that circulated a post suggesting that public libraries should carry more Marxist literature.

Two days after Ms. Avila Chevalier and two other self-described democratic socialists swept House primaries in New York, a group of centrist House Democrats signed a letter declaring, “We are capitalist, not socialist.”

Representative Don Davis, a centrist Democrat running for re-election in a battleground district in North Carolina, said in an interview that he had signed the letter because voters across his district had been expressing anxiety about communism.

“I have heard it from the northernmost portions of the district to the central all the way to the southernmost portions of eastern North Carolina,” he said. “Without any doubt, yes, there are genuine concerns.”

By the time the left-wing wave crashed into Florida last month, with the victory of the democratic socialist Angie Nixon in the Democratic primary for Senate, more lawmakers and the veteran Democratic strategist James Carville had agreed to sign the letter, too.

Most Americans have unfavorable views of socialism, according to polls. Communism polls much worse. And even as Mr. Trump mislabels Democrats as communists, some Democrats have jokingly blurred the lines themselves, referring to the area of New York City where one democratic socialist House candidate won as the “Commie Corridor.”

Jon Fleischman, a former executive director of the California Republican Party, said that “your options are limited when the president’s ratings on a lot of key issues, most notably the economy, are underwater.” But he added that describing Democrats as communists was “smart” strategically and would “freak out people.”

Hillary Clinton told Kara Swisher on the “Pivot” podcast that Republican messaging accusing Democrats of being communists would be “very effective” politically. She said Republicans had most likely tested it before making it their central attack.

“People on the left have to be prepared to answer that,” Mrs. Clinton said.

The deployment of over-the-top warnings about communism has become a staple of Mr. Trump’s speeches.

“These are not mere political disagreements like differences over taxes or regulations,” Mr. Trump said in a dark speech at Mount Rushmore the weekend of July 4, referring to communism more than a dozen times. “Communism is a mortal threat to American liberty. It is the greatest threat to our country, including World I, World War II, Pearl Harbor or even 9/11.”

Republicans have enhanced their standing with Hispanic voters in Florida by linking left-wing American leaders with authoritarian communist governments in Latin America, said former Representative Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican. But Mr. Curbelo was skeptical that the president’s claims of communism would be as potent with other voters.

Representative Don Bacon, a Republican from a swing Nebraska district who is retiring, said democratic socialists were a “good group to run against.” But he questioned the president’s approach of labeling them as communists.

“When you throw out the labels, people don’t know if it’s true or not,” Mr. Bacon said. Mr. Trump might be better off highlighting left-wing Democrats’ policy positions or inflammatory past statements, the congressman added: “I would quote these guys.”

Some Democrats say Republicans are embracing a straw-man argument.

Brad Lander, a self-described democratic socialist from Brooklyn who beat a Democratic congressman in a primary in June, said democratic socialists had “in many cases” been the “fiercest opponents of communists.”

“Democratic socialists want an extension of democracy into more parts of working people’s lives,” he said.

Even as Mr. Trump rages against the far left and seeks to tie it to communist governments, his administration has moved to expand the bounds of executive power — drawing accusations from Democrats that the president has more in common with autocratic communist leaders than they do.

The Trump administration has also been unusually aggressive in acquiring ownership shares of private companies, securing stakes in dozens of companies and reaching a deal that gave the government extraordinary influence over U. S. Steel.

And after Mr. Trump this week floated sending $5,000 to every adult American — but only if Republicans keep their congressional majorities in the midterms — some fiscal hawks in his party criticized what they said was a socialist-style gimmick.

Mr. Trump’s decision to speak so frequently and forcefully about communism is a throwback to the Cold War, said Barbara A. Perry, a presidential scholar at the University of Virginia. No president since George H. W. Bush has focused on communism in any meaningful way, she said.

Mr. Trump was a child during the so-called Red Scare, a period of political paranoia in the 1950s. In that era, Senator Joseph McCarthy, a Wisconsin Republican, led a series of investigations into supposed communist influence in the U. S. government.

Mr. Trump rose to prominence as a real estate developer in the 1970s and 1980s, when tension between the United States and the communist Soviet Union was high.

The president’s renewed focus on communism is in line with his long-running focus on the 1980s. Roy M. Cohn, Mr. Trump’s mentor and lawyer during that period, had decades earlier been chief counsel to McCarthy’s Senate investigations into communism. Those investigations became infamous for their overreaches.

Mr. Trump’s claims of an internal communism threat, rather than an external one, are particularly reminiscent of the Red Scare of the 1950s, Ms. Perry said.

Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, said Mr. Trump wasn’t qualified to lecture Democrats about communism, pointing to the president’s tendency to embrace President Xi Jinping of China, who leads his country’s Communist Party, and Kim Jong-un, the authoritarian leader of North Korea.

Mr. Trump has celebrated his “good relationship” with Mr. Kim, saying that they “fell in love” during his first term and that the North Korean leader had sent him “beautiful” letters.

Mr. Trump has said he plans to meet again with Mr. Kim by the end of the year.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

India Wants to Buy Fewer Chinese Imports, but Keeps Needing More

The New York Times September 12, 2026

Global Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Trade between India and China has nearly doubled in five years, leaving New Delhi with a widening deficit and a difficult choice over how to build its industrial future.

By Alex Travelli

Reporting from New Delhi

To understand India’s trade imbalance with China, look inside Indian factories.

Many of the big machines are Chinese, as are the electronic components and materials feeding them. An electric vehicle plant needs rare-earth magnets from China, while Indian drugmakers rely on Chinese pharmaceutical ingredients.

India has spent years trying to become less dependent on its giant neighbor. Instead, it has been buying more.

The total volume of goods exchanged between the two countries has nearly doubled over the past five years, to $151 billion a year. But the trade has become more unbalanced than ever. India now buys roughly seven times as much from China as it sells there.

That surge came even as relations between India and China went into a deep freeze. A bloody hand-to-hand skirmish at the Himalayan border in 2020 killed at least 24 soldiers and brought a run of high-level diplomacy to an abrupt halt. On Saturday, Xi Jinping, China’s top leader, will set foot in India for the first time in more than six years.

For India, the imbalance creates a difficult problem. Its industrial ambitions depend heavily on Chinese goods, even as that dependence exposes India to strategic risks and makes it harder for its companies to gain the scale needed to compete with Chinese rivals. Now, with the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran driving up energy costs, Chinese imports are widening India’s global trade deficit and weakening its currency.

India is not alone in struggling with a flood of low-cost Chinese goods. China’s record trade surplus reached nearly $1.2 trillion last year, deepening concerns among trading partners over the growing dominance of Chinese companies across industries.

Those tensions spilled into the open this month at a gathering of economic officials from the Group of 20 nations. The U. S. Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, accused China of blocking a joint statement criticizing countries “with excessive and persistent external surpluses.”

As India hosts China at the BRICS summit this weekend, analysts expect trade to loom large as a source of tension, alongside the two countries’ disputed border.

Both sides seem to prefer quiet along the border for now. The harder problem may be their economic relationship.

For India, keeping Chinese goods out is not an option.

“We will need to engage with them,” said Shekhar Aiyar, director of the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations. India should “aggressively invite Chinese firms in — especially in critical sectors like green technology, semiconductors, manufacturing, where China is the world leader,” Mr. Aiyar said. In batteries and solar power alone, he estimated, China has a 30 percent cost advantage over any other exporter.

After the 2020 border clash, India took an aggressive posture toward China. In retaliation, it banned TikTok and dozens of other consumer-facing Chinese apps and restricted Chinese companies’ ability to invest in Indian start-ups.

At the time, multinational companies were looking to move some supply chains out of China, and India appeared well positioned to benefit. For a brief moment, India looked capable of challenging China’s status as the “factory to the world.”

That did not happen. Vietnam and other Southeast Asian countries captured much of the investment, while China remained at the center of most supply chains.

Santosh Pai, a lawyer in New Delhi who advises Chinese and Indian companies, said Vietnam had secured large-scale investments as a manufacturing alternative to China — even though it, like India, imports heavily from China for essential equipment and materials. Vietnam’s supply chain, he said, is more integrated with China and the country courts Chinese investment more aggressively.

Mr. Pai said India’s efforts to reduce its economic dependence on China had produced mixed results. Even imports ostensibly coming from elsewhere are often Chinese goods processed or repackaged in Southeast Asia.

“The trade measures are well intentioned, but they don’t all work the way we want,” he said. “There is a lot of excess supply in China and a lot of excess demand in India.”

That leaves room for dealmaking. India wants to have access to Chinese money and technology. China wants India’s potentially enormous market.

But neither is willing to end up on the losing side of that exchange. Chinese companies do not want to miss the chance to build their brands in fast-growing India, even if its average consumer still has relatively little to spend. India, meanwhile, wants to protect its companies from far more efficient competitors.

The tension is sharpest in high-value, high-tech manufacturing. India wants Chinese investments, but investment that helps build an Indian industrial base. Apple’s iPhone manufacturing, about a quarter of which has shifted to India, is a prime example.

China has an obvious interest in keeping its position as the world’s indispensable manufacturer, even if individual Chinese companies want to take advantage of India’s young work force and government subsidies. Some of its restrictions on trade with India appear intended to preserve that advantage.

The struggle extends even to the movement of people.

For much of the five years after the 2020 clash, travel was constrained by tit-for-tat restrictions, beginning with India’s blocking Chinese business and tourist visas and China’s responding in kind, with Covid-19 restrictions further complicating travel.

India began issuing visas more freely last year. But China has tightened its exit rules, preventing some Chinese citizens from traveling to places like India if it deems them a threat to national industrial or technological security.

Visas are among the practical disputes that Mr. Xi and India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, could address at the summit, Mr. Pai said. “India will want some reassurances, both for business visas to China and engineers from China,” he said.

India has leverage, too. By working with companies like Taiwan’s Foxconn, one of Apple’s main contract manufacturers, it can gradually erode pieces of China’s industrial dominance. It can also restrict access to its domestic market of 1.4 billion people, a prize that will become more valuable as the average incomes in India rise.

But China has shown a willingness to use its dominance in strategic sectors as leverage. Rare-earth magnets, needed for electric cars and many other high-growth industries, are just one example. China has also gained enormous power over the production of many pharmaceutical ingredients, making India’s world-leading drug companies dependent on Chinese supplies.

Somnath Mukherjee, chief investment officer at ASK Wealth Advisors in Mumbai, worries about India’s global trade deficit.

It is “simple arithmetic,” he said, that the Indian rupee will remain under pressure as long as India buys more than it sells. The central bank can manage that, he said, even though higher oil prices and a flight to artificial intelligence stocks in the United States have made the task trickier.

“It is a fact that many countries, China and now the U. S. as well, have started weaponizing trade,” Mr. Mukherjee said. “China’s weaponized product access has become a source of massive concern.”

Keith Bradsher and Hari Kumar contributed reporting.

Alex Travelli is a correspondent based in New Delhi, writing about business and economic developments in India and the rest of South Asia.
